div.p: 2015 SWAP. These documents have been successfully guiding nongame and native fish conservation in Montana for 20 years, and they provided the foundation from which we built the 2025 SWAP. The development of Montana's 2025 SWAP involved contributions from numerous individuals across agencies and organizations, and we are deeply thankful to all of you for the time and expertise you devoted to helping create this plan. We thank the SWAP Steering Committee, whose leadership supported the revision through monthly meetings where key decisions were made that influenced the structure and function of this document. The SWAP Steering Committee also played a crucial role in setting a tone of importance for the SWAP, elevating its relevancy among agency personnel, lawmakers, and other Montanans. We greatly appreciate the work of the technical teams, who tapped into decades worth of experience with Montana's wildlife and their habitats and pored over an incredible amount of information to develop recommendations for Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) and the threats and conservation actions that affect them. The list on the following pages outlines those who served on the SWAP Steering Committee or SWAP technical teams at any time during the revision process. Finally, we are grateful to the external partners and subject matter experts who devoted their time and energy to offering input and critique of the 2025 SWAP (Appendix C). The dedication of Montanans from all corners of the conservation world was truly humbling, and we look forward to taking the connections we made during the development of the SWAP and turning them into meaningful actions on the ground in support of our state's natural heritage.

div.head: MONTANA FISH, WILDLIFE & PARKS MISSION
div.p: Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, through its employees and citizen commission and board, provides for the stewardship of the fish, wildlife, parks, and recreational resources of Montana, while contributing to the quality of life for present and future generations (FWP 2016).

div.head: MONTANA FISH, WILDLIFE & PARKS VISION
div.p: Montana is a place where people have abundant opportunities to connect with the worldrenowned fish, wildlife, and state parks resources that define our state, and where a responsive and relevant FWP has the resiliency and public support it needs to lead the way in making sure these resources remain an essential part of Montana's culture, economy, and high quality of life (FWP 2016). div.head: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
div.p: The 2025 Montana State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is the third generation of the SWAP, and the most comprehensive and collaborative fish and wildlife planning process ever completed for the state. The first SWAP was completed in 2005 (FWP 2005), reviewed and revised in 2015 (FWP 2015), and this version is the 2025 revision. For 20 years, Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks (FWP) and its partners have used the SWAP to guide conservation work in Montana, drawing upon the plan to prioritize projects, apply for funding, and implement actions that address specific threats to wildlife, fish, and their habitats. The 2025 SWAP continues with those efforts but with a stronger focus on the entire breadth of organisms that keep Montana's ecosystems functional, including invertebrates and plants.
Additionally, the 2025 SWAP puts a heavier focus on identifying threats to species and habitats and associated conservation actions to address those threats.

FWP is responsible for leading the development of the SWAP, but the 2025 revision was a collaborative effort, involving 95 individuals and staff from 15 organizations, as well as hundreds of partners that provided guidance and feedback. The 2025 SWAP uses the best available science to provide a roadmap for conserving at-risk species and habitats in Montana. It is intended to guide conservation work for FWP, but also foster collaborations with and among partners to collectively implement conservation measures for Montana's at-risk species and habitats.

Montana's 2025 SWAP identifies 52 Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN). Terrestrial HGCN were identified by selecting categories from the U.S. National Vegetation Classification and aquatic HGCN were identified by selecting categories from the Montana Natural Heritage Program's (MTNHP)'s aquatic community classification system. These selected HGCN represent habitats in the state that support the largest number and diversity of at-risk species and face significant threats that can be addressed by FWP and its partners.

Montana's 2025 SWAP identifies 375 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and 98 Species of Greatest Information Need (SGIN). SGCN and SGIN were identified using NatureServe's methodology for tracking and assessing the conservation status of species in the state. In addition to vertebrates previously included in the SWAP, Montana included invertebrates and plants for the first time in the 2025 SWAP. Aquatic and terrestrial invertebrate SGCN and SGIN were identified by teams of experts from 12 agencies and organizations across the state. Plant SGCN were adopted from the Montana Native Plant Conservation Strategy (Pipp et al. 2024), which was developed in a separate collaborative process that was led by the MTNHP.

Through SWAP technical teams and input from external partners, we developed the most comprehensive list of threats and conservation actions for SGCN and HGCN ever compiled for Montana. Thousands of threats and conservation actions were identified at the species level and for the habitats on which species rely. We first identified and focused on habitatrelated threats and actions, recognizing that actions at the habitat level will almost always help address threats to many SGCN. Next, we included threats and actions for SGCN that were specific to a particular species and were not covered by those developed for HGCN.

Montana's 2025 SWAP includes four new chapters containing information that is highly relevant to conservation of the state's SGCN and their habitats. Chapter 7 identifies beavers, woodpeckers, and prairie dogs as critical ecosystem engineers in Montana whose activities have an outsized, positive impact for multiple SGCN through the creation or modification of habitat. Chapter 8 highlights the importance of connectivity between intact habitats for the long-term persistence of Montana's flora and fauna. Chapter 9 includes an in-depth analysis conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey on 19 wildlife diseases in the state that could negatively impact SGCN. Chapter 10 outlines a vision and strategy for bolstering communication, education, citizen science, and wildlife viewing as critical components of fish and wildlife conservation in Montana. This chapter was developed recognizing that conservation of SGCN and HGCN hinges on people caring about Montana's wildlife resources, knowing about threats that could negatively impact them, and feeling empowered in understanding what they can do to help conserve at-risk species and habitats in the state. These additional chapters are important to ensure the 2025 SWAP is comprehensive in covering the range of issues related to wildlife conservation in Montana.

The 2025 SWAP represents FWP's most intensive effort to date in providing guidance for nongame wildlife and native fish conservation in Montana. However, we recognize that simply identifying at-risk species and habitats and what we can do to help them does not ensure the work will get done effectively and in strategic places. Monitoring is therefore a major component of the 2025 SWAP. While it is impossible to monitor the effects of all the different forms of conservation work in the state, we provide a strategy for tracking and evaluating the success of conservation actions on SGCN and HGCN.

Montana's 2025 SWAP is a blueprint for restoring, maintaining, and enhancing the incredible biological diversity that makes Montana one of the most outstanding states in the nation for natural resources and outdoor recreation. Through implementation of the SWAP, Montana's fishing, hunting, and wildlife watching resources will be maintained and improved, and the sectors of the economy that depend on them will be strengthened. The ecosystem services humans rely on from healthy, intact habitats and the species within them will be perpetuated into the future. And those of us who call Montana home will continue to be proud of the wild and scenic nature of The Last Best Place.

div.head: CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION 1.1 Introduction
div.p: Montana is comprised of diverse habitats ranging from the grassland and sagebrush seas of the northern great plains to the mosaic of wetlands across the prairie pothole region to the towering forests and alpine plateaus of the Rocky Mountains. And we are incredibly fortunate here in Montana that much of this habitat remains relatively intact. The incredible diversity of healthy habitats in Montana are home to an equally incredible diversity of plant and animal populations. There are 470 native vertebrate species in Montana, as well as more than 7,230 invertebrates, and more than 2,000 species of vascular plants.

Montana's fish and wildlife populations are some of the wildest and strongest in the nation, but still approximately one third of vertebrate species in the state are considered in need of conservation. Montana's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a strategy to identify those species, threats to their populations and their habitats, and actions to address those threats. This plan will help Montana focus limited resources to address the highest priorities: Species of Greatest Conservation Need and Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need.

Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks (FWP) is the state agency with statutorily assigned responsibility for the stewardship of Montana's fish and wildlife resources for present and future generations (MCA 87-1-201). While FWP is the lead wildlife conservation agency, comprehensive conservation of fish and wildlife cannot be achieved without collaboration and cooperation among willing partners. As such, FWP has a long history of working closely with state and federal agencies, tribes, private landowners, and conservation organizations to manage, conserve, protect, and enhance fish and wildlife populations and their habitats.

The first comprehensive strategies for fish and wildlife conservation were developed in 2005 by all 56 states and territories at the direction of Congress. These strategies came to be known as State Wildlife Action Plans (SWAPs), and they use the best available science to identify the threats and conservation actions for the species and habitats in greatest need of conservation. Year 2025 marks the 20th anniversary of SWAPs and Montana's third revision is the most comprehensive, science-based, partner-driven planning process ever completed for the state. It is intended to guide conservation work not just for FWP but also conservation partners, in a joint mission to implement conservation for Montana's at-risk species and habitats. Continued conservation success cannot occur without collaboration and support among partners.

div.head: Purpose of the SWAP
div.p: The U.S. Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-63, Title 1) established the State Wildlife Grants Program, which provides annual funding for conserving species with the greatest conservation need and their habitats (Federal Register 2001). The State Wildlife Grants Program provides funding to states for projects that work to stabilize, restore, enhance, and protect species and habitats. Congress stipulated that each state fish and wildlife agency is required to submit a State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) every 10 years to be eligible for State Wildlife Grants.

More importantly, Montana's SWAP and associated State Wildlife Grant funding supports Montana Fish, Wildlife and Park's (FWP) mission to provide "stewardship of the fish, wildlife, parks, and recreational resources of Montana, while contributing to the quality of life for present and future generations" (FWP 2016). The SWAP helps FWP's Wildlife and Fisheries Divisions identify and prioritize conservation actions to conserve Montana's most at-risk species and their habitats. Proactive conservation is critical in helping keep species off the endangered species list and avoiding costly and burdensome endangered species recovery efforts.

At its core, the SWAP identifies threats and conservation actions for Species of Greatest Conservation Need and Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need that help inform FWP's priorities. However, we hope the plan can assist other agencies and organizations in Montana with focusing their conservation efforts as well. Although FWP is responsible for leading the development of Montana's SWAP, the work identified in this plan far exceeds the available funding and capacity of FWP. Conservation partners are encouraged to use the SWAP to address conservation threats and create a unified effort to restore, maintain, and enhance Montana's tremendous biodiversity and vast public lands. The SWAP is intended to foster greater coordination between FWP and its conservation partners, enabling us to collectively address the conservation needs of Montana's at-risk species and habitats.

div.head: Elements 3 & 4: Threats/Stressors and Actions
div.p: The 2015 SWAP included threats and actions for S1-S2 species and did not include threats and actions for S3 species. In the 2025 SWAP, we are including threats and actions for all SGCN.

We believe it is important to include threats and actions for all S1, S2, and S3 SGCN. Greater staff capacity further facilitated inclusion of more SGCN threats and actions. The 2015 SWAP identified broad threats and actions for HGCN. The 2025 SWAP includes these broad threats and actions for HGCN and includes specific threats and actions for individual HGCN when appropriate. Some HGCN had important threats and actions that were specific to those habitats. Greater staff capacity further facilitated inclusion of more HGCN threats and actions.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Montana covers 146,923 square miles and is renowned for its vast and varied landscapes that support an incredible diversity of habitats (Figure 1). West of the Continental Divide, mountain ranges are separated by sagebrush and grassland valley bottoms, through which large rivers carve floodplains full of cottonwood forests and willow-dominant shrub communities. East of the Continental Divide, the Rocky Mountains give way to rolling prairie and sagebrush-steppe ecosystems occasionally broken up by unique island mountain ranges and vast badlands. Montana's immense variety of aquatic habitats support some of the most coveted and diverse populations of fish and other aquatic species in North America. The state's ecological diversity not only defines Montana's natural beauty but also plays a crucial role in providing ecosystem services to humans such as clean air and water, forage for livestock, pollination for crops, timber resources, and outdoor recreation opportunities, all while helping maintain state and regional biodiversity.

Montana's landscapes play an important role in conserving many at-risk plant and animal species. Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) are identified in the State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) to call attention to specific habitats in Montana that support the greatest number and diversity of Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and/or are at risk due to natural and human-caused factors. While all habitats are important for plants and wildlife in Montana, the purpose of the SWAP is to focus conservation investments in time, money, and energy where they will have the highest impact on conserving the state's flora and fauna.

Restoring, maintaining, and enhancing intact habitats provides resources for hundreds of plant and wildlife species at once. While in some cases single-species conservation actions may be needed to conserve at-risk species, addressing threats to HGCN is often the most efficient use of conservation resources in Montana. Nearly half (48%) of all identified conservation actions for SGCN in Chapter 5 were addressed by actions to protect and conserve habitat, which further supports using a habitat-focused approach in most cases. This emphasizes the need to address threats to species at the most fundamental level, the basic resources they need to survive and reproduce on Montana's landscapes.

Overlaid on Montana's diverse landscapes is a variety of landownership types. Just over 54% of the state is privately owned, while another 18% is managed by the U.S. Forest Service, 9% is managed by the Bureau of Land Management, 6% is managed by the State of Montana, and 1% is managed by the National Park Service. Tribal Nations make up 9% of the land base. The remaining 3% of Montana is owned or managed by local governments and other ownership types. Conservation easements on private lands held by nonprofit or state and federal government agencies account for 2.8% of the land base (2.6 million acres). The diversity of landownership in Montana highlights the importance of crossboundary conservation work. HGCN and SGCN do not recognize or adhere to these boundaries, yet they are substantially affected by differences in management between ownership types.

Figure 1. Map of land cover in Montana using existing natural vegetation communities as described at the Group level under the National Vegetation Classification system. Other land cover types include disturbances (e.g., burned areas, invasive plant communities), human land-use activities, and larger bodies of water (see https://msl.mt.gov/geoinfo/msdi/land_use_land_cover/ for additional information).

div.head: Selecting Terrestrial HGCN
div.p: In 2025, the Montana Natural Heritage Program (MTNHP) implemented mapping of Montana's terrestrial and wetland habitats using the U.S. National Vegetation Classification (NVC) system at the Group level to better align with national and international vegetation classification and mapping efforts and allow both global and state conservation status ranks to be assigned to vegetation communities (USNVC 2022). The NVC uses a consistent national approach to the classification of existing vegetation in the United States and is consistent with vegetation mapping and classification efforts being implemented in Canada. NVC is a hierarchical system designed to classify existing vegetation based on physiognomic and floristic criteria (USNVC 2022). For additional information on the application of the NVC in Montana see https://mtnhp.mt.gov/resources/ecology/nvcs/ Because FWP and MTNHP are so closely aligned in their work in Montana, especially on the development and implementation of the SWAP, the SWAP Habitat Team decided to use the NVC to identify terrestrial HGCN for the 2025 SWAP. The SWAP Habitat Team was first tasked with deciding at what level to include classifications from the NVC as HGCN. The NVC hierarchy consists of upper level (levels 1-3), mid level (levels 4-6), and lower level (levels 7-8) classifications, with greater specificity on plant communities at the lower level of classifications. In reviewing all habitats across the NVC levels, the team decided to select HGCN at Level 6 or "Group" level since this was the level vegetation communities would be mapped at in the 2025 land cover layer. Because all types of habitats in the riparian and wetland category support a disproportionately large number of SGCN, all subcategories are included as HGCN.

After the initial selection of the NVC level at which to classify HGCN in Montana, the SWAP Habitat Team decided which of the 59 Group classifications of native vegetation communities to include as HGCN in the 2025 SWAP. The team selected which habitats supported the most SGCN and which habitats were most in need of conservation investments to assure their continued ecological integrity in Montana into the future. After the initial list was developed, we compared the HGCN list to the SGCN list to confirm major habitats that support SGCN were not missed in the HGCN selection process.

div.head: Mapping Terrestrial HGCN
div.p: Terrestrial HGCN are mapped in the 2025 land cover layer which is a digital raster map of existing natural vegetation communities mapped at the NVC Group level, disturbances such as wildland fire, and human land use activities mapped at a scale of 30-meter x 30meter pixels. The base mapping NVC Groups was adapted from a NatureServe version of existing vegetation communities derived from the LandFire 2020 update that used 30meter resolution Landsat multispectral imagery that represented circa 2016 ground conditions. The LandFire mapping used decision tree models, field data, Landsat imagery, elevation, and biophysical gradient data. For more information, see the detailed metadata for the 2025 land cover layer on the state GIS Data List at: https://mslservices.mt.gov/geographic_information/data/datalist/ Because wetlands are too small to be represented in the land cover layer which is mapped using 30-meter x 30-meter pixels we recommend managers use the National Wetland Inventory (NWI) mapping that is available from the MTNHP's Map Viewer web application and the statewide GIS Data List when initially planning management actions for these HGCN. NWI mapping is available for approximately 87% of Montana. Aerial imagery, particularly color infrared imagery, can be used to identify the presence of wetlands in areas were NWI mapping is not yet available. NWI mapping and aerial imagery should not be used in place of on-site evaluations of these habitats. For more information on wetland mapping in Montana, see the Montana Wetland Framework from the Montana Spatial Data Infrastructure at: https://msl.mt.gov/geoinfo/msdi/wetlands/.

div.head: Selecting Aquatic HGCN
div.p: Although open water is mapped in the 2025 land cover layer many small streams, lakes, ponds, and wetlands are too small to be represented in the land cover layer which uses 30meter x 30-meter pixels. The SWAP Habitat Team therefore needed another method for selecting aquatic HGCN for the SWAP. The team considered using aquatic HGCN from the 2015 SWAP (formally called Community Types of Greatest Conservation Need) but decided that a more fine-scale consideration of aquatic habitats was needed for the 2025 SWAP.

MTNHP was in the process of developing an aquatic community classification system for standing and flowing waters with mapping from the medium resolution National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) as well as accounts describing these communities in the Montana Field Guide. The SWAP Habitat Team decided to use these aquatic communities to identify aquatic HGCN for the 2025 SWAP and worked with the MTNHP to finalize classification, mapping, and descriptions. The team first went through the list of aquatic communities and combined, removed, or renamed the categories based on expertise from around the state on the breadth of aquatic habitats, hydrology and geomorphology of waterbodies, and SGCN associations. The aquatic community classification separates flowing waters (lotic habitats) from standing waters (lentic habitats). Flowing water communities were categorized using: geographic areas (Statewide, Northern Rockies, Middle Rockies, Glaciated Plains, Northern Great Plains), stream size (small, medium, large), and flow type (perennial or intermittent). Alpine and subalpine streams were also added as separate categories for the Northern Rockies and Middle Rockies. Finally, small, medium, and large volume springs were added as habitat classifications, but these were not broken into geographic regions. The team selected all flowing water communities as HGCN except for the springs.

Standing water communities were not categorized by geographic region and included large lakes, small lakes/ponds, alpine lakes with fish, alpine lakes without fish, large reservoirs, small permanent reservoirs, and small seasonal reservoirs. The team selected large lakes and large reservoirs as HGCN.

The broad inclusion of most waterbody types in Montana as HGCN was done in recognition of the outsized importance of waterbodies in Montana, both for the SGCN they contain and support, and their role on the larger landscape supporting upland SGCN and HGCN, as well as human populations. Waterbodies and the riparian areas, floodplains, and wetlands they support contain the largest number and diversity of plant and animal species of any habitats in the state, and they are also a critically important source of water resources for agriculture and other human land uses.

div.head: Mapping Aquatic HGCN
div.p: The medium resolution National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) was used as a base GIS layer for mapping of aquatic communities. The aquatic communities described above were classified on this mapping using lake and reservoir size (> 13 acres), Continental Divide and ecoregional boundaries, digital elevation models, stream order, aerial imagery, National Wetland Inventory (NWI) mapping, Beaver Restoration Assessment Tool (BRAT) metrics and attributes, and known fish and aquatic invertebrate community data from the MTNHP. For more information on Montana's Hydrography Framework from the Montana Spatial Data Infrastructure see: https://msl.mt.gov/geoinfo/msdi/wetlands/

div.head: Terrestrial Habitat of Greatest Conservation Need
Introduction
div.p: One of Montana's greatest features is the incredible diversity of terrestrial and aquatic species that call the state home. Montana is one of the least populated states in the United States, with vast, intact landscapes and healthy ecosystems that support large numbers of native species alongside human land uses. It is with great pride that Montanans enjoy rich biological diversity while maintaining working landscapes and a thriving outdoor recreation economy. As the state becomes more popular and the human population expands, this biological diversity will face new challenges as development encroaches on native habitats and demand for natural resources accelerates. However, conservation of Montana's natural heritage is important to those who live and visit the state, and this shared admiration and respect for wild things and wild places crosses political, social, and economic divides.

Montana's native species include: 56 fish, 13 amphibians, 17 reptiles, 335 regularly occurring birds, 108 mammals, at least 7,230 invertebrates, as well as more than 2,000 species of vascular plants, over 2,500 species of non-vascular plants, algae, and diatoms, over a 1,000 species of lichens, and over 1,600 species of non-lichenizing fungi. The job of documenting and conserving all these species is truly overwhelming, emphasizing the need for careful consideration of where limited resources and time can be most effective in maintaining and enhancing this astounding biodiversity.

Montana's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a critical planning document for outlining the breadth of biological diversity in the state and forging a vision for how to restore, maintain, and enhance this diversity into the future. The 2025 SWAP identifies 375 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), including 153 vertebrate species, 113 invertebrate species, and 109 plant species. The SGCN list comprises species from all major taxonomic groups mentioned above and is the most comprehensive list of at-risk species in Montana's SWAP to-date.

div.head: Role of Conservation Status Ranks in Identifying SGCN
div.p: The Montana Natural Heritage Program (MTNHP) manages the conservation status ranks for species in Montana, which is the foundation for identifying which species are SGCN in the 2025 SWAP. MTNHP uses NatureServe's standardized conservation status ranking methodology to determine the state and global conservation status ranks of species (Salafsky et al. 2008; NatureServe 2020; Faber-Langendoen et al. 2012; Master et al. 2012). Conservation status ranks are calculated for each species using the best available science and most up-to-date data from three major categories:
1. Rarity: Assesses how widespread and/or common the species is within Montana.
2. Trends: Assesses the change in a meaningful metric using population, habitat, or range through time. Both the short-term and long-term trends can be evaluated.

3. Threats: Assesses the proximate activity or process that has caused, is causing, or may cause the destruction, degradation, and/or impairment to the species. Threats may be related to human activities or may be natural.

MTNHP and FWP are fortunate to have a long-term close partnership working on conservation efforts in the state, and the two agencies coordinate closely on the assignment of state conservation status ranks for animals. Each state rank for vertebrate species is assessed and approved by Montana's Species of Concern Committee, which is comprised of staff from MTNHP and FWP with input from species experts and members of the Montana Chapter of the American Fisheries Society. State ranks are now continually updated as new data and information become available, and the Species of Concern Committee meets annually to assess possible changes in ranks. If there are changes to ranks that affect a species' inclusion on the SGCN list, we will submit a SWAP minor revision to account for those changes prior to the 2035 SWAP revision.

Species that are at-risk in Montana are referred to as Species of Concern by MTNHP and SGCN by FWP and the SWAP. Although the Species of Concern and SGCN lists are very similar, the separation is needed because the SWAP-specific criteria for inclusion as SGCN varies slightly from MTNHP's Species of Concern list. Regardless of whether species are referred to as Species of Concern or SGCN, species are assigned status ranks ranging from S1 to S5 that reflect the relative degree of risk to the species' viability in the state of Montana (Table 6). NatureServe also assigns conservation status ranks ranging from G1 to G5 that reflect the relative degree of risk to the species' viability globally (Table 6). Some species are declining globally and we are seeing those effects here in Montana as reflected in their state rank. Conversely, some species may be doing well at a global scale but struggling here in Montana due to region-specific stressors to a species or its habitats. See the State Conservation Rank Criteria (MTNHP 2021; https://mtnhp.mt.gov/docs/Montana_State_Rank_Criteria_20211201.pdf) for more comprehensive information on the species status ranking process. Table 6. Definitions of conservation status rank and rank qualifiers for state and global ranks (MTNHP 2021).

div.head: S1 G1
div.p: Critically Imperiled -At high risk because of extremely limited and/or rapidly declining population numbers, range and/or habitat, making it highly vulnerable to global extinction or extirpation in the state.

The vertebrate SGCN list matches MTNHP's Species of Concern list that includes species with a state rank that includes an S1, S2, or S3 (Table 7). The vertebrate SGCN list deviates from the Species of Concern list by also including species with a state rank of S4 for which Montana has high stewardship responsibility because a substantial portion (≥10%) of the species' global population or range is in Montana (Table 7). MTNHP and FWP conducted a thorough review and update of Montana's state ranks in the years leading up to the 2025 SWAP revision to make sure the underlying data used to develop the SGCN list was as comprehensive and current as possible.

div.head: Invertebrate SGCN
div.p: New to the 2025 SWAP, we are including terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates as SGCN. This is in recognition of the critical role of invertebrates as a food source for many vertebrate SGCN and in overall ecosystem function, which supports all of Montana's fish and wildlife species. FWP has management authority for invertebrates under the definition of nongame wildlife as "any wild mammal, bird, amphibian, reptile, fish, mollusk, crustacean, or other animal not otherwise legally classified by statute or regulation of this state" ( § § 87-2-101 (8) and 87-5-102(6)(2025), MCA). The SWAP terrestrial and aquatic invertebrate teams led efforts to develop criteria for inclusion of invertebrate SGCN in the 2025 SWAP. In addition to FWP and MTNHP staff, the invertebrate teams were comprised of staff from 10 other agencies and organizations and relied heavily on the expertise of these experts from across Montana and the western United States.
The terrestrial and aquatic invertebrate SGCN list matches the MTNHP's Species of Concern list that includes all species with state rank that included an S1 or S2 (Table 7).

The terrestrial invertebrate SGCN list also includes species with a global rank that included a G1, G2, or G3, regardless of the state rank (Table 7). This addition showcases that aquatic invertebrates have higher quality ranks than the terrestrial invertebrates where global ranks are filling in gaps in our understanding of their status.

div.head: Plant SGCN
div.p: The selection of plant SGCN for the 2025 SWAP followed a different pathway than that for vertebrate and invertebrate SGCN. Selection methods and criteria for plant SGCN originated from the Montana Native Plant Conservation Strategy (Pipp et al. 2024). In developing this strategy, a committee of botanists, biologists, and ecologists from federal and state agencies, non-governmental organizations, and academia sought input and developed criteria for defining plant SGCN for vascular plants. The committee compiled information on distribution, population sizes, habitat conditions, threats, and other data from the MTNHP botany database, scientific literature, and professional expertise to refine the list of SGCN (Table 7). Important factors considered included the MTNHP's Species of Concern list, real or highly probable threats to the species in the short and long term, association with unique habitats or plant communities, and professional opinions on the status of common plants shared and expressed by different federal and state management agencies. Furthermore, species considered for inclusion had to be well documented in the state and lack any taxonomic problems. With approval from the larger partnership that guided the development of the Montana Native Plant Conservation Strategy, the committee created two pathways and sets of criteria for identifying Plant SGCN (Table 7).

div.head: Mapping for SGCN
div.p: Several types of spatial information are managed for all species tracked by the MTNHP, including SGCN. These types of spatial information include:

div.head: Structured Surveys
div.p: The MTNHP records information on the locations where more than 80 different types of well-defined repeatable survey protocols capable of detecting a species or suite of species have been conducted by state, federal, tribal, university, or private consulting biologists.

Examples of structured survey protocols tracked by MTNHP include: vegetation plot surveys for vascular plants, visual encounter and dip net surveys for pond breeding amphibians, point counts for birds, call playback surveys for selected bird species, visual surveys of migrating raptors, kick net stream reach surveys for macroinvertebrates, visual encounter cover object surveys for terrestrial mollusks, bat acoustic or mist net surveys, pitfall and/or snap trap surveys for small terrestrial mammals, track or camera trap surveys for large mammals, and trap surveys for turtles. Whenever possible, photographs of survey locations are stored in MTNHP databases.

div.head: Observations
div.p: The MTNHP manages information on over 6 million animal and plant observations that have been reported by professional biologists and private citizens from across Montana. The majority of these observations are submitted in digital format from standardized databases associated with research or monitoring efforts and spreadsheets of incidental observations submitted by professional biologists and amateur naturalists. At a minimum, accepted observation records must contain a credible species identification (i.e. appropriate geographic range, date, and habitat and, if species are difficult to identify, a photograph and/or notes on key identifying features), a date or date range, observer name, locational information (ideally with latitude and longitude in decimal degrees), notes on numbers observed, and species behavior or habitat use (e.g., is the observation likely associated with reproduction). Bird records are also required to have information associated with date-appropriate breeding or overwintering status of the species observed. MTNHP reviews observation records to ensure that they are mapped correctly, occur within date ranges when the species is known to be present or detectable, occur within the known seasonal geographic range of the species, and occur in appropriate habitats. MTNHP also assigns each record a locational uncertainty value in meters to indicate the spatial precision associated with the record's mapped coordinates.

div.head: Species of Concern Occurrences
div.p: The MTNHP evaluates plant and animal observation records for species of higher conservation concern to determine whether they are worthy of inclusion in a Species

Occurrence or "SO" (also known as an 'Element Occurrence'). An SO is an area depicting only what is known from direct observation with a defined level of certainty regarding the spatial location of a species or biological community. If an observation can be associated with a map feature that can be tracked (e.g., a wetland) then this polygon feature is used to represent the SO. Areas that can be inferred as probable occupied habitat based on direct observation of a species location and what is known about the foraging area or home range size of the species may be incorporated into the Species Occurrence.

div.head: Geographic Range Polygons
div.p: Range polygons have been created for native vascular plants and vertebrate animal species with sufficient data and are being created for other taxa as MTNHP staff time is available. Range polygons are refined over time with assistance of additional survey and observation data and predicted habitat suitability models. Range polygons are classified as native year-round, summer, winter, migratory, historical, and non-native year-round. Range polygons for native species and non-native aquatic species typically bound the extent of known or likely occupied habitats for non-migratory and relatively sedentary species and the regular extent of known or likely occupied habitats for migratory and long-distance dispersing species; polygons may include unsuitable intervening habitats. Unless predicted invasion risk models indicate unsuitable habitat for large portions of Montana, range polygons for non-native vascular plant species are typically mapped as statewide to reflect their possible invasion across Montana; please see relative density maps for reported distributions of these species. For most species, a single polygon can represent the year-round or seasonal range, but breeding ranges of some colonial nesting water birds and some non-native species are represented more patchily when supported by data. Some ranges are mapped more broadly than actual distributions in order to be visible on statewide maps (e.g., streams with fish are buffered for visibility).

div.p: The MTNHP constructs two types of predicted habitat suitability models for individual plant and animal species: (1)

div.head: Terrestrial Invertebrate SGCN List
div.p: We included 57 terrestrial invertebrate species as SGCN in the 2025 SWAP. Of these SGCN, 33 species had ranks that included S1 or S2 due to small population sizes, limited distribution, and/or affinity to specific environmental conditions coupled with direct or indirect threats. The terrestrial invertebrate SGCN list includes 1 ant, 1 arachnid, 9 bees, 2 beetles, 2 bugs, 11 butterflies, 1 fly, 5 grasshoppers, 5 millipedes, 15 mollusks, 1 moth, 3 skippers, and 1 springtail (Table 9). species are common on the landscape but observed by land managers from different agencies and/or tribal nations as in potential decline from various threats.

Table 11. List of plant Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) in Montana's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan, including information on their distribution, ranks, threat scores, and habitats. Species are arranged alphabetically by group, then by state rank, and then alphabetically by common name. In the HGCN columns, "Other" indicates the Plant SGCN is associated with a habitat that is not classified as a HGCN.

div.head: Terrestrial Vertebrate SGCN and HGCN Associations
div.p: The critical importance of habitat to the conservation of species is evident throughout the SWAP, with the majority of threats and actions identified for SGCN being related to their habitat. It is therefore also critical to explicitly link SGCN in the SWAP to associated HGCN. This allows for a holistic approach to nongame conservation by considering the entire range of threats to a species, both those that directly affect the species and those that affect the environment it lives in. Linking SGCN and HGCN also draws clearer threads between conservation actions, whether they be species-specific or habitat-specific. Those working on habitat conservation on the landscape can better understand which species are most at-risk in those habitats, and then focus conservation efforts on habitats with the highest potential to conserve those species. Those working on single-species conservation or management can relate their species of interest to a wider range of conservation work that, while not focused on a single species or group, can still be highly beneficial for the simple reason that good habitat supports a greater abundance and diversity of the plants and animals that live there.
Most terrestrial vertebrate SGCN in the 2025 SWAP are associated with one or more HGCN.

There are other habitats beyond those identified as HGCN in the SWAP that also support many SGCN, but those associations are not listed here. In order to link SGCN to HGCN, we only considered HGCN where the associated SGCN regularly breed or overwinter, or areas they travel through on migration routes. We then used the following information to assign SGCN to HGCN categories:
1. Incidental observations and structured survey results from various efforts across Montana via the MTNHP state-wide point observation database.

2. Review of literature that summarizes the breeding, overwintering, and/or migratory habitat requirements of each SGCN (Dobkin 1992, Hart et al. 1998, Hutto and Young 1999, Maxell 2000, Werner et al. 2004, Adams 2003, and Foresman 2012).
3. Evaluation of structural characteristics and distribution of each vegetation community associated with an HGCN relative to the species' range and habitat requirements.

4. Calculation of the percentage of observations associated with each HGCN relative to the percent of Montana covered by each HGCN to get a metric of the number of observations in the context of available habitat.

Species that breed in Montana were only evaluated for breeding habitat use. Species that only overwinter in Montana were only evaluated for overwintering habitat use. Species that only migrate through Montana were only evaluated for migratory habitat use. In general, species are listed as associated with a HGCN if it contains structural characteristics known to be used by the species. However, species are not listed as associated with a vegetation community if we found no support in the literature for the species' use of structural characteristics of the community even if point observations were associated with it.
Caspian Terns and Blue-gray Gnatcatchers were the only species without an associated HGCN.

div.head: Suggested Uses and Limitations
div.p: Species associations with HGCN should be used to generate potential lists of species that may occupy broader landscapes for the purposes of landscape-level planning. These potential lists of species should not be used in place of documented occurrences of species or predicted habitat suitability models (this information can be requested at: https://mtnhp.mt.gov/requests/), or systematic surveys for species and onsite evaluations of habitat by trained biologists. Users of this information should be aware that the land cover data used to generate species associations is based on satellite imagery from 2016 and was only intended to be used at broader landscape scales. Land-cover mapping accuracy is particularly problematic when the vegetation communities occur as small patches or where the land cover types have been altered over the past decade. Thus, caution should be taken when using the associations in assessments of smaller areas (e.g., evaluations of public land survey sections). Although a species may be associated with a particular HGCN within its known geographic range, portions of HGCN may occur outside of the species' known geographic range. Similarly, species are associated with a variety of HGCNs and these associations do not designate the relative importance of different HGCN.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Species of Greatest Information Need (SGIN) lack enough information about population status, trend, and/or threats to the species to determine their state status rank. SGIN are species that have the highest need for additional information because they lack baseline surveys, have outdated surveys, lack scientific information about important life history traits or habitat associations, and/or we have low confidence in the existing information about the species.

We emphasize that SGIN are not less important than SGCN; they are just lacking information largely due to difficulties in detecting or counting the species. For example, species that are cryptic and/or difficult to capture may require large amounts of time, funding, and person-power to obtain even basic data on current populations, much less evaluate those populations' trends over time. Our goal with identifying SGIN is to focus resources on gathering the most useful information with the greatest efficiency, resulting in an ability for the Species of Concern Committee to assign a state conservation status rank.

As species are removed from the SGIN list, they may be added to the SGCN list if their conservation status rank places them within the criteria for inclusion as SGCN. Threats and conservation actions were not developed for SGIN species, in recognition of the need for evaluating their status in the state first.

Montana's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) identifies 98 Species of Greatest Information Need (SGIN), including 12 birds, 11 fish, 14 mammals, 26 aquatic invertebrates, and 35 terrestrial invertebrates. These SGIN are considered SWAP species and are eligible for federal funding. We recognize the outstanding need to collect baseline data on all plants and invertebrates in the state. However, including all these species as Species of Greatest Information Need in the SWAP would be too long and cumbersome. We are including a small portion of plant and invertebrate species as SGIN in the SWAP based on feedback from species experts which we believe to be a key step towards expanding our knowledge about Montana's species and informing conservation needs and strategies.

div.head: Methods
div.p: The identification of SGIN stems from the same species status ranking process outlined for identifying SGCN in Chapter 3. However, the identification of SGIN necessarily acknowledges the lack of information for confidently assigning an S-rank to a species. Therefore, SGIN were selected almost entirely from species with no numerical S-rank, except for special circumstances (Table 16).

Table 16. Criteria used to identify Species of Greatest Information Need (SGIN) categories for vertebrates, terrestrial invertebrates, and aquatic invertebrates for the 2025 Montana State Wildlife Action Plan.

div.p: Vertebrate SGIN 1. State conservation status rank of SU.

2. State conservation status rank of S4 or S5 with either: a. Known declines in parts of the species' range outside of Montana and lacking information on whether the species is declining in Montana. b. Gaps in information for rarity (range extent, area of occupancy, or habitat associations), threats, or shortterm trends that, if documented, would allow the conservation status of a species to be more adequately assigned. Terrestrial Invertebrate SGIN 1. State conservation status rank of SNR or SU that were nominated by taxonomic experts. Aquatic Invertebrate SGIN 1. State conservation status rank of SU that were nominated by taxonomic experts. 2. Global conservation status rank of G1, G2, G3 that were nominated by taxonomic experts.

div.head: Vertebrate SGIN List
div.p: We included 37 vertebrate species as SGIN in the 2025 SWAP. Of these SGIN, 17 were classified as SU and an additional 20 species were included that were ranked S4 or S5, but for which critical information for determining their status as SGCN is missing or there are documented declines in other areas. The Vertebrate SGIN list includes 12 birds, 11 fish, and 14 mammals (Table 17).

div.head: Terrestrial Invertebrate SGIN List
div.p: We included 35 terrestrial invertebrate species as SGIN in the 2025 SWAP. The terrestrial invertebrate SGIN list includes 1 ant, 1 arachnid, 5 bees, 10 beetles, 6 butterflies, 1 cricket, 1 lacewing, 1 mantis, 8 moths, and 1 rock crawler (Table 18).

div.head: Aquatic Invertebrate SGIN List
div.p: We included 26 aquatic invertebrate species as SGIN in the 2025 SWAP. Of these SGIN, all 26 were classified as SU, and 24 were ranked as G1, G2, or G3, and were nominated by taxa experts. The Aquatic Invertebrate SGIN list includes 9 caddisflies, 7 crustaceans, 5 mayflies, 3 mollusks, and 2 stoneflies (Table 19). div.head: Element 4. Actions
div.p: The actions necessary to conserve SGCN and their habitats and the priorities for implementing such conservation actions

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In Chapters 2 and 3, we outlined Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) and Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) identified in the SWAP, setting the foundation for which species and habitats are highest priority for investments in conservation in Montana. But identifying species and habitats is only part of the larger picture of conservation, and the next step is to identify what threats make these species and habitats a high priority in the first place.

There is no use in identifying threats to HGCN and SGCN without pairing those threats with a plan for what we can do about them. We only identified a threat to a species or habitat if there were tangible conservation actions that could be taken to address that threat. Of course, almost always there were multiple actions that could address each threat, and similarly there were usually multiple threats that could be addressed by each action. As the SWAP technical teams and external experts compiled more than 6,000 threats and actions for the 2025 SWAP, the complexity of the interactions between threats and actions became apparent. One of the heaviest lifts in the process of revising the SWAP was organizing threats and actions, but the result is a comprehensive look at what is impacting our natural resources in Montana and what we can do about it.

This chapters covers a wide breadth of threats and actions for species and habitats in recognition that for most species and habitats, degradation and population declines are rarely the result of a single or small number of threats. Instead, many interacting threats come into play and which threats are most impactful changes across space and time. It is therefore important to outline the entire range of threats and actions so that FWP and its partners can then use more localized knowledge to identify which actions are most applicable to their geographic area or area of expertise and the specific threats that are most important in those contexts.

While we include a great many threats and actions in this SWAP, the format does not lend itself to fully capturing and communicating the entirety of the information compiled by the technical teams and external experts. The full detail of all the threats and actions identified as part of the SWAP revision will be included in a forthcoming SWAP dashboard. This dashboard will allow this complex web of interacting threats and actions to be databased, sorted, and queried by users looking for more in-depth information on a particular species or habitat. The SWAP dashboard, combined with the action-based focal area mapping (Chapter 6), will make the immense information we complied about conservation threats and actions easier to visualize, understand, and act upon for FWP and its partners.

div.head: Identifying Threats and Conservation Actions for HGCN
div.p: For Montana's 2025 SWAP, threats and conservation actions were identified for all Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN). As defined in Table 2, Elements 3 and 4, "threats" are problems for species and habitats, and "actions" are responses FWP and other partners can take to help reduce the adverse effects of those problems. Lists of threats and actions for each HGCN were assembled and reviewed by the habitat teams that worked to identify HGCN (see Chapter 2 for that process). Additionally, the SWAP habitat team hosted a partner engagement workshop at the Montana Chapter of The Wildlife Society (5 March 2025) that was attended by 37 people from 18 organizations. During this workshop, teams of partners, led by members of the habitat team, worked to brainstorm threats and actions for HGCN while considering the suite of SGCN those habitats support. Additional threats and actions were identified through expert experience and review of other State Wildlife Action plans and habitat management plans.

After lists of threats and actions were generated, they were categorized under the Conservation Measures Partnership Threats and Actions Classification System (Version 2.0, Salafsky et al. 2008, Appendix F). Because many threats and actions were shared across all HGCN, threats and actions are presented in a hierarchical structure, with threats and actions applicable to all HGCN presented first, and those applicable to specific HGCN presented within the HGCN habitat profiles. Threats and actions for HGCN can be considered threats and actions for the SGCN that use those habitats. In the SGCN threats and actions section, we outline any threats and actions that were specific to a particular SGCN and were not habitat related.

Through the process of compiling threats and actions for HGCN, the technical teams made decisions about grouping HGCN based on whether identified threats and actions were specific to certain types of HGCN or were widely applicable to all HGCN in a given category (Grassland, Shrubland, Forest and Woodland, Wetland and Riparian, River and Stream, Lake and Reservoir). In most cases, threats and actions were best communicated at the broadest level of HGCN classification (Tables 4 and5). We provide more specific threats and actions for some Forest and Woodland and Shrubland sub-categories, but for all other HGCN threats and actions are outlined at the broadest classification level.

div.head: Identifying Threats and Conservation Actions for SGCN
div.p: For Montana's 2025 SWAP, conservation actions and their corresponding threats were identified for all SGCN species. Lists of threats and actions for each species were then assembled and reviewed by a technical team consisting of two to five biologists, including a representative from FWP working with species experts from partner organizations. ). The intent of this classification system is to provide standard language for terms used by the conservation community (Appendix F). This classification system is also employed in MTNHP's species status assessments, and any new threats and actions identified through this SWAP revision will be reviewed for potential inclusion in species status rank revisions by MTNHP. All identified actions are linked to the threat(s) they address, allowing the same actions to be linked to multiple threats and vice-versa.
We employed a hierarchical approach to presenting threats and actions in the 2025 SWAP.

A majority of threats and actions identified for SGCN pertain to habitat and are directly addressed in the threats and actions for HGCN. Threats actions for SGCN that are addressed in the threats and actions for the HGCN those SGCN are associated with have therefore been excluded from the SGCN threats and actions tables. (See Section 3.7 for associations between SGCN and HCGN). As such, the threats and actions presented for SGCN are constrained to those that are species-specific. Habitat-related actions may still be included where they require species-specific information to implement.

Additionally, we have excluded actions pertaining to research and monitoring (Conservation Measures Partnership Threats and Actions Classification System Action 8.0) from the HGCN and SGCN summaries because these actions are being summarized and considered separately as forthcoming "Research Needs." For species with existing management plans (e.g., sage-grouse), a selection of key threats and actions have been included, and the species-specific management plans have been linked. In the forthcoming SWAP dashboard, habitat threats and actions that provide the foundation for species conservation will be linked to individual species accounts.

div.head: HGCN Profiles with Threats and Conservation Actions
div.p: Actions for the conservation of Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) are provided below, along with their corresponding threats, organized by the Conservation Measures Partnership Threats and Actions classification systems (Version 2.0, Salafsky et al. 2008, Appendix F). Threats and actions that are relevant to all HGCN are provided first, followed by tables relevant to specific HGCN.
In addition to the actions provided in the tables, addressing any of the threats herein would generally be aided by:
1. Providing decision makers with data, analysis, and interpretation regarding threats to HGCN and outlining effective conservation actions to address those threats.
2. Highlighting successful HGCN restoration, maintenance, and enhancement projects through a wide variety of media outlets.
3. Investigating the need for, and then creating or updating, guidance documents that are useful for minimizing negative impacts to HGCN.

4. Working with schools, universities, and the general public to include education around HGCN and threats and actions related to HGCN in curriculums. Highlight successful HGCN restoration, maintenance, and enhancement projects through a wide variety of media outlets.

div.head: Shrublands
div.p: The shrublands of Montana include a wide variety of habitats ranging from willow and alder thickets in the avalanche chutes of the Bitterroot Mountains to vast "sagebrush seas" overlooking the Missouri River Breaks. Combine all these varieties of shrubdominated habitats, which cover 17% of the state, and there are 53 terrestrial vertebrate SGCN that depend on them. Whether it is a shin-high cinquefoil or a 30-foot-high maple, shrubs fill the layer between the ground and the trees (if there are trees) with structure for nesting and evading predators and abundant food in the form of nutritious buds, delectable berries, and hordes of insects. Shrublands in Montana are often intermixed with grasslands, and similarly important to the state's ranching operations. These are also great habitats for wildlife-viewing and hunting, as it is a little bit easier to get close to wildlife when there are some plants to hide behind.

div.head: Riparian and Wetland
div.p: Riparian areas and wetlands cover a relatively small percentage of the land in Montana, but they are the biodiversity powerhouses of the state. The abundance of water in these habitats facilitates vigorous plant growth that occurs throughout the growing season. This leads to immense primary production (i.e., the base of the food web), which leads to a large number of SGCN that are dependent on riparian areas and wetlands. Despite largely existing as small patches and stringers in the larger Montana landscape, riparian areas and wetlands support 103 terrestrial vertebrate SGCN species. It is vital to consider that a great many SGCN, as well as all of the state's game and furbearer animals, are also dependent on water resources to survive. So, even though they may not spend their whole lives in this habitat, these other species will certainly need patches of riparian or wetland habitat in their home ranges to survive in the mostly arid environments of Montana.

div.head: Rivers and Streams
div.p: Montana is covered in a network of stream and river drainages that can take the form of everything from a small, crystal-clear seep or spring with barely a trickle of water to a giant muddy river more than 1/4-mile across. These streams and rivers are the lifeblood of Montana's ecosystems, transporting water from snowmelt and rain through sagebrush, grassland, and forested landscapes. In their healthiest form, these waterbodies form "river-wetland corridor" where channel migration and periodic flooding form broad riparian areas and wetland complexes used by the largest number of terrestrial SGCN of any HGCN in the state. Within the streams and rivers themselves swim some of Montana's most impressive animal populations: the fish and the aquatic invertebrates those fish rely on as the base of their food web. Montana is second to none in the U. S. for fisheries resources, and the allure of the state's streams and rivers brings in people from around the world. Alongside anglers are floaters, wildlife watchers, and hunters, who all escape to Montana's flowing waters to find abundant wildlife, cool temperatures, and some of the most beautiful and iconic scenery in the entire state. Streams and rivers make up a small percentage of the landscape in Montana, yet these habitats support well over 100 SGCN in both the aquatic and terrestrial realms. Work to expand the scope of streamside protection laws to include a buffer along stream and river channels in recognition of channel migration and the importance of riparian and wetland vegetation that is not directly adjacent to the waterbody. Bank stabilization to protect human infrastructure severs floodplain connectivity, reduces woody debris inputs into waterbodies, diminishes public access to waterbodies, facilitates increased development in and near floodplains, and perpetuates bank hardening downstream.

div.head: Action
div.p: Work to expand the scope of streamside protection laws to include a buffer along stream and river channels in recognition of channel migration and the importance of riparian and wetland vegetation that is not directly adjacent to the waterbody.

div.head: Household Sewage & Urban Waste Water
div.p: Excess nutrients contribute to eutrophication of waterbodies. Point source pollution (e.g., industrial effluents) and nonpoint source pollution (e.g., agricultural and urban runoff) contribute pollutants and excess nutrients to waterbodies, with cascading negative impacts to aquatic SGCN and their food base. Relatively new and emerging contaminants negatively impact SGCN or their food base (e.g., PFAS chemicals, 6PPD-Q, selenium).

div.head: Lakes and Reservoirs
div.p: Lakes and reservoirs in Montana are central to the state's fishing and boating economies but are also critical for storing water and managing it to benefit agriculture and municipalities. The creation of reservoirs for water management has also created some of the most sought-after fishing destinations in the United States. Places like Canyon Ferry Lake, Fort Peck Reservoir, and Nelson Reservoir are renowned fishing destinations but also boast immense wetland areas and a rich aquatic food web that provide resources for many terrestrial SGCN. These areas are important for animals that forage and breed in Montana but are also critical stopover points for continent-scale migrations of shorebirds, waterfowl, and other water-loving birds. Some lesser-known species are also dependent on still waterbodies such as bats that need still water to drink and find abundant insects to eat. Overall, Montana is still an arid state, and lakes and reservoirs make up a small percentage of the landscape.

Even with this small representation, over 100 terrestrial or aquatic SGCN are dependent on lakes and reservoirs at some point in their life cycle. Prohibit timber extraction in areas that serve as refugia that limit hydrological and thermal stress on this species.

div.head: Cassin's Finch Threats and Conservation Actions
Fire & Fire Suppression
div.p: Fire suppression leads to high intensity fires, which impacts Whitebark Pine with compounding effects from the loss of mature trees from beetle kill. Large replacement fires cause widespread mortality of all Whitebark Pine. Post-fire regeneration may be reduced due to a large proportion of cone-bearing trees having been previously killed, reducing available seed source/cone production. Altered fire regimes lead to Subalpine Fir/Lodgepole Pine encroachment and competition for resources.

div.head: Problematic Native Plants & Animals
div.p: Mountain Pine Beetle kills lead to large scale habitat loss and degradation of Whitebark Pine. Historic logging practices (i.e., large clearcuts in lodgepole forests) have led to overstocked even-aged stands of suitable DBH that combined with environmental conditions (i.e., drought, lack of sufficiently low winter temperatures) have led and continue to lead to Moutain Pine Beetle infestations that spread to adjacent Whitebark Pine stands. Predation by raptors (e.g., Great Horned Owl, Swainson's Hawk, Red-tailed Hawk, Cooper's Hawk, Golden Eagle).

div.head: Housing & Urban Areas
div.p: Housing and other development along lake shores reduces habitat through destruction of streamside vegetation and bank stabilization/modification, increases disturbance to nesting and foraging loons, and increases the introduction of pollutants and trash into lakes from yards, roads, waste storage areas, and access points.

div.head: Commercial & Industrial Areas
div.p: Commercial development along lake shores reduces habitat through bank stabilization/modification and destruction of streamside vegetation, increases disturbance to nesting and foraging loons, and introduces pollutants and trash into lakes from yards, roads, waste storage areas, and access points.

div.head: Tourism & Recreation
div.p: Development of recreation sites along lake shores reduces habitat through bank stabilization/modification and destruction of streamside vegetation, increases disturbance to nesting and foraging loons, and increases the introduction of pollutants and trash into lakes from campgrounds, boat ramps, roads, waste storage areas, and associated recreational activities.

div.head: Fishing & Harvesting Aquatic Resources
div.p: Ingestion of lead from fishing tackle causes direct mortality and is believed to be the top source of mortality for adult loons in Montana. Ingestion of fishing hooks and entanglement in discarded fishing line kills individual loons or diminishes their ability to hunt and raise young effectively. Disturbance from opening day for fishing on many lakes coincides with arrival and/or nest initiation.

div.head: Recreational Activities
div.p: Disturbance to nest sites and nursery areas from boaters, floaters, anglers, hikers, campers, bird watchers, photographers, and other recreationists causes nest abandonment or failure. Boat strikes cause direct mortalities of loons.

div.head: Invasive Non-Native/Alien Plants & Animals
div.p: Introduction of aquatic invasive species (e.g., invasive mussels) and plants can reduce or eliminate prey base for loons and increase the risk of botulism outbreaks that cause loon mortalities. Introduction of non-native fish species in lakes used by loons or planting of fish in formerly fishless lakes can reduce or eliminate prey base for loons (e.g., Northern Pike reducing silver salmon in Salmon Lake). Efforts to remove non-native fish for native fish restoration can cause loon mortalities or stress (e.g., gill-netting, piscicides reducing prey base) in the short term, but are generally positive for loon conservation in the long term.

div.head: Flammulated Owl Threats and Conservation Actions
Fire & Fire Suppression
div.p: Lack of fire disturbance leads to loss of dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forests that consist of widely spaced, largediameter trees, an open understory, and aspen stands. More frequent fire due to invasive plant species (e.g., Cheatgrass) removes understory shrubs and favors invasive species dominance, degrading habitat. Severely burned foothill forests may not recover to pre-fire conditions in the long-term, with compounding effects of climate change and invasive plant species.

div.head: Species Stewardship
div.p: Construct nest boxes on lands where suitable snags and injured trees for nesting are limited, as a temporary solution until suitable habitat conditions are restored. Work on conservation actions for Pileated Woodpeckers to promote robust populations of this keystone species which is an important next cavity excavator for Flammulated Owls.

div.head: Logging & Wood Harvesting
div.p: Salvage logging after fires and firewood cutting removes snags used for nesting. New and existing roads concentrate these activities in foothill habitats and more open forested areas. Timber harvest and vegetation management to restore mature and old-growth conditions and/or reduce fuel loads removes potential roost site features and escape cover (e.g., small patches of dense young conifers, trees with mistletoe growths, dense crowns, etc.). Vegetation management and timber harvest in dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forest types can remove large-diameter trees, snags, and downed woody debris critical for nesting and foraging.

div.head: Species Stewardship

div.head: Site/Area Stewardship
div.p: Prohibit livestock from grazing in peatlands while in the backcountry, as it is very hard to mitigate negative impacts in these systems. div.p: Small population sizes and isolation of populations in a few high elevation lakes that may provide little thermal refugia from increasing temperatures. For the 2025 SWAP, we are developing a suite of focal areas maps that are focused on conservation actions that can be taken to address threats to HGCN. We will do this by integrating spatial distribution maps for SGCN and HGCN to find areas of HGCN with relatively high numbers of SGCN. Then, we will select the top actions to address threats to those HGCN that can be mapped using remote sensing and refine the combined SGCN and HGCN maps based on those actions. The result will be focal areas that highlight where specific conservation actions should be undertaken on the landscape to have the biggest positive impact on the largest number of SGCN.

The new focal areas will present a continuous gradient of the level of impact to SGCN and HGCN across the state, instead of portraying explicit focal area zones as was done in the 2015 SWAP. By taking this approach, partners that work within a specific jurisdiction in the state can still identify the most impactful places to implement a conservation action to benefit SGCN and HGCN, even if those places may not be the most impactful in the context of the whole state. Our new approach to focal areas is fitting for Montana where half (48%) of all the conservation actions identified for species were related to habitat stewardship. To complete this new analysis, we first need time to process 6,000 conservation actions that were identified as part of the 2025 SWAP revision and create the links between HGCN, SGCN, and their associated threats and actions. Focal areas are one of the most used portions of the SWAP by our partners for identifying important areas for conservation work, and this new approach will incorporate all the feedback we got during the development of the SWAP and present it in a way that fosters on-the-ground action to focus limited habitat conservation and restoration investments. Throughout the process of developing focal areas, we will solicit and include partner feedback to make sure the focal areas make sense to those that will use them the most.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: FWP emphasizes conservation actions for Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) because creating, maintaining, and enhancing high-quality habitat addresses key threats to many Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) at once. Similarly, FWP recognizes that single-species management can also address conservation threats to many SGCN at once. This is especially true for species commonly referred to as "ecosystem engineers."

Ecosystem engineers are species that dramatically alter their environment to suit their needs, and those changes can be positive or negative for different species, or for biodiversity in general (Jones et al. 1997). The term "ecosystem engineer" is often used synonymously with "keystone species", though keystone species are considered to have an entirely positive influence on biodiversity by creating conditions that allow for certain plant and animals species to exist and/or thrive in an area where they may not otherwise (Power et al. 1996, Kotliar 2000). For the SWAP, we use the term "ecosystem engineer" to highlight the important role these species play in modifying the landscape, but all the ecosystem engineers in this chapter are also considered keystone species.

In Montana, we have a wide range of plant and animal species that are, or could be, considered ecosystem engineers. In this State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), we are focusing on a subset of ecosystem engineers whose activities can modify habitat to benefit a relatively large number of SGCN. Those ecosystem engineers are the North American beaver (Castor canadensis), woodpeckers, and prairie dogs (Cynomys spp.). The North American beaver is classified as a furbearer in Montana, while several woodpeckers and both white-tailed and black-tailed prairie dogs are classified as SGCN.

Projects, policies, and education around conserving and enhancing populations of these ecosystem engineers are effective ways to address multiple threats to many SGCN and HGCN. These are considered top-priority conservation actions that FWP and its partners should focus on in implementing the 2025 SWAP.

div.head: North American Beaver
div.p: Beavers (Castor canadensis) dramatically modify their environment through harvesting vegetation, digging tunnels and channels, and building dams. These activities can be a highly beneficial, if not essential, disturbance in the streams, rivers, and lakes beavers occupy. Dam building is especially beneficial, as beaver dams raise water tables, recharge groundwater, and reconnect degraded streams to their floodplains (Naiman et al. 1988, Wohl 2019, 2021). The impacts of thousands of beaver dams across a watershed can greatly enhance natural water storage and dampen annual hydrographs, providing water resources for wildlife and humans later into the summer and fall (Wohl 2019, 2021).

Restoring beavers to areas of their former range is considered one of the most important actions humans can take to mitigate negative impacts from excessive flooding, severe wildfire, and drought ( The impacts of beaver activity on plants and invertebrates were not evaluated as part of this effort. However, many studies have documented increased plant and invertebrate diversity and abundance in beaver-modified habitats, both at the scale of a single beaver colony and at the scale of an entire stream drainage (see reviews in Rosell et al. 2005, Muller-Schwarze 2011, and Rosell and Campbell-Palmer 2022). Therefore, it is reasonable to expect that some plant and invertebrate SGCN could benefit from beaver-modified habitats on the landscape. This is an area for future research and monitoring work.

div.head: Threats and Conservation Actions
div.p: High-quality riparian and wetland habitats can be maintained and enhanced by beaver activity, but beavers can also restore degraded habitats, and they can do it faster and cheaper than humans working alone (Pollock et al. 2014, 2017, Wheaton et al. 2019). "Beaver restoration" is an umbrella term encompassing all aspects of restoring beavers to areas of their former range and helping people address human-beaver conflicts. FWP published a comprehensive white paper on beaver restoration in 2023 (Ritter et al. 2023), and readers of the SWAP are encouraged to consult this document to learn more about conservation actions and management strategies for beavers in Montana.

Beavers are not considered at-risk in Montana, and their populations appear to be healthy in suitable habitats, though no statewide monitoring of populations occurs currently. The primary threats to beavers in Montana are disease, predation (including trapping by humans), and removal of beavers due to conflicts with human infrastructure and land uses. However, none of these threats are expected to cause a state-level population decline, though certain drainages may be negatively affected. Instead, the main limiting factor for beavers in Montana is historical loss of suitable habitat due to land use changes and stream degradation (Wohl 2021). These impacts have greatly reduced the extent of suitable streams where beavers can not only occupy the area, but remain in place long enough to bring about their beneficial effects on water storage, floodplain connectivity, and wildlife habitat.

Beavers are capable of breeding profusely and occupying available habitat rapidly (Muller-Schwarze 2011). So, even though their primary limiting factor is degraded habitat, they are also powerful agents of stream restoration (Pollock et al. 2014, 2017). A top conservation action for beavers is to identify those areas where relatively small investments in stream restoration can allow beavers to move in, take over the restoration work, and perpetuate those restoration investments into the future (Ritter et al. 2023). Expanding the distribution and connectedness of beaver populations across Montana's landscapes is an effective way to achieve landscape-scale stream restoration and bolster natural water storage.

The activities of beavers can cause major conflicts with humans, so beaver-human conflict resolution is another key conservation action to increase tolerance for beavers on the landscape and maintain connectivity between sub-populations. Beaver-human conflict resolution can take many forms, and may include:
• Lethal trapping of conflict beavers during regular furbearer trapping season or through FWP's beaver damage permit system.
• Installation of non-lethal beaver conflict resolution devices such as culvert fences, pond levelers, and tree wrapping (Shockey 2024a, 2024b).
• Capturing beavers from conflict situations and transplanting them into areas of their historical range.
• Deterrent measures such as electric fencing, motion-detecting floodlights, and fladry.
• Education about the benefits of beavers for situations where the beavers are not causing damage but are perceived as a negative influence on stream systems.
