Attitudes and opinions about beavers vary widely across the social spectrum in Montana, and myths about beavers and their impacts on the environment persist in many communities. Outreach and communication about beavers is another essential conservation action for reaping the benefits of beaver-modified habitats in Montana. This can include, but is not limited to, workshops, trainings, educational materials, and presentations on (1) the benefits of beavers to humans and wildlife, (2) lethal and nonlethal solutions for beaver-human conflicts, (3) restoration techniques to encourage beaver colonization, and (4) the role of trapping in beaver restoration and management.

div.head: Woodpeckers
div.p: In forested areas of Montana, numerous SGCN as well as other wildlife species rely on cavities in standing live or dead trees for nesting, cover, and thermoregulation. Many of these species are considered "secondary cavity nesters," meaning they are not capable of excavating a cavity themselves and are therefore reliant on "primary cavity nesters" to excavate cavities for them. Across North America, including Montana, woodpeckers fill the role as these primary cavity nesters (Hardin et al. 2020). Woodpeckers use their strong beaks and associated musculature to bore holes through the sapwood of trees to excavate chambers in the internal heartwood. The heartwood of trees is more susceptible to heartrot fungi than sapwood, and so the sapwood provides a strong entryway to the cavity while the softer heartwood can be excavated to form the internal chamber.

In Montana, primary cavity nesting woodpeckers occupy a wide range of forested habitats from ponderosa pine savannahs to river-bottom cottonwood galleries to recently burned forests. In all these habitats, their cavity excavating abilities modify the habitat in such a way that certain wildlife species would not be able to survive and thrive without the woodpeckers' efforts. All of Montana's woodpecker species can be considered primary cavity nesters, though some species have unique life history characteristics that make them especially adept at ecosystem engineering. For example, black-backed woodpeckers specialize in excavating cavities in standing dead trees in recently burned forests and may be the only species capable of excavating cavities in fire-hardened wood for many years after a burn. The impacts of woodpeckers on plants and invertebrates were not evaluated as part of this effort. It is likely that woodpecker activity in Montana may have significant impacts on invertebrates, as they are the primary food source for woodpeckers and large numbers of invertebrates take advantage of the same decaying wood that woodpeckers use for foraging and cavity excavation. It is unlikely that woodpeckers substantially affect any plant SGCN. Whether or not woodpeckers in Montana impact plant or invertebrate SGCN is unclear, and this is an area for ongoing research and monitoring.

div.head: Threats and Conservation Actions
div.p: In this SWAP, six woodpeckers are classified as SGCN (Lewis's Woodpecker, Black-backed Woodpecker, Pileated Woodpecker, Red-headed Woodpecker, Red-naped Sapsucker, and Williamson's Sapsucker). These woodpeckers occupy and modify a wide range of habitats, so threats and conservation actions for these ecosystem engineers are well-covered within the individual species threats and actions accounts in Chapter 5.

div.head: Prairie Dogs
div.p: Prairie dogs (Cynomys spp.) create unique habitat conditions in and around their colonies through the excavation of extensive burrow networks and the grazing of vegetation (Kotliar 2000). Many other species, including SGCN, key in on prairie dog colonies to take advantage of the array of resources they provide (Adams 2021 and

div.head: Threats and Conservation Actions
div.p: Prairie dog colonies are spread throughout the eastern part of Montana but represent a fraction of their former range. Burrowing by prairie dogs is disruptive to many human land uses, especially agriculture, and so they have been removed from large portions of their historical range. This represents a conservation threat to prairie dogs, but also to the SGCN that take advantage of prairie dog colonies. Removal by humans, alongside disease and predation, have led to both species of prairie dogs in Montana being classified as SGCN

div.head: CHAPTER 8: WILDLIFE CONNECTIVITY
div.p: Ecological connectivity (or simply "connectivity") refers to the capacity of landscapes and seascapes to allow species to move freely and for ecological processes to function unimpeded (UNEP 2019). Connectivity is fundamental for biodiversity conservation in an era of accelerating environmental change (Heller and Zavaleta 2009). As the landscape becomes increasingly fragmented, maintaining or restoring connectivity allows species to move safely between intact habitats to access necessary resources on a daily, seasonal, and annual basis. Over extended periods, connectivity maintains genetic diversity by preventing populations from becoming isolated and allows species to shift their ranges to track suitable conditions in response to changing environmental conditions (Tabor et al. 2014).

Increasing human population and associated infrastructure development and expansion alongside land conversion are growing threats to natural movement routes for wildlife. Barriers to movement and resulting loss of connectivity vary by species, but common barriers include linear infrastructure like roadways and fencing; other human structures such as buildings, dams, powerlines, and energy facilities; cross-boundary management and conservation issues that can be at the international scale for some species; and habitat fragmentation resulting from agricultural production and other human-related landuse changes. The loss of connectivity due to habitat fragmentation poses serious risks to wildlife populations (Ghoddousi et al. 2021). Wildlife populations become isolated, leading to increased competition for resources, inbreeding, increased risk of density-dependent diseases, and higher mortality rates. Disrupted movement patterns also force wildlife into human-dominated landscapes, escalating conflicts between people and animals and creating serious safety issues along transportation corridors.

Montana's Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) depend on connected landscapes across multiple spatial scales and habitat types for migration, dispersal, seasonal foraging, and reproduction. For nongame wildlife, connectivity needs range from a few meters to several kilometers, depending on their mobility and habitat use. Many species have small home ranges but need connections between habitat patches to avoid inbreeding. Nongame animals often exist in metapopulations-partially isolated groups connected through dispersal. Their movements may span long distances, linking between protected areas, riparian corridors, or wetland networks. Maintaining these connections supports recolonization after local extinctions, which is critical for population persistence in patchy or disturbed landscapes.
Most non-avian nongame species have lower mobility than wide-ranging mammals and can be highly affected by roads, fences, or minor development barriers (Cushman 2006).

Some organisms, such as amphibians, reptiles, and aquatic invertebrates, need access to different habitats throughout their life cycle, like wetlands, streams, and adjacent uplands (Semlitsch and Bodie 2003). Others, including rodents and insects with limited range, need continuous cover to move safely, while some rely on highly specific and often rare or declining habitat types. Avian nongame species are much more mobile but face increasing threats from the expansion of towers, tall buildings, airports and associated plane traffic, and other infrastructure. Avian species are also affected more broadly by increasing sound and light pollution and ongoing habitat loss and degradation. At the local scale, many forest, grassland, shrubland, and riparian bird species need contiguous or closely spaced habitat patches to move safely, especially during breeding and post-breeding dispersal. Many avian species migrate at a continental scale, emphasizing the need for full life-cycle species conservation that may cross state and international boundaries.

Connectivity conservation involves mitigating the barriers to species movement and maintaining and restoring landscape features, such as corridors or linkage areas, that facilitate species movement (Tabor et al. 2014). Ensuring connectivity for Montana's nongame species requires attention to multiple spatial scales and habitats. Strategies to conserve connectivity for nongame species include but are not limited to:
1. Protecting and restoring critical corridors and specific habitat types.
2. Collaborating with transportation and land-use planning entities to reduce barriers.

div.head: Integrating connectivity considerations into project review and funding decisions.
div.p: Generally, strategies should include protecting lands that include intact habitats consisting of elevation gradients, diverse vegetation structure, functional disturbance regimes, a high proportion of native plant communities, topographic diversity, and water availability.

To address barriers such as roads, creating new structures such as culverts or tunnels, or modifying existing drainage structures with dry shelves and fencing, can provide safe passage for smaller species, in addition to larger-scale crossings for larger species (Huijser et al. 2022). Creating protective cover habitat to avoid predation and maintain foraging routes or habitat niches (e.g., moisture and light regimes) is important for some species.

Windbreaks or riparian strips can serve as movement corridors in developed areas and agricultural landscapes. Nongame wildlife and their habitats, and particularly, SGCN and Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN), should be intentionally included in connectivity mapping and prioritization efforts that influence management decisions. Continuous engagement and collaboration with state and federal agencies is important to ensure projects and planning are complementary.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Infectious disease can present a notable and complex threat to wildlife survival, population resilience, and susceptibility to other stressors 1,2 . Impacts of disease on wildlife populations range widely, from relatively mild effects like reduced fitness or occasional deaths to more substantial effects like mass mortality events, population declines, and even population extinctions 1 . Healthy wildlife populations can often persist with pathogens or recover quickly after outbreaks through adaptive measures, such as developing immunity or tolerance to a disease 3 . Moreover, disease outbreaks often fade out over time as the number of susceptible hosts declines 4 . Thus, not all diseases cause long-term population declines, and disease is rarely the sole driver of species endangerment 5 .

Yet, there are important exceptions in which disease can lead to significant and lasting impacts in wildlife populations. Diseases like white-nose syndrome, chytridiomycosis, and avian malaria have caused high-profile, widespread declines and even extinctions [6][7][8] . In populations that are already imperiled due to other factors, disease can act as an additional stressor that disrupts recovery efforts or causes further reduction in numbers. In addition, small or isolated populations, such as those of imperiled species or populations involved in recovery programs, are less resilient to disease 9,10 . These populations may have low genetic diversity and reduced ability to develop immunity, and geographic isolation can prevent population recovery following outbreaks 1 . Diseases can impact populations rapidly if outbreaks cause mass mortalities. Alternatively, impacts can play out over many years (and in less visible ways), if disease persists as an underlying stressor that suppresses population growth rates or increases overall vulnerability to other threats 3 . In sum, although the magnitude of direct and indirect effects of disease are variable, diseases can be a relevant threat to the conservation and recovery of imperiled wildlife, including Montana's Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN).

Characterizing the distribution and impact of wildlife diseases is a significant challenge, and it is not always clear when and where disease management strategies are needed 11 . The impacts of disease can be highly variable across populations and through time. For example, changes in the environment or the presence of additional stressors like drought or habitat loss can enhance disease transmission or worsen disease outcomes 12 . The location of disease outbreaks can also be unpredictable. Climate variability, species range expansions, biodiversity loss, habitat change, and human activities (e.g., agriculture, recreation, transportation) can alter the distribution of hosts and pathogens, leading to introductions of pathogens to novel locations [12][13][14][15] . Larger impacts are expected when wildlife are exposed to new pathogens to which they lack immunity, a pattern that is increasing in frequency. Novel disease threats are expected to emerge over the coming decades, and may occur with little warning 2,14 .

Not only are disease distributions rapidly changing, but management is also challenged by significant uncertainty about the impacts of disease on wildlife populations. Disease surveillance can be costly and laborious, and few diseases are routinely monitored, leaving major gaps in knowledge about the geographic extent of wildlife diseases 16 . In addition, long-term impacts of diseases on wildlife populations are often difficult to assess because monitoring data on wildlife abundance is limited, especially for SGCN. Without information on the distribution of disease, the susceptibility of different wildlife species, and population impacts, it is difficult to identify the locations or populations in most need of management intervention 17 . Moreover, management strategies for wildlife diseases are limited, and commonly used interventions from human health or veterinary sectors rarely apply to wildlife populations 17 . Limited information and tools can inhibit preparedness for disease outbreaks and lead to delays in action during critical windows for managing wildlife disease outbreaks 18,19 .

This chapter aims to improve preparedness for wildlife health challenges by summarizing relevant information on 20 infectious diseases that may impact Montana's SGCN, including (1) potential wildlife species affected, (2) disease biology, risk factors, and potential impacts, (3) current knowledge about the disease's distribution in Montana, and (4) the potential for future disease spread. For each disease, a list of potential conservation actions supported by scientific research is provided, with the key caveat that interventions to limit wildlife disease are highly context-specific and, in some cases, techniques may be in the early stages of development.

div.head: Generating a Candidate Disease List
div.p: A list of high-priority infectious diseases that impact or could impact Montana's SGCN was generated using expert elicitation and targeted searches of the nationwide wildlife mortality database, Wildlife Health Information Sharing Partnership Event Reporting System (WHISPers) 20 . We searched the WHISPers database to identify diseases that have caused mortalities in Montana's SGCN since 1980. To conduct expert elicitation, we held workshops with wildlife health experts (n = 19) from Montana and surrounding states.

Participants were asked to identify relevant diseases across distinct vertebrate taxa including amphibians, reptiles, fish, mammals, and birds. The workshop also focused on discussing potential climate impacts on wildlife diseases and how to best compile conservation actions and assess disease threats in the face of uncertainty and rapidly changing conditions. This process generated an initial list of 48 diseases of potential relevance for Montana (Table 26). We could not thoroughly review all 48 diseases, so we selected a subset of 20 diseases that we designated as "high priority" to be reviewed for Montana's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP). We prioritized diseases that affected multiple SGCN, were identified as important by multiple experts, and were involved in mortality events in the WHISPers database. We also ensured that the list of high-priority diseases included diseases of fish, mammal, bird, and herptile species.

div.head: Literature Review and Synthesis
div.p: A targeted literature review was conducted for the 19 diseases designated as high priority for Montana's SGCN. Searches were performed using the scientific databases PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus. Initial search terms consisted of each pathogen's name (including synonyms or alternative scientific names) in combination with terms such as "wildlife," "free-ranging," or "wild." If needed, searches were further refined with additional keywords such as "management," "Montana," or "climate." Articles were included in the review if they demonstrated regional relevance within or around Montana, described impacts to wildlife at the individual or population level, or addressed key topics such as disease management strategies, climate sensitivity, host breadth, or vector dynamics. Articles were excluded from review if the study focused primarily on impacts to domestic species or humans, diagnostics, evolutionary dynamics, or surveillance studies outside region of interest. Findings from literature review were synthesized into disease summaries highlighting the pathogen and disease's ecology, host breadth (in Montana), disease drivers, impact, known presence in Montana, climate sensitivity, conservation actions, and knowledge gaps.

Host breadth is summarized in a table at the top of each disease's summary and was characterized by grouping species into four categories based on their susceptibility to disease impacts and conservation status within Montana:

1. SGCN with Known Impacts: Montana SGCN species (S1-S3) for which disease has been documented to cause negative health outcomes, such as clinical illness, mortality, population declines, or mass mortality events.

2. SGCN Susceptible to Infection: Montana SGCN species that are known to become infected with the pathogen but negative impacts have not been observed. This is either because species are asymptomatic or resistant to disease, or because the effects of the disease have not yet been quantified or observed in that species. These species could potentially become impacted by the disease or could serve as reservoir hosts or asymptomatic carriers.

3. SGCN Potentially Susceptible: Montana SGCN species in which infection has yet to be documented but are potentially susceptible based on evidence and taxonomic relatedness from known infected species. Species in this category highlight important data gaps in assessing potential risk to species of conservation concern.

4. Other Susceptible Montana Species: Montana species classified as S4 or higher or broad taxonomic groups that are known or suspected to be susceptible to infection. These species/groups may experience clinical disease or act as carriers and are important to consider due to their potential influence on disease distribution, transmission dynamics, and spillover to SGCN.

Disease drivers represent major ecological or anthropogenic factors that influence disease epidemiology and impact to wildlife 12 . Factors provided were well established in literature or recommended by subject matter experts. We highlight the major disease drivers in order to help identify environments or populations that may be particularly at risk and to provide potential management targets by emphasizing the factors that heighten disease occurrence, transmission, and severity.
Following completion of literature review and synthesis, each disease summary was reviewed by two subject matter experts to ensure information was both accurate and current.
actions that apply to wildlife diseases. Conservation actions were grouped into four broad categories:

1. Prevention: preventative measures aimed at reducing the likelihood of introduction of disease into species, populations, or locations 2. Disease Management: actions focused on reducing the prevalence or severity of infectious disease within affected populations 3. Species and Habitat Management: actions that promote overall species or population health, abundance, distribution, and adaptive capacity to disease by reducing other stressors or improving habitat 4. Surveillance and Monitoring: monitoring strategies and surveillance tools that improve the ability to detect outbreaks and prioritize disease management Actions provided in the disease summaries represent possible interventions to be considered on a case-by-case basis. While these actions are supported by literature and have been reviewed by subject matter experts, selection and implementation of actions will be based on a range of criteria, such as feasibility, goals, available resources, expertise, and expected impact 24 . In many cases, research on efficacy of certain actions is lacking or information pertaining to a disease or affected population is limited. In addition, as information related to a disease or at-risk population emerges and/or conditions change, management strategies will need the ability to adapt. Using adaptive management frameworks will increase the capacity and ability to respond to shifting conditions.

Novel disease threats that have not been identified in the SWAP may emerge over the next decade and may impact Montana's SGCN. Conservation actions listed in Table 25 and the following pages may apply to these novel, still-unknown diseases, and managers can consider referencing actions from this chapter as starting points for identifying salient management interventions.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This chapter provides an overview of the key diseases of concern for Montana's nongame wildlife and highlights opportunities to improve and sustain wildlife health through targeted disease management. Review of wildlife disease threats for Montana revealed multiple gaps in knowledge and critical research needs that are consistent with broader challenges in wildlife disease management. These include a lack of data on host (particularly SGCN) susceptibility to certain diseases, uncertainties regarding the distribution and population impacts of diseases within Montana, and limited knowledge of how disease extent may change in the future. We were able to identify a wide range of potential conservation actions for wildlife diseases; however, many of these actions have not been extensively implemented in wildlife populations, nor has their effectiveness been rigorously examined.

Overall, continued collaboration, research, and the adoption of adaptive management approaches will be key in addressing rapidly changing wildlife disease challenges and safeguarding the health of Montana's wildlife.

The determinants of healthy wildlife populations are complex and influenced not only by the presence or absence of disease, but by multiple other factors like resource availability, social structure, environmental conditions, and other stressors 25 . Consequently, wildlife health can be supported by a diversity of conservation actions that target multiple aspects of wildlife population resilience (as noted in other sections of the SWAP) and not just through actions that reduce the presence of pathogens. While certain actions, such as minimizing the spread and introduction of novel infectious diseases and improving the resilience of wildlife populations, are generally good practice, other interventions, such as environmental treatments, vaccinations, or pharmaceuticals, may only be necessary in limited contexts 17,24 . Although the following pages provide a list of potential conservation actions relevant to each disease, not all outbreaks or instances of wildlife disease will require intervention. How can managers identify those contexts where these conservation actions are needed? While increased disease surveillance may seem like the obvious answer, it is often resource-intensive, and surveillance programs or effective techniques are rare in wildlife. Population monitoring (i.e., to track abundance and distribution) may help identify specific locations where declines due to disease have occurred and where disease control efforts or further information on disease is most needed, along with supporting other management goals. Therefore, we emphasize that broader efforts to monitor and conserve imperiled populations are critical to addressing disease threats 17 .

Table 24. Rubric used to evaluate degree of threat represented by each disease. We modified NatureServe's Threat categories (Scope, Severity, and Timing) to apply to wildlife diseases and added a fifth category pertaining to future spread from climate variability (Climate Risk). The total risk score was computed as: 3 x (population impact) + 2 x (relevance to Montana) + 2 x (host range) + 1 x (outbreak timing) + 1 x (climate risk). Diseases could receive a final score between 9 and 45.

div.head: Negligible
div.p: Pathogen is not present in US; conditions in Montana are likely to limit pathogen presence.

div.head: Host Range (SCOPE IN WILDLIFE) Weight: 2x
div.p: Description: the number of species affected by the disease (lower range: species affected by the disease; upper range: species potentially susceptible to the disease) Score >10 SGCN affected and multiple taxa are affected and at least 10 non-SGCN are affected >10 SGCN affected and either multiple taxa are affected or at least 10 non-SGCN are also affected

div.head: High
div.p: Epizootic outbreaks occur regularly but do not last multiple years OR disease may persist as enzootic for multiple years.

div.head: Moderate
div.p: Sporadic outbreaks are likely to occur multiple times per decade but are short lived.

div.head: Low
div.p: Outbreaks occur only sporadically and may occur only 1-2x over the next few decades.

div.head: Insignificant
div.p: Threat is in the past and unlikely to return.

div.head: Climate Risk Weight: 1x
div.p: Description: the likelihood of disease expansion or increased severity under changing climate conditions Score High
Disease is known to be expanding due to climate change, with increasing risk in Montana.

div.head: Serious
div.p: Disease is known to be highly sensitive to climate change; impacts in Montana unknown.

div.head: Moderate
div.p: Disease has traits making it climate-sensitive, but relationships have not been well quantified or rigorously examined.

div.head: Slight
div.p: Disease has few or no traits that are climate-sensitive; however, impacts from climate change or susceptible species may lead to disease expansion.

div.head: Impacts
div.p: WNS has caused severe population declines and near-extirpations of bat populations, particularly in Myotis and Perimyotis species and in populations located in the eastern U.S. and Canada. Scientists estimate that infected bat populations have decreased by 30 percent to 99 percent annually, with some species having an overall estimated population decline of 90 percent 2,5 . As of 2025, Pd is confirmed in 40 U.S. states and 9 Canadian provinces 6 . Seven of Montana's 15 bat species are known to be susceptible to WNS, in addition to six species in which Pd has been detected without evidence of clinical disease 7 .

It is suspected that some of these species may serve as vectors for disease 1 . While the risk that WNS poses to western bat populations is clear, differences in species ecology may alter disease severity and risk of major declines. Such factors include reduced aggregation, alternative hibernacula selection (fewer caves or mines), shorter seasonal migrations, and colder hibernacula with increased temperature fluctuation 9 . However, substantial information gaps still exist for these factors and their influence on WNS's impact to western bat populations.

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Because Pd is a fungal pathogen, WNS prevalence and severity are closely tied with environmental conditions. The growth temperature range for Pd is less than 68 degrees F (ideal range is 41 to 57 degrees F). However, evidence exists that infectious spores may be viable up to 98 degrees F, allowing for increased dispersal opportunities 10 . The theorized impacts of climate variability on WNS are mixed. Warmer, longer autumns may allow for increased fat accumulation for bats pre-hibernation (improving survival rates), while increased temperature variability during winter may lead to increased arousals and energy expenditure or alter hibernacula microclimates that either favor or reduce Pd growth 11,12 . Finally, effects of future climatic shifts, especially increased drought conditions in the west, are predicted to pose significant challenges to overall bat population health, impacting reproduction, range restrictions, and survival 13 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Prairie dogs and black-footed ferrets are most severely impacted by sylvatic plague, although other populations such as chipmunks and ground squirrels may occasionally be impacted. In prairie dog colonies, disease tends to shift between enzootic and epizootic phases. Epizootic phases involve rapid, large-scale die-offs, in which complete colony extirpations often occur 6 . Enzootic phases occur when Y. pestis is maintained at low levels in the environment, usually through transmission between relatively resistant small mammal hosts (e.g., deer mice and voles) and their fleas, without causing widespread mortality 7 . For black-footed ferrets and prairie dogs, without major interventions (e.g., vaccination, insecticides), infection is almost always fatal, with individuals usually succumbing to the disease within three to four days. Odds of survival for black-footed ferrets are further reduced by loss of their primary prey base (prairie dogs) during epizootics. Plague's impact is also felt not only on the level of individual species but across ecosystems. The burden of disease reduces prairie dogs' ability to fulfill their ecological role as ecosystem engineers, threatening the conservation of other species such as predators and grassland SGCN birds, like burrowing owls, mountain plovers, and chestnutcollared longspurs 8,9 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Data from outbreaks suggest that climate may have a significant influence on plague cycles [11][12][13] . In the U.S., plague tends to occur in semi-arid regions of the west, with epizootics most frequently observed in mid to late summer when fleas are most abundant. Wet summers, moderate temperatures and moisture tend to favor increased rodent activity and provide favorable conditions for flea hatching, contributing to increased potential for epizootics 11,14,15 . Extended periods of hot, dry conditions can reduce both flea and Y. pestis survival, but the pathogen may be able to persist under the protection of cooler underground burrows 11 . Under future climates, longer, warmer summers and increased fluctuations in precipitation are expected to occur, which may extend the transmission season for plague and allow increased opportunity for outbreaks. In some instances, extended drought periods may limit plague activity but will also lead to stress in host populations, leaving them more susceptible to disease. Altogether, due to the complexity of drivers of plague dynamics, the relationship between climate and plague still remains poorly understood and in need of further investigation.
Monitor for other indicators of plague activity, such as decline in active prairie dog colony area, decline in prairie dog abundance, presence of carcasses, and burrow abandonment [19][20][21] .

• Monitor flea species type and abundance in prairie dog colonies and other nearby rodents. If the number of fleas per prairie dog trend upwards, this may signal an increased risk of a disease outbreak [19][20][21] .

div.head: Literature Cited
div.p: end hosts because they do not transmit the virus back to feeding mosquitos. Some birds (e.g., the American robin) play a larger role in the spread of WNV because they are better at passing the virus to mosquitos than other bird species 9 . WNV causes neurologic disease in both birds and mammals. Birds that succumb to disease typically die within a few days to a few weeks following infection, while surviving birds can have long-lasting immunity to the virus 10 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: WNV has caused significant mortality and been linked to population declines in multiple avian species. Most notably, greater sage-grouse have demonstrated a high susceptibility to WNV, marked by substantial mortality, reduced survival rates, and limited resistance 1,11,12 . Other species of birds, such as corvids, thrushes, and raptors, have demonstrated significant mortality or population declines as a result of WNV, though some populations appear to have developed resistance to the disease 4,7 . Future impacts of WNV on wildlife will be driven by WNV-prevalence in vectors, overall vector abundance and distribution, and climate. Many of the species that are affected by WNV are also involved with important ecological processes, such as scavenging of carcasses, seed dispersal, and control of insect pests, suggesting secondary, ecosystem-level impacts are possible with increased WNV spread and severity 7 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ WNV has been associated with multiple, large-scale die offs in mixed avian populations (e.g., variety of waterfowl, crows, and American white pelicans) in Montana over the last two decades 13 . ▪ The most recent report to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) WHISPers database occurred in 2016 at the Bowdoin National Wildlife Refuge, where both WNV and botulism type C were isolated from dead birds 13 . Other reports of avian mortality in Montana describe WNV as either a confirmed or suspected diagnosis. These reports tend to occur in populations of waterfowl where other diseases (e.g., botulism type C, salmonellosis, and avian cholera) are of concern and sometimes diagnosed in conjunction with WNV. ▪ Greater sage-grouse in southern Phillips County have experienced WNV-associated mortality and impacts since its emergence in the area in 2003 1 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Warming temperatures and changes to precipitation are predicted to have significant impact on WNV distribution and timing, likely resulting in increased disease occurrence 14 . Milder winters and longer warm seasons lengthen and intensify the mosquito breeding season, providing more opportunity for contact with bird hosts and disease amplification. As habitat generalists, mosquitos are also often tolerant to drought conditions and have even demonstrated population surges as a response to drought due to its negative impact on mosquito larvae predators (e.g., fish, other aquatic insects) 15 . Evidence already exists that milder winters have allowed for overwintering of the virus in mosquito populations, allowing for earlier spread and infection to wildlife 16 . Due to the virus's capacity to infect a wide range of avian hosts combined with mosquitos' general durability, WNV is expected to withstand extreme shifts in climate and potentially lead to an increase in the number of outbreaks.

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Develop integrated pest management plans for vector control in collaboration with state public health agencies 6 .
• Engage with landowners or managers of wetlands to develop protocols or strategies for minimizing suitable habitat for virus-carrying mosquitos 3 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • During outbreaks, continue to reduce mosquito abundance and larval habitat to minimize risk of WNV transmission (e.g., reduction of stagnant water, use of chemical or biological pesticides) 3,6,16,17 .
• Consider vaccination against WNV in highly vulnerable species 6 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Locate and preserve key roosting sites for susceptible bird species as communal roosting may reduce WNV impact by reducing the number of mosquitos feeding per bird 18 .
• Consider strategies to prevent other avian diseases (e.g., avian cholera, botulism, etc.) to reduce cumulative host stress 17 .
Conduct avian serosurveys to understand potential distribution of WNV and what populations are vulnerable 11,6,14 .
• Monitor mosquito populations and WNV prevalence in vectors 6 .

• Develop public education campaigns to promote awareness about WNV transmission cycle and impacts to birds, and to monitor for unusual deaths in wildlife. Over 100 of Montana's bird and mammal species can be infected with HPAI.

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: -Mixing of populations at wetland habitats 3 -Habitat location relative to migratory pathways 4 -Contact with poultry 5 -Seasonality 6,7

div.head: Background
div.p: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is caused by strains of the avian influenza (AI) virus that are highly transmissible and cause particularly severe diseases. Outbreaks of HPAI have been associated with mass mortalities in wild birds, mammals, and domestic poultry 1,5,8 . HPAI is an emerging disease in the United States, with the first observations in North American wild birds occurring in 2021 5,9 , and information on HPAI is rapidly changing as research and surveillance efforts grow 6 . The virus is transmitted through direct contact, aerosols, contaminated water, and surfaces, and infected birds often shed virus in their feces 10 . Influenza viruses can remain infectious in waterbodies for several months after shedding 10,11 . Symptoms of infection include respiratory distress and neurological signs (lethargy, lack of coordination, seizures) 8,10 . Hundreds of wild bird species and many mammals can be infected with HPAI 1 . Waterfowl and shorebirds are commonly infected with the virus but may or may not develop severe disease symptoms 5 . Other wild birds, including raptors, may contract HPAI by consuming infected waterfowl or through contact with contaminated waterbodies 6 . Wild mammals, particularly scavengers, may also be affected 6,8 . Outbreaks typically coincide with migration, with deaths peaking in spring and fall, and are facilitated by mixing of birds at wetland sites 3,4,6,7 . There are many different strains of avian influenza, and they evolve rapidly, meaning that even mild strains have the potential to mutate into highly pathogenic strains 11 . This complicates vaccine development and the likelihood for populations to develop immunity 11 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Outbreaks of HPAI have caused large mortality events in wild birds across the globe, affecting thousands of individuals in some cases 6 . Economic impacts of HPAI (i.e., in dairy cattle and poultry production) can be highly consequential and have received more attention than effects on wild populations 5 . However, HPAI is considered a threat to wild birds that are listed as threatened or endangered. Species with colonial nesting behaviors can be particularly at risk; for instance, the Caspian tern has suffered population declines in excess of 50 percent during a single season 6 . Given the relatively recent spread of HPAI within wild birds of the United States, the diversity of strains, and the rapid evolution of the virus, there are still substantial uncertainties regarding the long-term and population-level impacts of HPAI.

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ HPAI is found throughout Montana, having been detected in at least 40 species of wild birds in Montana across 20 counties [12][13][14] . Montana FWP tests suspected cases where deemed warranted (e.g., where multiple birds are found dead or where human exposure occurs) 14 . ▪ In Montana, the most commonly reported species with HPAI are mallards, Canada geese, great horned owls, red-tailed hawks, American wigeons, and blue-winged and green-winged teals 2 . ▪ Mortality from HPAI has been observed in Montana's wild birds, including hundreds of individuals during a 2022 outbreak 12,13 . Mass mortality events affecting thousands of wild birds have been observed in neighboring states (North Dakota, South Dakota) 13 . ▪ HPAI has been detected in wild mammals in Montana, including grizzly bears, mountain lions, red foxes, striped skunks, and raccoons. This includes cases where individuals were thought to have died due to HPAI or cases where animals suffered clinical signs and died of secondary causes 12,14 .

div.head: Literature Cited
div.p: opportunity for recovery, when water temperatures are below optimal range for T. bryosalmonae (59 degrees F) 3 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: PKD has caused multiple, large-scale die-offs in free-ranging fish throughout western North America and Europe 2,3,8 . Surveys indicate that the parasite is often widely distributed and highly prevalent in fish populations 2,7 . Disease tends to be worse in younger fish, with one report citing a 90 percent loss in abundance of young-of-the-year brown trout in PKDaffected streams 9 . Outbreaks, disease severity, and mortality risk are primarily temperature-dependent and are exacerbated in warming water conditions 5 . In some cases, PKD may not be the direct cause of fish mortality but can contribute to lower fitness and exacerbate declines in populations affected by pollution, low-oxygenated waters, secondary pathogens, or other stressors 7 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: The emergence and impacts of PKD have been directly linked to warming temperatures and shifting environmental conditions 3,5,7,8 . Warming waters and changes in precipitation patterns in the Northern hemisphere have led to an increase in PKD outbreaks and disease severity 7,8 . Clinical PKD is known to occur when water temperatures exceed 59 degrees F (15 degrees C) for several weeks or longer, which promotes the release of T. bryosalmonae spores and the proliferation of bryozoan colonies. Importantly, warming waters also lead to increased stress and immunosuppression in fish overall, and when combined with reduced or altered water flows, such as those resulting from drought, fish suffer habitat loss and increased exposure to infected bryozoans. In Montana, severe outbreaks have been

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ Distribution of bryozoans in Montana and factors that enhance growth of colonies or lead to infectious spore release ▪ Susceptibility to PKD in Montana fish species and impacts of subclinical infection ▪ Transmission and shedding dynamics of T. bryosalmonae in Montana fish species ▪ Relationship between PKD, climate, hydrologic events, and stress on fish populations in Montana ▪ Use of climate science to predict high-risk locations and periods for improved monitoring and management

div.head: Background
div.p: Avian cholera is a highly contagious disease among wild and domestic birds that is caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida 1,2 . Cases of avian cholera in wild birds have been documented in the U.S. since the 1940s 2 . Since that time, it has emerged as a significant threat to avian populations worldwide, particularly among waterfowl and shorebirds 5 . Outbreaks tend to be explosive in onset, often involving hundreds to thousands of birds at a time, and occur in densely populated bird colonies or along migration routes 2 . Mortalities may occur year round; however, birds are usually affected while in their wintering grounds and during spring migration. Avian cholera is transmitted through contact with infected birds or carcasses, secretions or feces of infected birds, ingestion of contaminated food or water, and in some cases, inhalation of contaminated water droplets 3 . Once introduced into a dense population of waterfowl, infection can spread rapidly, with some highly susceptible species (e.g., ducks, geese, and swans) dying as soon as 6 to 12 hours after exposure 1,3 . The clinical course of cholera can be so rapid that infected birds may fall out of the sky or die while feeding with no other signs of illness 3 . The bacteria can persist and remain infectious in water for several weeks, and it is suspected that some birds can become chronic carriers, continuing to transmit the pathogen for years 6 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: While most bird and mammal species can be infected by P. multocida, not all exhibit disease or experience mortality. In waterfowl, however, mass mortality events involving thousands of birds per day are regularly observed, with some outbreak events culminating in the deaths of tens of thousands of birds 5,7 . As a result, avian cholera is considered one of the most highly impactful diseases of wild waterfowl. The population impacts of avian cholera are not well understood in wildlife, but significant impacts have been observed on individual breeding colonies and at particular wintering locations 3 . Imperiled waterfowl that stage or winter in Montana or have limited/highly concentrated breeding areas may be particularly at risk. In recent years, outbreaks are frequently associated with snow geese as they start to migrate south, with mortalities continuing throughout winter until departure in the spring (Robert Dusek, USGS, pers. comm.).

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ There have been several outbreaks of avian cholera recorded in Montana since the 1970s, including in Ponderosa, Gallatin, Phillips, Teton, Sheridan, Cascade, and Flathead counties 8 . ▪ Outbreaks have killed hundreds (or more) of snow geese, northern pintails, northern shovelers, mallards, California gulls, Canada geese, American wigeons, American coots, ring-billed gulls and Ross's geese 8 . ▪ Locations along waterfowl migratory pathways (e.g., the Pacific Flyway in western Montana) are most at risk 3 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: The effects of climate factors on avian cholera are not well-understood. As a bacterium, P. multocida is likely impacted by temperature changes. Indirectly, warming temperatures, seasonal shifts, and changes to precipitation patterns can impact avian cholera by altering habitats, food availability, and migration patterns, which could lead to changes in animal stress, densities, and disease transmission 4,9 .

div.head: Conservation Actions
div.p: Prevention ▪ In some instances, a vaccine for avian cholera can be administered to improve survival rates in chicks. This practice has mostly been used to protect colonies of endangered seabirds, and vaccines are species-specific [10][11][12] .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: ▪ Once an outbreak occurs, if feasible, promptly remove sick and dead birds to help reduce the spread of the bacteria 3 . ▪ Consider actions (e.g., deterrents) that limit scavenging by gulls and crows, which are involved in spread to new locations 3 . ▪ Consider use of deterrents, hazing, and draining of waterbodies to limit wildlife use of contaminated waterbodies 3 . ▪ Consider the manipulation of habitat attributes (e.g., water temperature, water quality) that affect bacterial persistence and prevalence 3 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: ▪ Enhance habitat quality at non-impacted waterbodies that may serve as refugia 3,6 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: ▪ Monitor habitats for sudden mortalities, particularly in highly susceptible species (e.g., snow geese, eared grebes), and determine cause of death to extent possible 8 . Priority sites for monitoring include waterbodies with high concentrations of waterfowl, a history of past outbreaks, or high use by migratory birds 1,3,4 . ▪ Be aware of indicators of an avian cholera outbreak (e.g., large numbers of dead waterfowl in a short time). Sick birds may not be observed because death is often rapid. If sick birds are observed, they may show the following signs: convulsions, erratic flight or swimming patterns, lethargy, and/or mortality shortly after handling 1,3,4 .

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ The long-term consequences of avian cholera outbreaks on wild bird populations are not well understood. ▪ Research on the impacts of temperature and water quality on the survival of P. multocida could identify risk factors and control strategies that could be used on specific wetlands.

div.head: Background
div.p: Botulism is a fatal non-infectious disease affecting warm-blooded animals and some fish species. It is caused by intoxication with neurotoxins produced by Clostridium botulinum bacteria 1 , which are widespread in the environment. Intoxication may occur through ingestion of decaying tissue contaminated with the botulinum toxin or the bacteria, or through consumption of invertebrates that have fed on contaminated tissue (i.e., maggots concentrate toxin within their bodies after feeding on affected carcasses) 5,6 . Animals may also develop disease via a wound contaminated by the bacteria 5,6 . Toxin accumulation in affected individuals leads to paralysis and death. There are multiple toxin strains produced by C. botulinum, with Types C and E most often associated with wildlife mortalities, particularly in waterfowl and other aquatic wildlife 6 . Optimal conditions for the growth of C. botulinum include warm temperatures, low oxygen levels, and high levels of organic materials (e.g., decaying animal carcasses); however, outbreaks may still occur without these conditions being present 1,5 . Increases in pesticides and other agricultural pollutants, wetland flooding and draining, and anoxia of the wetland bottom that lead to increased wildlife mortality can promote C. botulinum growth and toxin production in the environment 1,3,5,6 . Due to the various routes of exposure, a few mortalities due to botulism can rapidly amplify into large-scale die-offs involving hundreds to thousands of birds 7 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Botulism type C outbreaks are responsible for mass mortality events in wild birds, usually waterfowl species, and have caused hundreds of thousands of deaths in a single event 5,6 .
Migrating birds are most susceptible, and large die-offs are most likely to occur in sensitive species with smaller population sizes 2,5,6 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ More than a dozen outbreaks of botulism have been recorded in Montana since 2000, including in Sheridan, Phillips, Yellowstone, Musselshell, Cascade, and Teton counties. Over 100 outbreaks have been recorded since 2000 in neighboring states and Canadian provinces 2,3,6 . ▪ Outbreaks in the early 2000s in Montana killed thousands of ducks, pelicans, and gulls, and a more recent outbreak in 2019 caused die-offs in ducks and shorebirds 8 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Higher temperatures (77 to 104 degrees F; 25 to 40 degrees C) and longer warm seasons provide optimal conditions for C. botulinum growth. Drought can also lead to warm, stagnant water and die-offs in aquatic life, which increase the likelihood of an outbreak 9 .

During drought years, birds are likely to concentrate at remaining wetlands in higher numbers, putting a greater number at risk. Botulism risk is likely to increase in the coming decades with warmer temperatures and more frequent drought conditions.

div.head: Conservation Actions
div.p: Prevention ▪ Consider removal of carcasses from large die-offs of aquatic animals (e.g., fish kills) to limit proliferation of C. botulinum, especially if area is highly trafficked by water birds and other wildlife. Carcass removal is the most effective means for preventing the expansion of outbreaks 1 . ▪ Mitigate or avoid abrupt changes in water levels from factors like drought or water management 3,9 . ▪ Maintain water quality by limiting pesticide and agricultural pollution 3,9 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: ▪ In high priority habitats, survey outbreak sites regularly to remove carcasses. Consider the use of cadaver dogs to improve efficiency of carcass removal 1,6 . ▪ In some limited cases (such as highly imperiled populations), consider clinical treatment for intoxicated individuals through the use of botulinum antitoxin 6 , but be aware that this option is not widely available due to the limited availability and high cost of botulinum antitoxin. ▪ Consider using deterrents to temporarily discourage wildlife visitation to affected wetlands 1,6 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: ▪ Control the spread of aquatic invasive species (e.g., zebra mussels) that may play a role in botulism outbreaks 3,9 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: ▪ Conduct routine surveillance at sites with known history of outbreaks and which are important habitat for imperiled populations. ▪ Be aware of signs of a botulism outbreak, including multiple animal carcasses and animals with paralysis or limited movements in close proximity to a water source 1,6 .

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ Information on botulism's impacts on fish populations is limited 9 . ▪ Invasive species (e.g., zebra mussel, round goby) play a role in botulism transmission in the Great Lakes 9 , but the effects of invasive species on botulism in Montana are not known. ▪ The long-term effects of botulism outbreaks on bird populations are poorly understood 1,6 .

div.head: Canine Distemper
div.p: SGCN with Known Impacts 1

div.head: Drivers
div.p: Black-footed Ferret -Seasonality and temperature 5 -Age and previous exposure 4 -Spatial connectivity and contact rates among carnivore populations 3,4 -Unvaccinated domestic animals (e.g., dogs, ferrets) in proximity to wildlife 3,4 SGCN Susceptible to Infection 1 Grizzly Bear Swift Fox Canada Lynx Fisher Wolverine Other Susceptible Montana Species [1][2][3][4] Most carnivores (including cougars, bears, foxes, coyotes, raccoons, skunks, and weasels) can be infected with CDV.

div.head: Background
div.p: Canine distemper virus (CDV) is an RNA virus in the family Paramyxoviridae (Canine morbillivirus) that causes the disease canine distemper. Despite the name, CDV infects a wide range of carnivores besides canids, including cougars, bears, racoons, and members of the weasel family. The virus is highly contagious and is primarily spread through contact with respiratory particles or bodily fluids (i.e., urine, feces, secretions) 2 . It does not survive long in the environment, although cold temperatures can allow the virus to remain viable for up to a few days 2,3 . Clinical signs include discharge from the eyes and nose, difficulty breathing, pneumonia, fever, and a neurological phase that can result in seizures, wandering, and aggressiveness 3,5 . Some species, especially mustelids, experience high mortality rates (50 to 100 percent) and in most species, juveniles are more susceptible to severe disease than adults 5 . Outbreaks of CDV are often seasonal and in wildlife typically occur during spring and summer due to increases in susceptible (i.e., juvenile) individuals 5 .

In urban settings, outbreaks may also occur during winter when the virus persists longer in the environment and when individuals are breeding and in close contact 5 . Due to its high mortality rate, low environmental persistence, and the fact that survivors experience longlasting immunity, CDV generally fades out in small, isolated populations. In wildlife systems of the western U.S., maintenance of the virus likely requires the presence of multiple, interconnected populations and transmission between several carnivore species 4,6 . In particular, raccoons and coyotes appear to play an important role in maintaining CDV and transmitting it to other wildlife species 4,6 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Mustelids, including black-footed ferrets, often experience high rates of mortality from CDV, in some cases up to 100 percent 7,8 . CDV likely contributed to the near-extinction of the black-footed ferret, and vaccination is now an important part of the recovery strategy for this species 7 . Periodic outbreaks of CDV in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem have caused significant mortality in gray wolves, particularly pups 6,9,10 , but the disease has not threatened overall recovery. Similarly, CDV has caused mortalities in swift foxes in Wyoming, but longer-term population-level impacts have not been observed 11 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ CDV has a near-global distribution and a wide host range, and it is not uncommon in Montana wildlife, particularly among raccoons, coyotes, and skunks 12,13 . ▪ In Montana, cases are most frequently observed in spring and early summer when there is an increase in young, highly susceptible animals (J. Ramsey, Montana Fish, Wildlife, & Parks, pers. comm.). ▪ CDV appears relatively common within carnivores of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem (GYE). For instance, a recent study found that 30 to 60 percent of wolves and 30 to 40 percent of grizzly bears in the GYE were exposed to CDV 14 . Outbreaks have typically occurred every two to five years.

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Climate variability does not appear to play a strong role in CDV dynamics in the western United States, although links between CDV mortality and temperature have been detected in other countries 15 . Warmer winter temperatures could, in theory, reduce transmission by facilitating faster viral inactivation. Climatic shifts could also alter movements, population connectivity, and contact rates among carnivores in ways that change CDV transmission patterns.

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Continue to encourage vaccination of domestic dogs to reduce the reservoir of CDV and risk to wildlife 2 .

• Be aware that most CDV vaccines are not designed for wildlife and that some species may experience harmful effects from available CDV vaccines 3 . Consider the use of vaccines in highly imperiled populations for which approved, effective vaccines exist (e.g., black-footed ferrets are commonly vaccinated during reintroductions) 2,3 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • Evaluate the need for control of reservoir hosts (e.g., coyotes and raccoons) in cases where they may spread disease to vulnerable populations 2,3 .
• If feasible, consider removing infected carcasses to reduce transmission risk during outbreaks 5 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Continue to improve the population size of threatened species to improve their ability to withstand periodic CDV outbreaks 6 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Encourage the public to report unusual behavior in wildlife, which can be a sign of CDV or other viruses, like rabies.

• Continue passive surveillance efforts for CDV through morbidity/mortality investigations and opportunistic serologic testing during captures (Jennifer Ramsey, Montana Fish, Wildlife, & Parks, pers. comm.).

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ The distribution and impacts of CDV in vulnerable SGCN like swift foxes, lynx, and wolverine is not well known. ▪ Understanding contact rates and connectivity between vulnerable populations and reservoirs can help identify risk factors and potential targets for management.

div.head: Literature Cited
div.p: Iridoviruses SGCN with Known Impacts -Water temperature and quality 2,3 -Seasonality and life-stage 3 -Presence of reservoir species 3,4 *Potential concern as a reservoir species

div.head: Background
div.p: Iridoviruses are a broad family of viruses primarily affecting cold-blooded species including amphibians, fish, and reptiles 1 . The family includes several species of Ranavirus (e.g., Frog Virus 3 [FV3], Ambystoma tigrinum virus [ATV], largemouth bass virus) as well as related viruses that cause fish diseases like White Sturgeon iridoviral disease (WSIV) and Missouri River sturgeon iridovirus (MRSIV). Infection typically occurs through exposure to viral particles in water, ingestion of infected tissues, or direct contact. Some Iridoviruses appear to be specialists, while others (e.g., FV3) may be transmitted across a wide range of hosts, including between fish and amphibians 1 . Generally, loss of organ function related to hemorrhage and necrosis is the most common cause of death and may be preceded by signs like irregular swimming behavior, redness of limbs or vent, lethargy, lesions on the body, skin hemorrhaging, inappetence, and edema (swelling) 5 . Viruses can survive in water for weeks, and potentially months. In amphibians, ranaviruses can cause sporadic, shortlived, and intense outbreaks, which may intensify over a period of just a few days 6 .

Mortalities typically occur during summer, primarily affecting larvae or recently metamorphosed individuals 3,5 . There is some evidence that outbreaks are more likely in areas with high human influence, such as suburban or cattle ponds 3,7 ; however, surveillance in wild populations is rare and thus the true distribution of ranavirus in remote populations is not well characterized.

MRSIV (a related Iridovirus) is of particular concern for efforts to recover the pallid sturgeon via hatchery breeding. Outbreaks at hatcheries in Montana have killed up to 60 to 100 percent of juvenile pallid sturgeon or shovelnose sturgeon 8 . Survivors of outbreaks may become carriers, continuing to transmit the virus without showing clinical signs. Transmission occurs through exposure to infected tissues (e.g., in water or in feed) or cohabitation with infected fish. Vertical transmission may also be possible. It is presumed that wild fish harbor the pathogen and, when it is introduced to the hatchery environment, large outbreaks are possible 8 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Although Iridoviruses can affect a wide range of fish, amphibian, and reptile species, impacts are of particular concern in hatchery-raised fish and in amphibians that are already rare and exhibit aggregation behavior in waterbodies 3 . Outbreaks of ranaviruses in wild amphibian populations have caused large mortality events, with mortality rates reaching 100 percent in some affected populations. But while the virus can strongly reduce abundances in the short term, to date, ranaviruses have not been associated with longterm population declines in North American amphibians 3 . In fish, outbreaks of Iridoviruses can drastically reduce hatchery survival rates (up to 100 percent mortality) and can threaten the success of recovery programs relying upon stocking efforts, such as those for pallid sturgeon 9 . Generally, the impacts of Iridovirus outbreaks in wild fish populations are not well-known, but in some populations, evidence of potential immunity and populations rebounding is emerging 10 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Few ranavirus outbreaks have been reported in Montana; however, two separate outbreaks in 2001 were associated with large die-offs of western toads (Ravalli County; 1000 reported dead) and Columbia spotted frogs (Gallatin County; 30 reported dead) 11 .

A die-off of tiger salamanders in the Powder River Basin in 2008-2009 appears to be driven by a ranavirus (ATV) outbreak. ▪ Surveys of the Prairie Pothole Region in 2017 found low occurrence of ranavirus in amphibian larvae and waterbodies 12 , whereas amphibian monitoring projects in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem indicated multiple mortality events from 2000 to 2014 occurring over a wide distribution 13 .
• Select appropriate tissue samples (e.g., internal organs, fin clips, etc.) for surveillance, in accordance with study goals and species 2 .

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ The host range of many Iridoviruses is unknown. Therefore, which of Montana's SGCN are potentially affected is difficult to characterize. ▪ Effects of Iridoviruses in free-ranging fish populations are poorly understood. ▪ Research suggests that water temperature can impact Iridovirus transmission and pathology, but questions remain about whether temperature modifications can effectively be used for treatment, or how temperature-disease relationships vary among Iridovirus strains or hosts 2 .

div.head: Literature Cited
div.p: and northern leopard frog are the most susceptible to Bd, demonstrated by significant historical population declines in the Rocky Mountain region [17][18][19][20] . The northern leopard frog suffered severe population declines that effectively extirpated it from its former range in western Montana 1 . However, in Montana and across much of North America, evidence exists that Bd may be functioning as an endemic disease with host-pathogen coexistence 4,17 . The dynamics and distribution of this disease are complex and appear to be highly influenced by the community structure of host species and environmental factors 21,22 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Bd has been found in the northeast and western parts of the state; however, there is little published surveillance data from eastern Montana. Bd has been detected in Montana's western toads, Idaho giant salamanders, tiger salamanders, long-toed salamanders, northern leopard frogs, and Columbia spotted frogs 21,22 . ▪ Western toad populations in Montana have historically experienced moderate to high prevalence of Bd with evidence of population decline in some regions 1,17,18 . ▪ The Columbia spotted frog, which appears tolerant to infection with Bd, likely serves as an important reservoir species 1 . ▪ While Bd has been present in Montana amphibian populations for about 40 years, current evidence indicates that there are no further declines in northern leopard frog and western toad populations (B. Maxell, Montana Natural Heritage Program, pers. comm.). However, there may be sporadic individual mortalities, and the long-term impacts to overall species fitness are still under investigation.

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Generally, Bd favors cool, moist environments, and laboratory experiments indicate the fungus does not tolerate temperatures above 80 degrees F (27 degrees C) or below 50 degrees F (10 degrees C) 23 . However, increasing climate variability and extreme weather events could impact amphibian immunity and alter habitat and community structures that favor pathogen survival and pathogenicity [24][25][26] . Factors such as snowpack and timing of precipitation have demonstrated a strong influence over amphibian population health. In years where snowpack is low and Bd is present in the environment, amphibian survival is significantly reduced 27 .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Establish standard biosecurity measures (i.e., disinfection protocols) for work and recreation in wetlands and aquatic habitats [28][29][30] .
• Restrict or minimize human activity around sensitive habitats [28][29][30] .

div.head: Whirling Disease SGCN with Known Impacts
Drivers
div.p: To date, significant impacts on SGCN have not been reported.
-Stream/river morphology and flow rate 1 -Habitat suitability for T. tubifex (requires fine sediment, low flows)

div.head: Background
div.p: Whirling disease (WD) is a disease of certain salmonid fish species caused by the parasite Myxobolus cerebralis. It is associated with severe population declines and outbreaks in rainbow trout throughout the Intermountain West. The parasite targets and consumes cartilage tissue in fish, resulting in neurologic impairments and skeletal deformities typically characterized by a crooked, blackened tail and deformed head 3 . Severe disease is more likely to occur in fish with higher parasite loads, in younger fish, and in more vulnerable species 3 . In Montana, rainbow trout and cutthroat trout are the most vulnerable to severe disease 2 .

The life cycle of M. cerebralis is complex, requiring both a salmonid fish host and an aquatic, bottom-dwelling worm, Tubifex tubifex. Fish become infected by spores released from the Tubifex worm, which penetrate the skin and migrate to preferred tissues (cartilage) within the fish host. Infection risk is tied closely with environmental suitability for the release of spores from T. tubifex, which can vary widely across watersheds and may depend on the strain of T. tubifex present. Generally, however, water temperatures above 40 degrees F are optimal for parasite development and spore release, leading to peak infectivity in spring and fall for most areas 1 . Spatial spread of M. cerebralis may be facilitated by human-mediated transport, stocking, and digested spores in the fecal matter of fish-eating birds 4 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: In Montana and surrounding states (Wyoming, Idaho, Utah, Colorado), whirling disease has been identified as the primary agent of population declines in many wild rainbow trout populations 3 . In addition, it has been documented as a significant threat to cutthroat trout conservation efforts in Colorado and Yellowstone National Park [5][6][7] . The disease was first identified in Montana in 1994 following a severe population decline (>90 percent) in rainbow trout in the Madison River 8 . Although M. cerebralis has the potential to drive population-level impacts [9][10][11] and has been present for many decades, impacts from disease are variable and appear to be site-specific. Impacts are largely based on factors influencing habitat suitability for T. tubifex, environmental conditions for parasite development (i.e., water temperature), fish species composition, immunity, and timing of spawning 9 . In addition, in areas with historical impacts of disease, fish populations appear to have developed resistance to whirling disease through natural selection 12 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Following the Madison River outbreak in 1994, intensive statewide monitoring revealed that the pathogen was widespread throughout western Montana, with disease present at varying levels of severity 10 . ▪ There is a lack of recently published data on current distribution of whirling disease in Montana, but based on the pathogen's relationship with its hosts and environment, it still appears widespread throughout Montana waters (K. Staigmiller, Montana Fish, Wildlife, & Parks, pers. comm.).

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Water temperature is a key factor in controlling the life cycle and release of M. cerebralis spores and also influences the growth and abundance of T. tubifex 13 . Warming temperatures speed the parasite's development, resulting in increased release of spores from worms 3 . The Tubifex worm also favors habitat consisting of fine sediment and low water flow, both of which can increase in the event of excessive erosion and/or human disturbance 14,15 . Under the influence of climate warming, these factors may be exacerbated and increase the risk of whirling disease and compromise overall fish health.

div.head: Background
div.p: Avian trematodiasis is caused by infection with parasitic flatworms known as trematodes. While many trematode species can infect birds, most cause only mild or subclinical disease and only occasionally result in mortality. However, several species-Cyathocoytle bushiensis, Sphaeridiotrema globulus, Sphaeridiotrema pseudoglobulus, and Leyogonimus polyoon-are associated with recurrent, large-scale mortality events in waterfowl during spring and fall migrations 1 . Birds become parasitized by eating infected faucet snails (Bithynia tentaculata; also known as the mud bithynia), an invasive mollusk that harbors the parasite. The snail (and thus the occurrence of the disease) is typically found in freshwater ponds and shallow areas (<6 m) of lakes 3 . Major outbreaks of trematodiasis in avian populations are driven by a combination of infected snail abundance, waterfowl density and species composition, avian host status (i.e., nutrition, age, exposure), and favorable environmental conditions for both the parasite and snail hosts 4 . Infection of birds with pathogenic trematode species leads to severe intestinal disease (e.g., inflammation, bleeding) and disruption of nutritional absorption 2 . Depending on the concentration of parasites within snails that are consumed, birds may ingest a lethal dose in as little as a few hours to several days, succumbing to trematode-associated disease within three to eight days 1 . Due to the rapid onset of disease, signs preceding mass mortality events are rarely observed, but may include an inability to fly or dive, emaciation, diarrhea, and bloodstaining around the vent 4 . Survivors appear to develop some resistance to future infections but can further the parasites' life cycle and spread the disease to other waterbodies 5 . C. bushienesis and Sphaeridiotrema spp. are the trematode parasites of greatest concern to Montana bird populations.

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Pathogenic trematode species have been associated with repeated, seasonal, large-scale die-offs of North American waterfowl over the last 40 years (or more) 3,5 . Outbreaks have caused losses of hundreds to thousands of birds at a time and have triggered population declines of some species in certain areas (e.g., 40 percent decline in scaup in Wisconsin in 2006) 2 . The geographical distribution of outbreaks overlaps closely with the distribution of the invasive faucet snail, which is well-established in Montana and much of the midwestern and northeastern United States 6 . Lesser and greater scaup and American coot are the avian species most frequently impacted; however, other water birds (e.g., diving ducks, swans) may also be affected 7 . It remains unclear why infection has a disproportionate impact on certain waterfowl species. Yet, while trematode infections may not lead to direct mortality in more resistant avian species, chronic parasitism can serve as a contributing factor for ill health and increased susceptibility to other diseases. Overall, this disease represents an additional stressor for already declining waterbird populations.

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Episodic outbreaks in Montana involving C. bushiensis and Sphaeridiotrema spp. have been reported since 1988, occurring (on average) every few years in spring and fall months 8,9 . Events involve hundreds to thousands of bird fatalities, with common species including American coot, lesser scaup, northern pintail, mallard, green-winged teal, American wigeon, northern shoveler, ring-necked duck, canvasback, gadwall, redhead, etc. Recent events have occurred in Flathead, Yellowstone, and Granite counties, including locations mentioned below where faucet snails have been identified 8 . ▪ The invasive faucet snail has been identified in multiple regions across Montana (primarily in the western half) with recently confirmed locations including Blanchard Lake, Georgetown Lake, McWenneger Slough, Smith lake, Upsata Lake, Rattlesnake Reservoir, and Whitefish Lake 10,11 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Bacterial Kidney Disease SGCN with Known Impacts

div.head: Background
div.p: Bacterial Kidney Disease (BKD) is a disease of salmonid fish caused by the bacterium Renibacterium salmoninarum. BKD is a systemic infection that can lead to high rates of mortality in affected populations (e.g., >80 percent) 1 . The clinical signs of BKD are quite variable and include lethargy, skin darkening, blood-filled blisters, skin ulcers, bulging eyes, hemorrhaging around vent, and unusual swimming behavior 1,2 . Internally, BKD leads to chronic inflammation and swelling in the kidneys and lesions on internal organs. However, some fish may be infected without displaying any outward signs, which complicates the detection of BKD. The pathogen is transmitted horizontally through contaminated water and contact among individuals, as well as vertically, in which bacteria are passed directly from an infected female to her eggs 3 . The bacterium can persist in sediment and fish feces for several weeks. All salmonids are considered susceptible to infection by R. salmoninarum; however, not all species experience severe disease.

div.head: Impacts
div.p: It can take many months for disease signs to appear after R. salmoninarum is introduced into a population. Infected fish can carry the pathogen and continue to transmit it for life. For those reasons, BKD is often associated with slow, prolonged declines over a long time period. BKD has been detected in both farmed and wild fish, and while R. salmoninarum bacteria are likely widespread within inland trout populations, it is not considered a major threat to most inland wild fish populations, and most populations do not appear to be strongly impacted by the disease 4 . Population-level impacts in wild populations have mostly been observed in Chinook salmon and other Pacific salmon 1 . Thus, the primary relevance of BKD to Montana fish conservation is the introduction of the bacteria into hatchery populations and the potential impact on captive rearing of endangered salmonids 1 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ The pathogen R. salmoninarum has been detected in both wild and hatchery fish in Montana. While testing is common within hatcheries, the extent of the pathogen in wild populations is not known [5][6][7] . However, BKD does not appear to be associated with significant impacts to wild fish in the state. ▪ BKD has been detected in wild trout in nearby states, including Wyoming (Yellowstone National Park and southeastern Wyoming) [8][9][10] . An outbreak affecting wild brook trout in Wyoming was tied to a stocking event 11 . A recent study in Colorado reported the pathogen in all 68 of the streams tested and suggested the distribution is widespread 4 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: BKD appears highly sensitive to temperature; therefore, future climate variability and change could alter the timing and severity of BKD outbreaks. Outbreaks of BKD tend to occur after peaks in water temperature, and mortality rates increase with warmer temperatures 1,13,14 . However, other studies suggest that warming temperatures, particularly beyond 59 degrees F (15 degrees C), will lead to declines in BKD 15 . For fish, warmer temperatures may have a mixed effect. In certain species it may enhance immune response and increase disease resistance 12 , while in others (e.g., cold water-adapted salmonids), it can lead to increased stress and immune suppression. Future climatic shifts may reduce stream flow, the size of pools, and water quality; these factors have been linked to increased outbreak severity 11 .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Continue to test brood fish coming into the hatchery system to prevent introduction of BKD 1 .
• Continue to test fish prior to movement and/or stocking to prevent release of fish from BKD-infected hatcheries 1 .
• Educate the public on BKD and the risk of spread from fish movements.
• Explore opportunities to invest and support hatchery infrastructure to protect the integrity of the water supply for hatcheries raising conservation broodstock 1 .

div.head: Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease
div.p: SGCN with Known Impacts 1

div.head: Drivers
div.p: Pygmy Rabbit -Human-mediated transmission; domestic rabbit and rabbit product trade 2
-Periods of increased activity/commingling (e.g., host breeding or rearing season) 3 -Environmental persistence of pathogen 3,4 -Presence of vectors (e.g., insects, birds, predators) 3

div.head: SGCN Susceptible to Infection
div.p: To date, no additional SGCN confirmed as susceptible Other Susceptible Montana Species

div.head: Background
div.p: Rabbit hemorrhagic disease (RHD) is a highly contagious viral disease affecting rabbits and hares.
