"Classical" rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus (RHDV) and a recently emerged strain (RHDV2) are the primary causative agents of RHD and can be found in almost all parts of the world. However, due to its recent impacts on native wildlife, RHDV2 is the variant of highest concern to North America 3 . In comparison to RHDV, RHDV2 has a broader host range (capable of infecting both rabbits and hares versus RHDV, which affects only European rabbits), can infect animals of almost any age, and can readily infect and cause mortality in rabbits previously exposed to RHDV (i.e., lack of cross-protective immunity) 4 . In wildlife, signs of disease are rarely observed as death tends to occur within several days following infection 5 . In some cases, blood may be observed around the nose or mouth and eyes can appear reddened 6 . Individuals that survive infection are likely to become chronic carriers, capable of shedding the virus into the environment for several months or longer 1 .

Major factors for RHD's spread are that viral agents are highly resistant to environmental conditions and can easily be spread via direct contact with infected hosts, carcasses or meat, bodily fluids, or contact with contaminated surfaces 7 . Insects, birds, predators, or humans can also serve as mechanical vectors of disease, meaning that they can incidentally move infectious virus particles around when they come into contact, leading to geographical expansion of disease 8 . In wild populations, seasonal variation in outbreaks appears to be tied to periods of increased rabbit activity, with spring (breeding season) being the peak period for observed mortality in North America (though mortalities have been observed in all months) 3 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Both short-term and long-term population declines due to RHD have been observed in rabbit populations around the world, with spread of the disease being primarily facilitated by human activities (e.g., transport of live rabbits and rabbit products) 3 . RHDV2 first emerged in North America in feral domestic rabbits in 2016, after which it occurred sporadically over the next several years as small, localized outbreaks 1 . A major outbreak occurring in the southwestern U.S. in 2020 marked the first time that natural infection was observed in native North American species 9 . Since then, RHDV2 has spread across 14 states and is now considered endemic throughout the west. Challenges in surveillance have made it difficult to estimate the impact of these outbreaks on wild populations in the U.S. Studies have indicated that mortality rates from RHDV2 infection are more variable (50 to 80 percent 5 ) than RHDV (70 to 100 percent 2 ). While reduced mortality from RHDV2 may limit risk of extirpation, it increases the likelihood for rabbits to become carriers and further spread disease. Today, detections of RHDV2 are sporadic. It is difficult to determine if this is attributed to a reduced incidence in wildlife, effective management strategies (e.g., vaccination in domestics and decreased spillover), challenges in monitoring, or a combination thereof. Nonetheless, special concern exists for the impact of RHDV2 on imperiled species, such as the pygmy rabbit, which has a restricted range and is highly susceptible to RHD, with evidence of a possible disease-associated decline occurring in Nevada in 2022 10 . A final consideration is the bottom-up effect that may occur on predator communities following a major decline in a key group of prey species, should a severe outbreak occur 11 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ The most recent report of RHD in Montana occurred in a domestic rabbit in fall of 2024 in Lewis and Clark County 12 . ▪ In free-ranging rabbits, the most recent report occurred in Musselshell County in summer 2023 (species unidentified). Several cases were reported in Yellowstone County (feral domestic rabbits and mountain cottontails) and in or around Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming (unidentified cottontail) in spring of 2021 13 , as well as Big Horn, Stillwater, Musselshell, Fallon, and Gallatin counties in recent years 14 . The extent of RHD in wild populations during these events is unknown.

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: RHD viruses are very environmentally durable, capable of resisting desiccation, heat, and freeze/thaw cycles 7,15 . Therefore, they may be relatively resistant to the effects of climate variability. Both the impact and the number of outbreaks of RHD tend to be higher in of dead animals, since sick animals are rarely observed due to the rapid course of the disease (death usually occurring within 2 to 10 days post-infection).

Francisella tularensis is found in both terrestrial and aquatic environments. Rabbits, hares, and small ground rodents are particularly susceptible to infection and are important for persistence and amplification of F. tularensis in terrestrial ecosystems, whereas beavers, muskrats, and voles may become infected and amplify F. tularensis in aquatic environments [1][2][3] . In susceptible species, it requires very few bacteria to cause disease. This, in combination with the multitude of transmission pathways, wide host range, and environmental persistence, makes tularemia a highly adaptive and ecologically complex disease.

div.head: Impacts
div.p: While F. tularensis is known as one of the most infectious pathogens to vertebrates, reports of long-lasting population-level impacts or declines in wildlife are uncommon. Mass mortality events are occasionally observed in aquatic rodent populations (e.g., beavers and muskrats) and susceptible terrestrial rodent and lagomorph populations, but typically disease fatalities occur sporadically 4,5 . However, cases in humans have trended upward over the last 20 years 3,6 , leading to concern about the potential for expansion and increasing impacts on wildlife populations. Moreover, the impacts of tularemia on beavers in particular are a concern due to their important roles as ecosystem engineers and because of the widespread desire to restore beavers within Montana. Impacts on beavers could therefore create indirect effects on a variety of SGCN that use beaver habitat. Generally, the disease threat can be variable, context-dependent, and prone to change over time, depending on shifts in environmental conditions, host abundance, community structure, and human activity.

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Recent reports have found tularemia-associated mortalities in mountain cottontail rabbits (2024, 2020) and beavers (2024) in Lewis and Clark County (Montana Fish, Wildlife, & Parks, unpublished data), and tularemia is suspected to have caused mortalities in desert cottontail rabbits and deer mice in Phillips County (2015) 7 . ▪ Mortalities in beavers continue to be documented within the state 8,9 , including relatively large die-offs in the upper Madison River and upper Gallatin River drainages in 2016 and 2017. Tularemia is suspected to have contributed to beaver die-offs in the Centennial Valley and Ruby Valley around the same period. ▪ Past serologic studies occurring in Greater Yellowstone Area have shown a 21 percent prevalence of antibodies against F. tularensis in coyotes 10 , but no antibodies were observed in snowshoe hares 11 . ▪ Outbreaks have occurred in domestic sheep herds (which frequently share habitat with wildlife) in Montana following severe winters and heavy tick infestations 12 .

had severe impacts on wild fish populations in the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes regions and both wild and farm-raised fish (typically marine species) along the Pacific Coast. Fish become infected via contact with waterborne virus, direct contact with other infected fish or fish excretions (urine, reproductive fluids), or by consuming infected individuals 3 . Outbreaks typically occur in spring when water temperatures are still cold and within the virus's optimal range. Clinical signs include reddened areas (hemorrhages) around the eyes, gills, base of fins, or other areas of the body, bulging eyes, swollen abdomens, darkening of the skin, and abnormal swimming behavior. Infection severity and mortality rates tend to be higher in juvenile fish but can occur in any age 5 . Environmental persistence of VHSV is mediated through reservoir hosts (susceptible fish) and incidental hosts such as freshwater turtles, microcrustaceans (amphipods), and leeches 5 . Additionally, fish that survive the disease may continue to shed the virus for long periods of time (15 weeks or more), especially following stressful events 8 . Fish-eating birds may also serve as mechanical vectors for introducing VHSV into new areas 9 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: VHSV is associated with severe disease outbreaks in both wild and farmed fish, with up to 100 percent mortality in some cases 9 . One particular strain of VHSV (the IVb strain) has caused multiple large die-offs in wild, freshwater fish (including freshwater drum, round goby, and yellow perch-species all present in Montana) in the Great Lakes region since it was first detected in 2005 4 . Since that time, it has been detected in inland waters throughout the Midwest and mid-Atlantic regions 9 . Current evidence suggests that VHSV outbreaks in North America are sporadic, with prevalence and environmental persistence appearing to wax and wane over a period of several years 5 . Mass mortality events are typically reported in common, relatively abundant species without evidence of sustained population declines. However, potential impacts to hatcheries and farm-raised fish are a concern. To date, VHSV has not been detected in Montana, but it remains a potential threat. Montana fish belonging to the orders Salmoniformes, Perciformes, and Cypriniformes should be considered most susceptible 1 , yet the wide host range and difference in susceptibility between species makes predicting potential impact for Montana species difficult. Introduction of the virus would most likely occur via humanmediated transmission (e.g., transport of contaminated water, gear, or infected fish) 10 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ VHSV is routinely tested for in Montana hatcheries and wild fish populations but, to date, has yet to be detected.

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Survival and infectiousness of VHSV is heavily influenced by water temperature. Disease due to VHSV can be observed in water temperatures ranging between 34 to 64 degrees F (1 to 18 degrees C) 9 . It can survive outside the host for up to 14 days in ideal conditions, but it is highly susceptible to heat and desiccation 8 . Warming temperatures or increases in drought conditions may reduce viral spread. However, stressful events or changes to aquatic habitats that lead to crowding and fish seeking deeper, cooler waters may result in disease outbreaks. Therefore, it remains unclear to what degree climate variability may influence VHSV risk.

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Implement and promote regulations on import of live fish or fish products from affected areas and maintain strict adherence to aquatic invasive species prevention guidelines 6 .
• Clearly communicate with anglers about the risk of VHSV spread from activities like baitfish transport and release and using contaminated boats and gear 6 .
• Develop response and management plan in the event of an outbreak 11 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • If severe outbreaks occur, consider manipulations to increase water temperature or draining and drying out of affected sites to eliminate virus 6,11 .

In environments where it is feasible (e.g., on equipment, in case of transport, or in hatchery environment), use disinfectants and UV light to inactivate the virus and treat water or contaminated surfaces 2 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Reduce stressors (e.g., regulating fishing access, conserve/restore habitat, mitigate pollutants, etc.) to promote healthy, robust fish populations 3,11 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Monitor for mortality events and provide training to public to watch for signs of disease 11 .
• Continue routine surveillance efforts for VHSV in both wild fish and hatchery fish in Montana.

div.head: Background
div.p: Salamander chytrid disease, or salamander chytridiomycosis, is an emerging infectious disease caused by the fungal pathogen, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal). The disease has severely impacted certain species in Europe, but as of 2025, Bsal has not been detected in North America. Similar to B. dendrobatidis (Bd) in anurans (frogs and toads), Bsal invades the host's skin, leading to reddened or ulcerated lesions, increased shedding, and thickening 2 . Other clinical signs associated with infection include lethargy, anorexia, and abnormal movement or posturing prior to death 2 . Highly susceptible individuals typically succumb to infection within two to three weeks following exposure 3 . Transmission occurs through contact with fungal spores in the water, contact with contaminated surfaces (moist substrates, leaf litter, etc.), or direct contact with infected amphibians. Infective Bsal spores have also shown the ability to adhere to the feet of waterfowl, potentially facilitating widespread dispersal 4 . Understanding what species are susceptible to salamander chytridiomycosis remains ongoing, but disease appears most severe in adult salamanders in the families Salamandridae and Plethodontidae 4,5 . Some members of the Salamandridae family (e.g., newts) and certain anurans appear susceptible to infection with Bsal with or without clinical signs, indicating potential disease reservoirs 2,6 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: First discovered in the Netherlands in 2010, Bsal is associated with mass mortalities and extirpation of the European fire salamander and other native European populations 7 .

Populations have struggled to recover due to the sustained and disproportionate mortality observed in adults 4 . So far, eight species have been detected as infected in the wild in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, and Spain 5 , but experimental trials indicate many more species are susceptible to infection 5 . A laboratory study on North American amphibians revealed that Bsal caused infection in 25 (consisting of both salamanders and frogs) of the 35 species exposed to the pathogen, with eight of those species experiencing moderate to very high mortality 1 . Montana's salamander SGCN were not included in this study; however, the Coeur d'Alene Salamander (Plethodon idahoensis) belongs to a family (Plethodontidae) in which researchers saw moderate to high mortality in tested species 1 .

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Bsal has not been detected in North America as of 2025 8 . ▪ A geographic risk analysis for Bsal suggests that invasion risk potential is highest in the Northwest region of the U.S., posing a threat to Montana's amphibian species 1 .

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: In culture, Bsal favors 50 to 60 degrees F (10 to 15 degrees C), but it has been detected on salamanders in water temperatures over 78 degrees F in the wild 9 . Infective spores have also been shown to survive and remain infective in filtered pond water for over 30 days 2 . As a fungal pathogen, Bsal is likely to be highly influenced by environmental conditions; however, the precise impacts of future climatic changes on Bsal distribution and pathogenicity are not currently known.

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Establish standard biosecurity protocol for work in wetlands and aquatic habitats (see Disinfection Protocols for Herpetofaunal Pathogens) 9,10 .

• Reduce the risk of spillover from captive to wild amphibians by supporting regulations on the import of certain high-risk species (Asian or European-origin amphibians) and the use of salamanders as bait 10 .

• Create a communication plan that includes messages on the importance and value of amphibians, the risks Bsal poses, and how target audiences (researchers, captive amphibian owners/breeders, hikers, etc.) can prevent introduction and spread of Bsal 10 .
• Restrict or minimize human activity around high-priority or sensitive habitats 9,10 .
• Consider proactive management actions prior to Bsal invasion, such as connectivity reduction, habitat modification, and water treatments [9][10][11] .

▪ Only a few reports have evaluated Oo's presence in snakes in the western U.S. Of these, a survey on military lands identified infection in only a single individual (western milksnake in Idaho), which was asymptomatic for SFD 5 . A second report diagnosed SFD in a California kingsnake in California 14 . ▪ There are no known published reports evaluating the presence of Oo in Montana as of 2025.

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Oo can grow in a wide temperature range 15 . However, cool, moist environments are most likely to promote fungal growth and persistence in the environment. Prevalence and evidence of clinical disease in snakes have been linked to emergence from overwintering [3][4][5][6] . Temperature increases during hibernation or increases in hot, dry weather patterns could drive snakes to spend more time underground. This might increase optimal Oo growth conditions, alter snake immunity, or increase contact rates among snakes, leading to heightened prevalence and worsened disease outcomes 3,[15][16][17] .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Employ strict disinfection protocols when using invasive marking techniques (e.g., radiotelemetry devices, scale clipping, cauterization, etc.), especially in areas where SFD is present 5,18 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • For species of concern, capture and treatment programs may be considered for SFDaffected individuals; however, efficacy of treatments is still under investigation 19,20 .
• Avoid disturbance of snake populations; consider restricting or minimizing human activity around habitat if concern for disease emergence exists 18 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • If deemed necessary, consider methods that reduce fungal load in the environment and/or improve adaptive capacity to disease, such as habitat modifications (e.g., increase basking sites, reduce moisture in denning habitats, improve habitat connectivity) or application of environmental treatments (e.g., antifungals) 21,22 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Monitor for clinical disease or evidence of increased mortality in snake populations that may indicate an outbreak 18 .

• Explore multimodal approaches for monitoring for disease in wild populations, such as collecting swabs of individuals and conducting PCR to detect pathogen 5 and using ultraviolet light to identify skin lesions in free-ranging snakes 23 .
• Develop communication plan to inform the public about SFD and consider public monitoring programs.

div.head: Literature Cited
div.p: This second recommendation resulted in the Fish and Wildlife Relevancy Roadmap (AFWA 2019), a compilation of nonprescriptive recommendations that are based on the best available research, insight, and experience of conservation professionals. Expanding conservation relevance to unengaged constituents, while continuing to engage those who are already allies, will allow FWP to be successful today and into the future.

Addressing the threats and implementing the actions identified in the SWAP isn't just a roadmap for conserving SGCN and HGCN; it presents an opportunity to build a broader, more supportive, and better-informed public that will support FWP's mission. This chapter provides options to enhance conservation of SGCN and their habitats through outreach, education, citizen science, and wildlife viewing. It outlines the strategy that FWP will use to expand the agency's relevance to otherwise unfamiliar constituents and improve customer service to all Montanans. We have organized the strategy around four avenues for delivering messages that will increase FWP's success in conserving SGCN and their habitats: communication, education, citizen science, and wildlife viewing.

div.head: Communication
div.p: Effective wildlife management and conservation in a state as large and diverse as Montana necessitates clear and frequent communication between FWP, partners, and the public. Strategic communication can help increase public awareness of and involvement in agency decision-making, simplify complex science behind management decisions, and support public resource stewardship, all of which help FWP meet its mission.

In recent years, FWP has created targeted and successful statewide, multimedia communications campaigns that integrate outreach with education related to bear safety and awareness, combating aquatic invasive species, improving hunter understanding of chronic wasting disease and the importance of testing game for disease, and more. These campaigns all identify various objectives related to the knowledge, beliefs, and behaviors of target audiences; identify messages that will resonate with those audiences; and employ an arsenal of communications tools ranging from print to digital and new to traditional media.
FWP's Communications Bureau will support the SWAP in the following ways:

1. Work with the Wildlife Division and other partners to develop and implement one or more statewide, integrated communication/education campaigns related to the SWAP's top priorities. Examples may include developing messages around the various values of nongame species, the importance of wetland and riparian habitat, or how landowners and urban wildlife watchers can help conserve and improve wildlife habitat on their properties.

2. Working from specific conservation actions identified for SGCN and HGCN that are related to communication, the communications and nongame wildlife bureaus will partner to identify strategic communications objectives, audiences, messages, and tools to meet conservation objectives.

div.head: Education
div.p: FWP recognizes the important role of conservation education in supporting the agency's mission and creating positive conservation and management outcomes for wildlife and habitat. Research, however, has shown that the connection between education and conservation-minded behavior is not linear. Rather, there is a complex web of interactions between an individual's knowledge, attitudes, values, and behaviors as well as the direct and measurable environmental impacts from those behaviors (Ardoin et al. 2020).

A 2020 review (Ardoin et al.) examined environmental education programs and their direct conservation impacts. The study highlighted a few key factors for success. It emphasized the importance of a local program focus, leveraging partnerships for program implementation, and integrating actions (e.g., weed pulling, bird surveying) into the program itself. These recommendations, which align well with FWP's existing program offerings, can guide future education program and partnership development as well as field trip and citizen science opportunities that collectively address SWAP priorities.

FWP offers a variety of place-based interpretive and educational programming at many of its 56 state parks and at the Montana WILD Education Center in Helena. Montana WILD is a premier education destination that welcomes K-12 students from across the state for educational programs (field trips) and is also open to the public for programs, live raptor viewing, and exhibit hall exploration. Similarly, many state parks provide interpretive programs for K-12 students throughout the year with hands-on learning opportunities.
FWP has identified several ways to support SWAP goals through education:
1. Integrate Species of Greatest Conservation and Inventory Need into existing educational programming.

Montana WILD offers high quality, hands-on educational programs that meet K -12 standards across a variety of species and topics, including bats, songbirds, raptors, reptiles, amphibians, fish, macroinvertebrates, mammals, and more. Education staff frequently update programs to incorporate new data and information, hands-on elements, and recommended behaviors. Using SWAP as a guide, FWP educators will evaluate existing Montana WILD programs as well as Aquatic Education, which is delivered statewide, and integrate SWAP target species, habitats, threats, and actions whenever possible.

In addition, FWP educators host professional development trainings for teachers across Montana using the Project WILD Curriculum Guide, a collection of lessons curated by the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies that is used nationwide. As part of teacher trainings, educators often partner with biologists to facilitate field research experiences such as surveying for greater short-horned lizards and seine netting minnows. When these teachers return to their classrooms, they are empowered to deliver high-quality education on a variety of species, extending the reach of the material well beyond FWP's capacity. FWP will continue to prioritize and create place-based field trip opportunities for teachers and the public to further SWAP goals.
2. Create new educational programs and capacity to support SWAP.

FWP's education and interpretation specialists are well-poised to apply their skills in curriculum development and place-based educational techniques to highlight species, threats, habitats, and actions outlined in this plan. Using Level 3 conservation actions that teams of experts identified in the SWAP for 159 vertebrate SGCN and 52 HGCN, staff from the nongame and education bureaus will partner to create new education messaging and programs that aim to change human behaviors that threaten conservation or enhance human behaviors that contribute to conservation. Outcomes will yield regionally tailored programs in support of wildlife watching, key habitats and species of concern, ecosystem function, and more.

With the recent addition of seven regional Educational Technicians and an Education and Outreach Specialist in Helena tasked, in part, with SWAP implementation support, the agency will have increased capacity to support SWAP priorities through education starting in 2025.
3. Update interpretive signage and exhibits to highlight SGCN.

Working through the agency's interpretive work group-a collaborative effort between biologists, parks and recreation, and education staff-FWP will look for opportunities to integrate species and messages outlined in the SWAP into existing and new statewide interpretive signs and digital platforms. Biologists and education staff will work to develop new messaging on the threats and conservation actions for SGCN and habitats that are identified in the SWAP.

Montana WILD will explore ways to integrate a new exhibit highlighting species and habitats of concern (e.g., wetlands) in the education center's exhibit hall. In addition, the new Avian Center on the Montana WILD campus in Helena will provide on-demand opportunities for the public to view FWP's 10 to 15 ambassador raptors. These birds, including a variety of hawks, falcons, owls, and eagles, support educational programming highlighting birds, their habitats, and ecological importance. Ambassador raptors can be a highly impactful document species distribution, build predictive habitat suitability models, and inform environmental reviews.
FWP has identified several ways that citizen science can be used to help conserve SGCN:
1. Identify SGCN and SGIN that can be surveyed or monitored effectively by citizen scientists.

The SWAP identifies vertebrate, invertebrate, and plant SGCN and SGIN. FWP biologists will determine which species are good candidates for citizen science projects and develop or refine survey methods to produce the data needed to meet information needs. New citizen science projects could be established for species that lack baseline data, or for which distribution data is inadequate. Citizen scientists can also resurvey locations where FWP biologists have established a baseline occupancy rate for a species, but periodic surveys (e.g., once every 10 years) are required to monitor trends.
2. Encourage participation in citizen science projects managed by partners that help FWP meet conservation and management objectives for SGCN and SGIN.

FWP will identify existing citizen science projects developed and managed by partner agencies, universities, and conservation organizations that meet SWAP goals. Examples include the Montana Bumble Bee Atlas and Project FeederWatch. FWP will also build relationships with partner organizations and look for opportunities to codevelop and implement citizen science projects that target SGCN and SGIN.
3. Increase the public's awareness and use of mobile apps that allow users to log plant and wildlife observations.

Outdoor recreation is a way of life for Montanans. A survey of outdoor recreation use by residents found that 87% of households use hiking trails (SCORP 2025). If even a small fraction of recreationists were trained in how to use mobile apps to record species observations, this would generate a tremendous amount of data on plants and wildlife. iNaturalist is particularly powerful for obtaining distribution data for plants and invertebrates; the user simply takes a photo, submits it, and a worldwide community of experts will identify the observation. When citizens submit observations of SGCN and SGIN vertebrates, invertebrates, and plants, they are feeding information into a database that is used to inform environmental review and avoid negative impacts to sensitive species and habitats.

div.head: Wildlife Viewing
div.p: Wildlife viewing is broadly defined as closely observing, feeding, or photographing wildlife; maintaining plantings or natural areas for the benefit of wildlife; or taking trips to parks and natural areas for the primary purpose of wildlife viewing outdoor recreation is a core value for Montanans, with 97% indicating that outdoor recreation is important for maintaining their quality of life and 90% indicating the importance of preserving natural areas and wildlife in recreation areas. When asked about which recreation facilities and areas they use the top response from Montanans was hiking trails (87%). Natural or wild areas was 4 th (79%), wildlife viewing areas was 11th (63%), and interpretive trails was 14th (53%).

These results indicate that wildlife viewing is already popular and that there is tremendous opportunity for enhancing access and improving quality of life for even more Montanans. We know that compared to other states, Montana offers fewer developed wildlife viewing opportunities and less interpretive programming despite abundant opportunities and increasing user demand. Wildlife viewing can be further leveraged to help FWP implement SWAP goals. Research shows that wildlife viewers are more likely to participate in conservation behaviors, such as maintaining habitat for wildlife and supporting state wildlife agencies (Sinkular et al. 2022; Jennings 2024). FWP will leverage wildlife viewing experiences to deliver information on SGCN and their habitats and convey actions that lead to better conservation outcomes.
FWP has identified several ways to support SWAP goals through wildlife viewing:
1. Enhance wildlife viewing opportunities at existing FWP sites.

FWP staff from the wildlife, communications and education, and parks and outdoor recreation divisions will work collaboratively to develop a list of FWP sites, including parks, wildlife management areas, and fishing access sites, with exceptional wildlife viewing opportunities. Site evaluations will be conducted to document the types of wildlife viewing available, opportunities for enhancement, and whether updates are needed to ensure ADA compliance. All sites will be included on FWP's wildlife viewing website, and those that meet specific ADA requirements for bird watching will be entered into the Birdability Map https://gis.audubon.org/birdability/.
2. Work with partners to identify and develop new wildlife viewing areas.

FWP has previously partnered with other agencies and conservation organizations to develop wildlife viewing opportunities. A recent example is the Reed's Slough Wildlife Viewing Area, a collaboration in which the Flathead Valley Land Trust secured a conservation easement on private property to protect important habitat for migratory birds, and FWP secured an access agreement with the landowner and developed the parking lot and other infrastructure to create a safe space for the public to access the site.
3. Build a wildlife viewing webpage on FWP's website under the Activities menu.

FWP staff from the wildlife and parks and outdoor recreation divisions will collaborate to build a webpage with wildlife viewing information, including a map of wildlife viewing areas and opportunities managed by FWP. The long-term vision is to include wildlife viewing information and opportunities maintained by other agencies, city and county development groups, and other partners on a common platform.
4. Incorporate wildlife viewing opportunities along trail systems.

Wildlife viewing provides opportunities to mesh State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) and Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP) objectives. Enhancing trail networks, pathways, and recreation connectivity is a core goal in the SCORP, and one action in the plan is to identify and designate wildlife viewing opportunities along trail systems. Incorporating wildlife viewing and interpretive information into trail systems offers multiple benefits that align with the objectives of both plans. Trails designed with wildlife viewing opportunities enhance the overall outdoor experience, attracting a broader range of users, including birdwatchers, photographers, and nature enthusiasts.

Guiding recreation to specific trail corridors helps minimize disturbance to sensitive habitats by concentrating visitor use in appropriate areas. Trail systems with designated wildlife viewing points can also be used to help monitor species occurrences and habitats (e.g., direct users to log observations in wildlife apps), providing valuable data to inform SWAP-related conservation and management decisions.

Finally, well-designed trails with wildlife viewing features can boost local ecotourism, generating revenue for nearby communities. They are also more inclusive and provide fully accessible opportunities for all ages and abilities.
5. Develop interpretive signage with targeted messaging on SGCN and HGCN.

Interpretive signage and information at FWP sites and along trails educate visitors about local wildlife species, their habitats, and conservation needs. This raises public awareness about biodiversity and the importance of protecting ecosystems. Adding interpretive elements creates a more engaging and meaningful visit, increasing repeat use and positive word-of-mouth about sites and trail systems. Such educational opportunities can foster stewardship and support for conservation initiatives outlined in SWAP, encouraging responsible recreation and wildlife-friendly behaviors.

Interpretive programs can guide visitors on how to reduce impacts, helping sustain both recreational access and wildlife habitats over the long term. In summary, wildlife viewing within trail systems enhances the visitor experience, supports education and conservation goals of SWAP and SCORP, encourages sustainable outdoor recreation, and benefits communities economically and socially. This approach harmonizes recreation with wildlife stewardship, fostering a deeper connection between people and nature. Many SGCN fish species are monitored via the Montana Statewide Fisheries Management Plan (2023-2026), which provides management direction for both native and non-native sport fish. Monitoring fish populations and collecting ecological health data to describe trends in fish abundance, distribution, and genetic variation provides staff with essential information to manage Montana's fisheries. Monitoring is used to identify factors limiting fish populations, including habitat quality and environmental variables (e.g. flow, temperature), evaluate impacts of angling or harvest, determine the effectiveness of stocking waterbodies, and detect diseases in a population. Genetic samples of numerous fish species throughout the state are collected annually to address a wide variety of native fish management and conservation needs. For example, genetic data are necessary for species identification in cryptic species or life stages (e.g., larval pallid sturgeon), quantifying native vs. non-native genetic ancestry in individuals and populations of cutthroat trout, and documenting the amount of genetic variation in a fish population. This information is used to prioritize management actions (e.g., translocations) that address undesirable or limited genetic variation and potential inbreeding . Genetic data also play a fundamental role in helping identify and demarcate conservation and management units (e.g., populations), which in turn directly informs the spatial scale at which populations are monitored and managed.

FWP enhances its monitoring efforts by using information from incidental observations of species submitted via citizen science efforts and other platforms such as the Montana Natural Heritage Program, Fishes of Montana, eBird, iNaturalist, eMammal, and Bumble Bee Watch. FWP and partners contribute to many of these efforts through funding and/or staff time to conduct surveys. Investment in surveys that extend beyond Montana's boundaries has proven key to understanding Montana's role in stewarding species both within the state and within the region because these broader efforts provide spatially explicit density and trend information. Investments in these survey programs would be inherently less valuable without our partnership with the Montana Natural Heritage Program (MTNHP), which collates structured survey and incidental observation data from the aforementioned programs as well as data that have been submitted directly to them. Importantly, state resource agencies (e.g., FWP, Montana Department of Resources and Conservation, Montana Department of Environmental Quality) are statutorily mandated to submit collected species data to MTNHP (MCA 90-15-303), centralizing these data in one place. With these data, MTNHP supports a variety of tools that use monitoring data to help inform SGCN management. These include:

• Map Viewer: This tool, which supports viewing of species occurrence and habitat suitability model information, is used by nearly 1,800 agency personnel for environmental review, permitting, and planning processes across Montana.
• Montana Field Guide: This tool provides accounts with information on the distribution, status, general biology, and ecology of nearly 18,000 species and habitats that are known to occur in Montana.
• Invasive Weeds, Non-Native Watchlist, and Aquatic Invasive Species Incident Management: These tools are used to prioritize survey and control efforts and respond to invasions of non-native species.
• Montana Beaver Restoration HUB: These tools are used to support management and restoration of beavers, which provide habitat for a large number of SGCN.

Additionally, MTNHP incorporates observation data into regular re-evaluations of the conservation status of species at a state scale, and they coordinate with NatureServe on similar updates at a global scale. This process provides an opportunity to understand whether species status or trends have changed substantially given new information.

div.head: Adapting Conservation Actions to Changing Conditions
div.p: Most SGCN do not have a dedicated management plan. Monitoring data nevertheless informs conservation actions, primarily through identification of locations where actions should be implemented. The tools provided by MTNHP leverage monitoring data to inform conservation and management, and to minimize environmental impacts from human causes (see section 10.1). Monitoring data are also used to identify information gaps that can be addressed via research that examines the relationship of a threat or action to a species status or trend.

While an overwhelming amount of information about SGCN exists that could be used in conservation and management, no single agency has sufficient time to keep track of all new information for all SWAP species. Our collective goal is to identify and respond to reductions in SGCN populations and/or their habitats, and our primary means of accomplishing this is through partnership. Some of the work partners conduct offers deeper insight into threats and actions for species, and sharing this work provides broader benefits.

div.head: Monitoring the Effectiveness of Conservation Actions
div.p: Ecological responses to conservation actions are often slow to occur and difficult to assess given the complexity of factors impacting a given ecosystem. For some actions, there is reasonable evidence to support their effectiveness (e.g., https://www.conservationevidence.com/) , so project-specific effectiveness monitoring would not provide enough additional insight to warrant the dedication of limited resources.

Given this, we aim to implement effectiveness monitoring when the insight it offers is of high value in understanding the impacts of actions on the threat to a SGCN or Habitat of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) the action was meant to address. We therefore do not plan to outline monitoring objectives or undertake effectiveness monitoring for all actions outlined in the SWAP. We aim to follow several best practices when engaging in effectiveness monitoring:

• Assess metrics that are anticipated to be responsive to the treatment within the timeframe of the assessment. In some cases, these may be variables related to changes in habitat features instead of species occurrence or abundance patterns.

• Determine whether there is likely to be adequate statistical power produced by our monitoring efforts to assess the change or difference anticipated. If greater effort is needed, then we can partner with other entities undertaking similar actions to perform an assessment that can be more broadly informative. Some funding sources for actions will require effectiveness monitoring, which we will engage with even if the potential inferences are limited. In these cases, working on small-scale effectiveness monitoring within a larger framework (e.g., Integrated Monitoring in Bird Conservation Regions) will make the greatest contribution toward broader understanding of impacts of actions on SGCN and HGCN.

• Use the most informative approach to monitoring given the constraints of the resources available to conduct the monitoring. It is better to fully answer a smaller question than assemble a data set that does not have adequate power to address a more desirable question.
• Use a combination of genetic and demographic metrics to monitor populations and consistently evaluate novel techniques to improve precision and effectiveness of monitoring SGCN.

div.head: Monitoring the Effectiveness of Montana's SWAP
div.p: FWP is working in collaboration with MTNHP to build a forthcoming SWAP dashboard, which we will use to track conservation actions implemented in relation to SGCN, HGCN, and other SWAP objectives. By tracking the spatial and temporal implementation of actions, we hope to gain and provide better insight into where, how, and for which SGCN and HGCN we are having the greatest impact. We also intend to use the SWAP dashboard to facilitate continued and improved collaboration with partners through shared understanding of priority actions and locations where those actions are needed.

div.head: Partnering with FWP to Address Monitoring
div.p: Conservation of species and habitats is a collaborative endeavor in which different partners have different capacities, abilities, priorities, and constraints. For example, some partners directly manage habitat, while others can work to develop and test new conservation strategies or facilitate landowner access to cost-share opportunities and technical support. In the context of monitoring, an important component of collaboration is sharing information across ownership to better assess conservation needs and impacts.

In particular, all partners can encourage the reporting of wildlife observation and survey data through platforms like iNaturalist or eBird, or directly to MTNHP. This steady accrual of occurrence data for different species forms the basis of our understanding of SGCN in Montana. Observations in habitats and parts of Montana that are under-visited are particularly valuable.

Explicit acknowledgement of the constraints and prioritization processes shaping the work we undertake can facilitate more efficient collaboration. Each year, FWP's Wildlife and Fisheries Divisions consider priorities for monitoring efforts that are not already dedicated through recovery or species management plans (Section 9.1). These considerations are informed by:

• ESA candidate species petitions and designations for which information on the species in Montana is needed to contribute meaningful data for a U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS) Species Status Assessment.
• MTNHP species status ranking needs, including addressing baseline distribution information, especially for species for which Montana has disproportionately high stewardship responsibility.

• Opportunities where FWP participation in a collaborative monitoring project can meet Montana objectives that we cannot meet on our own (e.g., participating in multi-state monitoring projects that span a species' entire range).

• The need to understand how human-related stressors or management actions may impact HGCN condition or SGCN population status (e.g., developing protocols for assessing the use of bridges by bats for roosting).

New research or monitoring projects that require FWP resources, including staff time, supplies, equipment, data collected by FWP staff, or money from any FWP-managed account; or require FWP sanction (e.g., to use our logo or describe FWP as a "partner") are vetted through FWP's Research Prioritization Process (Version 2024-April-3). FWP defines research to include "every new study, monitoring method, or project except established, ongoing monitoring of fish or wildlife populations, habitats, or communities, and user harvest, user effort, or recreational use, or application of established monitoring methods to new species, situations, or areas."

The FWP Fisheries and Wildlife Divisions operate research steering committees that are the vehicle for vetting, prioritizing, and recommending approval of research projects by the FWP Director. The committees consist of the division administrator, bureau chiefs, regional program managers, and the primary contact from the Research Unit; each division also may include other relevant staff in proposal review and prioritization at their discretion. These committees meet twice annually (spring and fall) to evaluate research and new monitoring proposals. Proposals are scored based on the following criteria:

• Meets information needs or research obligations identified in FWP plans, legislation, by FWP-sponsored public working groups; or by commitments made by the director, governor, or in legislative or commission processes.
• Informs or improves FWP's management, conservation actions, or programs in a tangible way.
• Addresses concerns of vocal, influential, or large constituency groups or has significant economic impacts.
• Uses appropriate methods and techniques (analytical and technological), and products are realistically achievable in the specified timeline with identified resources.

div.head: War, Civil Unrest & Military Exercises
div.p: Actions by military forces without a permanent footprint (e.g. training exercises and ranges, munitions testing)

div.head: Work & Other Activities
div.p: People spending time in or traveling in natural environments for reasons other than recreation, military activities, or research (e.g., law enforcement, drug smugglers, illegal immigrants, vandalism)

div.head: Natural System Modifications
div.p: Threats from actions that convert or degrade habitat in service of "managing" natural or semi-natural systems, often to improve human welfare

div.head: Fire & Fire Suppression
div.p: Suppression or increase in fire frequency and/or intensity outside of its natural range of variation

div.head: Dams & Water Management/Use
div.p: Changing water flow patterns from their natural range of variation either deliberately or as a result of other activities

div.head: Other Ecosystem Modifications
div.p: Other actions that convert or degrade habitat in service of "managing" natural systems to improve human welfare (e.g., land reclamation projects, abandonment of managed lands, rip-rap along shorelines, mowing grass, tree thinning in parks, beach construction, removal of snags from streams)

div.head: Removing/ Reducing Human Maintenance
div.p: Absence or reduction of current or historical maintenance regimes important for key ecological attributes. Includes regimes historically maintained by protected area staff, farmers and ranchers, indigenous peoples, private landowners, or any other resource manager.

div.head: Invasive & Other Problematic Species & Genes
div.p: Threats from non-native and native plants, animals, pathogens/microbes, or genetic materials that have or are predicted to have harmful effects on biodiversity following their introduction, spread and/or increase in abundance

div.head: Invasive Non-Native/Alien Species
div.p: Harmful plants, animals, and microbes not originally found within the ecosystem(s) in question and directly or indirectly introduced and spread into it by human activities

div.head: Problematic Native Species
div.p: Harmful plants, animals, or microbes that are originally found within the ecosystem(s) in question, but have become "out-of-balance" or "released" directly or indirectly due to human activities

div.head: Introduced Genetic Material
div.p: Human altered or transported organisms or genes (e.g., pesticide resistant crops, using nonlocal seed stock, genetically modified insects for biocontrol)

div.head: Pathogens & Microbes
div.p: Harmful native and non-native agents that cause disease or illness to a host, including bacteria, viruses, prions, fungi, and other microorganisms

div.head: Pollution
div.p: Threats from introduction of exotic and/or excess materials or energy from point and nonpoint sources

div.head: Household Sewage & Urban Waste Water
div.p: Water-borne sewage and non-point runoff from housing and urban areas that include nutrients, toxic chemicals and/or sediments

div.head: Industrial & Military Effluents
div.p: Water-borne pollutants from industrial and military sources including mining, energy production, and other resource extraction industries that include nutrients, toxic chemicals and/or sediments

div.head: Agricultural & Forestry Effluents
div.p: Water-borne pollutants from agricultural, silvicultural, and aquaculture systems that include nutrients, toxic chemicals and/or sediments

div.head: Garbage & Solid Waste
div.p: Rubbish and other solid materials including those that entangle wildlife

div.head: Air-Borne Pollutants
div.p: Atmospheric pollutants from point and nonpoint sources

div.head: Excess Energy
div.p: Inputs of heat, sound, or light that disturb wildlife or ecosystems (e.g., noise from highways or airplanes, heated water from power plants, lamps attracting insects) Restoring missing or severely degraded ecosystems and ecosystem functions and processes, especially on a large scale

div.head: Species Management
div.p: Actions directly managing or restoring specific species or taxonomic groups

div.head: Species Stewardship
div.p: Enhancing viability of/ mitigating stresses to specific taxa within their current range

div.head: Species Re-introduction & Translocation
div.p: Transferring species or genetic material to places where they formerly occurred or to suitable future habitat or benign introductions of species to an ecosystem

div.head: Ex-situ Conservation
div.p: Protecting specific taxa in artificial settings with the aim of ultimately restoring them to their natural settings

div.head: Awareness Raising
div.p: Actions making people aware of key issues and/or feeling desired emotions, leading to behavior change

div.head: Outreach & Communications
div.p: Promoting desired awareness and/or emotions and subsequent behavior change by providing information to target audiences through appropriate channels

div.head: Protests & Civil Disobedience
div.p: Promoting desired awareness and subsequent desired behavior change by conducting protests, naming and shaming, civil disobedience, or sabotage activities

div.head: Law Enforcement & Prosecution
div.p: Actions monitoring and enforcing compliance with existing laws and policies at all levels to deter threats or compel conservation action

div.head: Detection & Arrest
div.p: Detecting, directly stopping, and/or deterring violations of existing laws and policies

div.head: Criminal Prosecution & Conviction
div.p: Ensuring appropriate application of sanctions for violations of existing laws and policies

div.head: Non-Criminal Legal Action
div.p: Threatening or bringing non-criminal legal action to get individuals, organizations, agencies or firms to change or deter undesired behaviors or compel conservation action

div.head: Livelihood, Economic & Moral Incentives
div.p: Actions using livelihood, other economic and moral incentives to directly influence attitudes and behaviors

div.head: Linked Enterprises & Alternative Livelihoods
div.p: Developing enterprises that directly depend on the maintenance of natural resources or provide substitute livelihoods as a means of changing attitudes and behaviors

div.head: Better Products & Management Practices
div.p: Developing, promoting and/or providing more environmentally friendly products or practices that substitute for environmentally damaging ones

div.head: Market-based Incentives
div.p: Using market mechanisms to change behaviors and attitudes

div.head: Direct Economic Incentives
div.p: Using direct or indirect payments or ascribing economic value to change behaviors and attitudes

div.head: Non-Monetary Values
div.p: Using intangible and moral values to change behaviors and attitudes

div.head: Conservation Designation & Planning
div.p: Actions directly protecting sites and/or species

div.head: Protected Area Designation and/or Acquisition
div.p: Legally or formally establishing or expanding public or private parks, reserves, and other protected areas

div.head: Easements & Resource Rights
div.p: Legally or formally establishing protection of some specific aspect of the natural resources on public or private lands

div.head: Land/Water Use Zoning & Designation
div.p: Designating land/water uses or designating conservation areas outside of formal parks or wildernesses

div.head: Conservation Planning
div.p: Planning for management of sites, species, or thematic conservation projects

div.head: Site Infrastructure
div.p: Building or maintaining the physical infrastructure for protected areas and other conservation sites

figure.figDesc: Overall, 140 people representing 37 partner organizations served on these species expert teams. The teams reviewed threats documented by the Montana Natural Heritage Program (MTNHP), as well as threats and actions listed in Montana's 2015 SWAP. They also identified additional threats and actions by drawing on scientific literature, conservation plans, and expert opinion. For species that are native in one part of the state and introduced in other parts of the state, the species teams were instructed to consider threats and actions for species only for the native portion of the population. For example,

note.p: snapping turtles are native east of the Continental Divide in Montana but are introduced and problematic for other SGCN west of the Continental Divide. Therefore, threats and actions presented herein for snapping turtles apply only to the native portion of the species range. Conservation actions and threats for SGCN were categorized according to the Conservation Measures Partnership Threats and Actions Classification System (Version 2.0; Salafsky et al. 2008, Appendix F), as recommended in the Best Practices for State Wildlife Action Plans Voluntary Guidance to States for Revision and Implementation developed by the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA 2012

figure.figDesc: East of the Continental Divide is Montana's portion of the Great Plains, an immense grassland and sagebrush ecosystem that covers roughly 60 percent of the state. Other grasslands cover alpine plateaus or are splattered across largely forested habitats as meadows. Overall, grasslands cover 28% of the land area in Montana (2017 Montana Land Cover Layers) and support 48 terrestrial vertebrate SGCN species. Many of these species, such as the thickbilled longspur and Sprague's pipet, are facing some of the most dramatic declines of any species on Montana's SGCN list. Grasslands in Montana are central to the state's farming and ranching operations, are highly valued for wildlife viewing and hunting, and are considered some of the last best places for many North American grassland wildlife species.

figure.figDesc: This includes the sprawling conifer forests of western Montana's mountain ranges and the wooded draws and ponderosa pine savannahs of eastern Montana's open landscapes. Forests and woodlands are some of Montana's most iconic habitats and support important parts of Montana's economy such as timber harvest and outdoor recreation. Forests and woodlands bring vertical structure to the landscape, providing key resources to wildlife in form of safe nesting and resting sites, shade, and a whole lot of buds, berries, and insects for SGCN to eat. Overall, 68 terrestrial vertebrate SGCN depend on Montana's forests and woodlands.

row.cell: 1. Land/Water Protection 1.1 Site/Area Stewardship Avoid/minimize bank hardening to only situations where it is needed to protect infrastructure. If bank hardening is needed, use naturalized bank stabilization whenever possible and re-vegetate waterbody-adjacent slopes with native riparian vegetation. Remove and rehab hardened banks where bank hardening is no longer necessary to protect infrastructure. Conduct hand-thinning operations in floodplain areas that have shifted to dense conifer forests to avoid future high-intensity wildfires in valley bottoms. Retain canopy cover, streamside vegetative complexity, and coarse woody debris in the stream channel and in streamside habitats to create/maintain moist microsites to reduce thermal stress from increased water temperatures. 1.2 Ecosystem & Natural Process (Re)Creation Strategically evaluate and act on opportunities to improve passage for SGCN and restore connectivity (e.g., to lake systems, between main rivers and tributaries) by identifying and removing movement barriers, improving native fish corridors, restoring habitat, and/or by installing fish passage structures. 2. Species Management 2.1 Species Stewardship Restore, maintain, and enhance beaver populations and habitats in areas of their historical range to increase natural water storage, reduce the severity of floods and wildfires, and maintain natural stream processes that create, enhance, and maintain habitat for SGCN. B. Behavioral Change/ Threat Reduction 3. Awareness Raising 3.1 Outreach & Communications Implement education and outreach campaigns about the importance of beavers to ecosystem services and natural stream processes and techniques for mitigating beaver-human conflicts catered to agricultural communities, water users, road crews, fire-prone communities, local watershed groups, irrigation districts, conservation districts, and local governments. Implement education and outreach campaigns in agricultural communities about the importance of healthy floodplains, riparian areas, and wetlands for providing ecosystem services and maintaining natural stream processes that result in more water available on the landscape. 4. Law Enforcement & Prosecution 4.3 Non-Criminal Legal Action Increase enforcement of local, state, and federal laws around the protection and conservation of floodplains, riparian areas, and wetlands to address the culture of ignoring these laws or treating fines as fees for illegal activities (e.g., streamside vegetation removal, unpermitted bank hardening and bridge/culvert construction, driving vehicles around in floodplains and wetlands, etc.). This may require strengthening of state and federal laws around floodplains, riparian areas, and wetlands reduce protections for these HGCN to facilitate holding violators accountable. 5. Livelihood Economic & Moral Incentives 5.2 Better Products & Management Practices Advocate for water-use management and dam operations to improve instream flows, prevent dewatering, mimic natural hydrologic regimes, and improve and maintain natural stream/river form and function. Work with dam operators to minimize water level fluctuations during important SGCN nesting seasons and avoid water level lowering ahead of or during heat waves. Do not stock fish in currently fishless waterbodies. Use piscicides to remove non-native fish from lakes and streams and restore fishless conditions or native fish assemblages. Follow guidance in Montana's Aquatic Invasive Species Management Plan. Follow the Statewide Fisheries Management Plan and/or individual waterbody management plans, where applicable. Implement both lethal and non-lethal beaver conflict mitigation measures and programs to address conflicts with aquatic SGCN conservation and to increase tolerance for beavers on the landscape. Maintain adequate vegetated buffers between human development, agricultural areas, logging projects and waterbodies to maintain the most critical habitats, help capture runoff of nutrients and pollutants, provide visual and auditory screening for SGCN, and minimize noise and light pollution. Use native plants in buffers when possible to maintain natural characteristics of riparian communities. Minimize or avoid the use of culverts for stream crossings in favor of bridges or large culverts that accommodate full stream width and marginal habitats with low stream velocities to facilitate movement for SGCN unless a culvert is an important movement barrier for non-native or problematic native species. Remove dams and barriers where appropriate to restore connectivity, except where the barrier provides necessary protection of an SGCN. Minimize use of agricultural fertilizers especially on fields adjacent to floodplains, riparian areas, and wetlands. 6.2 Easements & Resource Rights Continue and increase efforts to maintain adequate stream flows via instream flow protections and water leases. 6.4 Conservation Planning Conduct channel migration mapping on all major river and streams in Montana to Pursue channel migration easements on large rivers to allow for natural channel migration to maintain and restore critical floodplain processes for natural establishment of riparian plants and important floodplain features for SGCN (e.g., backwaters, floodplain pools, beaver-modified habitats, etc.). improve land-use planning efforts that can benefit HGCN. Develop and implement grazing management plans that meet or exceed riparian health objectives and exclude grazers from unlimited riparian access. 7. Legal & Policy Frameworks Secure instream water rights or leases to maintain flows during low-water periods. Re-establish or improve flows in intermittent reaches of streams where intermittency is an unnatural condition. 7.1 Laws, Regulations & Codes Advocate for aquatic connectivity during Federal Energy Regulatory Commission relicensing.

Bank stabilization to protect human infrastructure severs floodplain connectivity, reduces woody debris inputs into waterbodies, diminishes public access to waterbodies, facilitates increased development in and near floodplains, and perpetuates bank hardening downstream. Introduction of Aquatic Invasive Species via recreational activities (watercraft, waders, etc.). Loss of movement barriers allows non-native fish and other species to become established and spread in new areas. Reducing/removing human maintenance of HGCN that can degrade without human intervention. Hot climatic conditions contribute to increased plant and algae growth and longer growing season length may make some emergent and submergent plant species and algal blooms problematic for aquatic and semi-aquatic species through direct mortalities, changes to prey base, reduced water clarity, or reduced swimming ability/efficiency. Undersized culverts, perched culverts, and other waterbody obstructions interrupt connectivity for aquatic SGCN. Irrigation and/or hydropower dams result in partial or full passage barriers for aquatic SGCN. note.p: 1.1 Site/Area Stewardship Applying seasonal closures for motorized use to discourage concentrations of hunters in critical seasonal habitats (e.g., during late big-game seasons) when Greater Sage-Grouse are present. Encourage recreationists to avoid continuous or concentrated use within 1.5 miles of leks from 15 March-15 May. Notify user group of the impacts of disturbance during the sensitive nesting period. 4.1 Roads & Railroads Roads contribute to habitat loss and population declines. Roads/off-road travel can cause habitat fragmentation, habitat loss, and a potential decline or shift in populations. Vehicle use on federal, state, and tribal lands impacts habitat quality. Recreation/commercial activities (energy facilities and high-volume road traffic) impacts breeding and reproduction through disturbance and reduces habitat quality through spread of invasive plants. Plowing and introduction of cultivated crops or other nonnative species for pasture leads to the long-term loss of Greater Sage-Grouse habitat. As habitats become more fragmented by conversion to cropland, nests are more susceptible to predation, which significantly reduces productivity. Grazing affects sagebrush-grassland habitat through direct effects on plants and indirect effects on soil and microclimate. Continuous use by domestic livestock and wild ungulates might not leave suitable cover or maintain the feeding of livestock in winter habitat and around leks.

figure.figDesc: Introduction of aquatic invasive species (e.g., invasive mussels) and plants can reduce or eliminate prey base for loons and increase the risk of botulism outbreaks that cause loon mortalities. Introduction of non-native fish species in lakes used by loons or planting of fish in formerly fishless lakes can reduce or eliminate prey base for loons (e.g., Northern Pike reducing silver salmon in Salmon Lake). Efforts to remove non-native fish for native fish restoration can cause loon mortalities or stress (e.g., gill-netting, piscicides reducing prey base) in the short term, but are generally positive for loon conservation in the long term.

Invasion of open, dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forests by invasive plants (e.g., Cheatgrass, knapweed, toadflax) degrades habitat for prey species and leads to changing fire regimes that can reduce or eliminate habitat in the long-term. Encroachment of development into dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forest types and removal of dead, downed, and dying trees to "clean up" private property destroys or degrades habitat. Encroachment of development into dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forest types increases human-caused sources of mortality (e.g., outdoor cats, European Starlings, corvids, window strikes, vehicle collisions).

figure.figDesc: New and existing roads concentrate these activities in foothill habitats and more open forested areas. Timber harvest and vegetation management to restore mature and old-growth conditions and/or reduce fuel loads removes potential roost site features and escape cover (e.g., small patches of dense young conifers, trees with mistletoe growths, dense crowns, etc.). Vegetation management and timber harvest in dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forest types can remove large-diameter trees, snags, and downed woody debris critical for nesting and foraging.Lack of fire disturbance leads to loss of dry Ponderosa Pine and Douglas-fir forests that consist of widely spaced, largediameter trees, an open understory, and aspen stands. More frequent fire due to invasive plant species (e.g., Cheatgrass) removes understory shrubs and favors invasive species dominance, degrading habitat. Severely burned foothill forests may not recover to pre-fire conditions in the long-term, with compounding effects of climate change and invasive plant species.

figure.figDesc: Ephydatia cooperensis and Heteromeyenia baileyi, both aquatic invertebrate Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Montana.Montana's 2015 SWAP identified 257 aquatic focal areas and 116 terrestrial focal areas spread across the state. Focal areas were meant to guide attention to specific geographical areas of Montana that have a high number of HGCN and SGCN to help focus conservation efforts in areas with the highest need and the best potential return on conservation investments. We are currently developing new methods to identify focal areas for the 2025 SWAP, and we anticipate a new list of focal areas will be completed by October 2026. We will add the new focal areas to the 2025 SWAP through a minor revision and will notify our partners when the new version is available. In the meantime, we encourage partners to continue using the focal areas in the 2015 SWAP until new focal areas are complete.

figure.figDesc: Beechie et al. 2013, Fairfax and Whittle 2020, Thompson et al. 2021, Jordan and Fairfax 2022, Wohl 2024).Beavers are not only beneficial for the ecosystem services they can provide on the landscape, they also create and maintain diverse stream-wetland corridors that provide resources for dozens of species across Montana, including many SGCN(Ritter et al. 2023). In 2022, biologists with FWP and the Montana Natural Heritage Program (MTNHP) conducted a literature review and expert analysis on the impacts of beaver activity on the 128 SGCN identified in the 2015 SWAP(Ritter et al. 2023). The results of this analysis, summarized in Table20, reveal that beaver activity can be a significant benefit to the majority of terrestrial SGCN in the state. While aquatic SGCN are much more complicated in terms of the effects of beaver activity, in the right situations there are substantial benefits to aquatic SGCN as well. It is important to note that beaver activity was not assessed to be entirely negative for any SGCN in Montana other than western pearlshell mussels (Margaritifera falcata). A full list of SGCN from the 2015 SWAP that can benefit from beaver activity is provided in Table21. Overview of the impacts of beaver activity on SGCN from the 2015 SWAP based on an analysis included inRitter et al. (2023). For five aquatic SGCN, there was too little information on the effects of beaver activity on the species to classify impacts.

Red-headed woodpeckers and sapsuckers are found in riparian areas throughout eastern Montana and are the key primary cavity nesters in less heavily forested parts of the state.The cavities woodpeckers create ca" be 'sed by dozens of species over their lifespan. These cavities can remain on the landscape and available for species to use anywhere from a single breeding season to many decades. figure.figDesc: . The burrows prairie dogs create facilitate soil turnover and increase permeability of the soil to precipitation(Davidson et al. 2012, Sierra-Corona et al. 2015). These burrows are also used by many other species for nesting, foraging, and cover(Davidson et al. 2012, Adams 2021). Through grazing, prairie dogs maintain short vegetation communities that allow them to see over long distances in flat terrain. This grazing pressure creates and maintains unique plant communities, increases forage quality, increases invertebrate abundance and diversity, and prevents encroachment by shrubs(Coppock et al. 1983, Whicker and Detling 1988, Davidson et al. 2012, Adams 2021). Prairie dogs can be highly abundant where they are allowed to maintain colonies, and they provide a rich food resource for many species of raptors and terrestrial carnivores(Davidson et al. 2012).

figure.head: Literature Cited 9.4 Wildlife Disease Profiles White-nose Syndrome SGCN with Known Impacts 1
figure.figDesc: WNS) is a fungal skin disease of hibernating bats that has had devastating impacts since its North American emergence in New York in 20064 . It is caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd), which infects bats during fall and winter months. Bats are exposed through direct contact with contaminated surfaces or other infected bats2 . Infection leads to increases in arousal frequency during hibernation and physiological stress, which result in dehydration, starvation, and frequently, death. If infected bats survive to spring emergence, they may later die of severe inflammation associated with disease impacts, further contributing to population declines4 . Peak transmission occurs in late autumn or early winter as bats return to infected hibernacula and come into contact with one another 3 ; as disease progresses, mortality rates and overall prevalence are usually highest by the end of winter. Roosting behavior, hibernaculum conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity), and species-specific tolerance are key factors that influence which bat populations are most at risk from WNS 2 . Body condition also plays a role, as bats with increased body mass appear better able to survive infection5 .

figure.figDesc: The first detection of Pd in Montana occurred in the spring of 2020, followed by detection of WNS in spring of 2021. Both occurred in eastern Montana 1. ▪ Between 2021 to 2022, Azure Cave (Phillips County) experienced a 98 percent population decline in its hibernating little brown myotis colony due to WNS 8 . ▪ As of 2024 state-wide monitoring efforts, Pd and WNS have been detected in the central and eastern portions of the state. It has yet to be detected in regions west of the Continental Divide 1 . ▪ Pd and WNS have been confirmed in the three largest remaining winter Myotis colonies in the state: Lick Creek Cave, Cascade County (Pd in 2023, WNS in 2024); Mystery Cave, Carbon County (Pd and WNS in 2023); and Whitaker Sink, Judith Basin County (Pd and WNS in 2024). It is predicted that these hibernacula will experience significant diseaseinduced declines in the next one to two years 1 . ▪ Acoustic surveillance data from 2020 to 2022 suggests that WNS is causing detectable population declines in the eastern half of the state, which is consistent with observed declines reported by field staff in affected counties 1 .

In spring of 2025, a mountain lion in Beaverhead County was confirmed to have died from plague (Jennifer Ramsey, Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, pers. comm.). ▪ USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) Wildlife Services surveillance indicates that Y. pestis is widespread across Montana 3 . Based on data taken since 1970, Y. pestis has been identified in either an animal or flea sample in almost all counties in Montana 10 . ▪ Plague management (e.g., insecticide, vaccination) efforts occur at all black-footed ferret reintroduction sites in Montana (UL Bend National Wildlife Refuge, Ft. Belknap Reservation, and Crow Reservation).

The first recorded outbreak of PKD in free-ranging fish in North America occurred in Montana at Middle Creek Reservoir in the summers of 1990 and 1991, causing considerable mortality in Yellowstone cutthroat trout1 . ▪ A large-scale mortality event occurred in late summer of 2016 on the Yellowstone River, in which tens of thousands of mountain whitefish died as a result of PKD, initiating an unprecedented closure of over 180 miles of the Yellowstone River 2 . ▪ Recent surveillance efforts in Montana demonstrate that T. bryosalmonae is widely distributed across watersheds in the central and western parts of the state 2 , and it is likely to occur wherever suitable habitat for bryozoans exists (K. Staigmiller, Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, pers. comm.). During surveillance efforts, wild-caught fish routinely test positive for exposure to T. bryosalmonae DNA (J. Veilleux, USFWS, pers. comm.), suggesting the potential for high infection prevalence in Montana fish populations.

(US DOI et al. 2016). More than half of Americans participate in wildlife viewing; the 2022 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation estimated 148.3 million wildlife watching participants (US DOI 2022). Results from this national survey of U.S. residents have found that wildlife viewing is one of the fastest growing forms of outdoor recreation, and more Americans participate in wildlife viewing than fishing (39.9 million) and hunting(14.4 million) (US DOI 2022).Here in Montana, we know that interest in outdoor recreation has never been higher; FWP has seen increased use at state parks, fishing access sites, and other FWP properties. State parks welcomed over 3.2 million visitors in 2024. This number is a 3.8% increase from 2023, a 21.9% increase from pre-pandemic levels and nearly a 50% increase in the past decade. The Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP) is Montana's strategic roadmap in the development of outdoor recreation opportunities. The Land and Water Conservation Fund program requires states to produce a SCORP every 5 years to remain eligible for LWCF funding. The SCORP identifies recreation trends, assesses existing outdoor recreation facilities and demands, and sets priorities for future investments and initiatives over a five-year planning cycle. div.head: CHAPTER 9: WILDLIFE DISEASE
div.p: Work on the wildlife disease chapter was supported through funding by the U.S. Geological Survey North Central Climate Adaptation Science Center. We would like to thank subject matter experts for their time and expertise in reviewing the wildlife disease profiles for this chapter.

div.head: Disease Threat Assessment
div.p: We developed a scoring system to evaluate the level of threat each disease represented for Montana's SGCN (Table 24). The level of disease threat was a combination of scores across five categories: (1) population impact, (2) relevance to Montana, (3) host range, (4) timing, and (5) climate sensitivity. These categories were adapted from previously established conservation ranking systems and addressed the scope, severity, and timing of each disease threat [21][22][23] . Scores of 0 through 5 were applied (e.g., 5 being most severe) for each category. When there was uncertainty or lack of information within a category, we used a range (minimum, maximum) of scores to capture the current state of knowledge. Impact, relevance, and host breadth were weighted higher than climate sensitivity and timing, as recommended by experts participating in our workshop. The total score for each disease, representing its level of threat was: 𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙 𝑠𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒 = 3 × 𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑡 + 2 × 𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑒𝑣𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 + 2 × ℎ𝑜𝑠𝑡 𝑏𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑡ℎ + 𝑐𝑙𝑖𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑒 + 𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑔. Where uncertainty was present, we performed this calculation using the minimum score for each category and maximum score, and then took the median. Diseases could receive a final score between 9 and 45. We present the threat ranking for the 20 diseases in Figure 2.
