div.head: Background
div.p: Yersinia pestis is a bacterium and the causative agent of plague, a major disease of both humans and animals. Sylvatic plague (the disease affecting wildlife) causes severe, periodic episodes of high mortality (>90 percent) in certain species of rodents and blackfooted ferrets. Fleas serve as the primary vectors of Y. pestis, and rodent communities can help maintain high densities of fleas, thus plague dynamics are strongly influenced by the distribution and abundance of rodent and flea communities 4 . A wide range of wildlife species are susceptible to plague, and individuals become infected through flea bites or exposure to infected rodents (via direct contact, ingestion, or inhalation of aerosolized bacteria) 5 . Susceptibility to clinical disease and death varies among species, with mortality typically resulting from the rapid spread of bacteria throughout the bloodstream, leading to shock and organ failure. Generally, felids, lagomorphs, certain rodents, and mustelids (particularly black-footed ferrets) are susceptible to severe disease, while other taxa, like canids, badgers, weasels, bears, and even ungulates, may become infected but are typically resistant to disease and may play an important role in spreading it to new areas 3,5 .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Consider use of insecticides (e.g., deltamethrin dust 16 , fipronil-treated grain 17 , and fipronil bait pellets 18 ) for flea control in prairie dog colonies, but make sure decisions regarding application integrate information on product's durability, weather conditions, and the life cycle/ecology of both hosts and vectors [16][17][18] .
• Continue to vaccinate captive black-footed ferrets and consider continued vaccination in released and wild-born ferrets 6 .
• Develop an integrated plague management plan based on current and future needs, goals, and available resources.

In the event of plague outbreaks, consider wider application of insecticides (especially burrow dusting), but be aware of the risk of developing resistance in flea vectors 17,[19][20][21] and potential impact on non-target species [19][20][21] .

• Vaccination of prairie dogs (i.e., with oral baits) can be used for partial protection, and benefits may accumulate over time. If vaccination is chosen, consider appropriate timing, the likely vaccination rate, and combining it with other strategies 22 .
• Be aware that, while prairie dog colony control measures may reduce rodent abundance, they can also worsen outbreaks 7 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Develop public campaigns or messaging to advertise prairie dogs' importance to the environment and their role as a keystone species and need for conservation.
Protect key prairie dog habitats and colonies, including through supporting programs that promote coexistence between private landowners and prairie dog ecosystem conservation [19][20][21] .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Conduct serologic screening in species of interest (e.g., rodents, carnivores) to help determine disease foci and potential trends in plague activity [19][20][21] .

div.head: Background
div.p: West Nile virus (WNV) is a mosquito-borne disease that affects birds and some mammals. It is primarily transmitted by mosquitos in the genus Culex with C. tarsalis being the vector of main concern in the western U.S. The virus is known to infect over 300 species of birds in North America, leading to high fatality rates and population declines in some species 1,7,8 . The disease is propagated through a transmission cycle involving infected birds and mosquitoes. Horses and humans occasionally become infected but are considered dead-

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: The spread, impact, and evolution of HPAI may be sensitive to aspects of climate variability. Migration is an important factor driving the long-distance spread of new strains, and aspects of migration (timing, number of individuals, migratory locations) are sensitive to climate factors 15 . Changes in migration patterns may bring new populations of wild birds in contact with one another, or with agricultural species, leading to the introduction and mixing (i.e., evolution) of new strains 15 . However, warmer conditions under future climates may also extend breeding seasons, improve individual fitness during migration, and lead to higher capacity to fight infection 15 . Warmer temperatures and freeze-thaw events can also reduce viral persistence in the environment 16 . Thus, the net effect of changing climate conditions for HPAI risk in Montana is still uncertain.
Work with agricultural producers to limit contact between wild and domestic birds 5 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • Avoid concentrating wildlife around bait or other attractants during outbreaks 5 .
• Limit nonessential banding, capturing, or other efforts during active outbreaks 5 .
• Alert public of active disease outbreaks to help mitigate additional disturbance or risk to humans.

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Consider methods to manipulate waterbodies (e.g., pH, temperature, salinity, water levels) to facilitate viral inactivation 16 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Encourage the public to report cases of sickness and death in wild birds, and consider citizen science platforms to facilitate reporting 17 .

• Be aware of and investigate mortality events that may indicate HPAI: (1) those involving waterfowl, (2) a mortality event affecting more than five individuals at a given time, (3) mortalities affecting scavengers and raptors, (4) mortalities involving neurological signs, acute death, or respiratory symptoms 12 . Consulting decisionmaking tools related to avian mortality may be particularly useful 18 .
• Participate in national surveillance programs and keep up to date on current distributions and develop protocols for consistent reporting and saving of HPAI data in Montana wildlife 19 .
Conduct environmental surveillance at important aquatic sites (i.e., analysis of fecal material or collection of environmental DNA) 19 .

div.head: Proliferative Kidney Disease
div.p: SGCN with Known Impacts 1

div.head: Drivers
div.p: Cutthroat Trout -Presence and abundance of bryozoans 3 -Water temperature and quality (eutrophication)

div.head: Background
div.p: Proliferative kidney disease (PKD) is an infectious disease of salmonid fish caused by the parasite Tetracapsuloides bryosalmonae. This parasite has a complex life cycle in which it alternates between fish and secondary host species, bryozoans (a class of freshwater, filter-feeding invertebrates). Bryozoans release infectious T. bryosalmonae spores, which are spread throughout waterbodies where they may infect susceptible fish species. Some fish species appear more tolerant than others, and generally fish are considered to be either intermediate or accidental hosts for T. bryosalmonae (depending on the species) 3 . Once fish are infected, the parasite may spread through the blood stream, where it invades and proliferates within the kidneys and can cause impaired function. Fish transmit T. bryosalmonae back to bryozoan colonies through urinary excretions. Frequently, fish are infected with the parasite without showing evidence of disease. However, if disease progresses, outward clinical signs are characterized by pale gills, lethargy, abdominal swelling, and bulging eyes 1 . PKD outbreaks are most likely to occur in late summer once bryozoan colonies, spore shedding, and infections have had adequate time to proliferate in the warmer months 3,7 . Fish that survive exposure to T. bryosalmonae are likely to develop immunity or tolerance to the parasite. Disease signs can be reduced, allowing fish an preceded by multiple years of unusually warm summers, low water flows, and mild winters 2 .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Continue routine screening for T. bryosalmonae in hatchery stock and avoid stocking (when possible) to prevent the spread of disease, especially in waterways in which T. bryosalmonae has not been detected 7 .
• Inform anglers and water recreation users about the risks and transmission routes of PKD (contaminated gear/boats, fish transport) and enforce aquatic biosecurity protocols.
• Conserve water and avoid low flows during high-risk years to reduce outbreak potential 7 .
• Implement habitat modifications to decrease colonization of bryozoans, such as encouraging turbulent water flow and reducing algal growth 7 .

div.head: Disease management
div.p: • Be aware of the effects of climate variability on PKD impacts and incorporate information on climatic trends into decision-making processes for disease management 5,7 .
• If severe outbreaks occur, consider conservation stocking methods (e.g., developing PKD-resistant or temperature-resilient native fish stock) to restore imperiled populations 7 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Implement fishing closures as needed when high water temperatures and/or low water flows occur to reduce fish stress 7 .
• Maintain water quality, reduce pollution and runoff, and support habitat restoration and climate adaptation projects to promote overall fish health and resilience 4,5,7 .
• Promote habitat connectivity to encourage natural selection, improve adaptive capacity, and provide fish species the opportunity to migrate to cooler waters 7 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Support and advance the use of noninvasive surveillance technologies such as environmental DNA (eDNA) to monitor T. bryosalmonae and bryozoan colonies 2 .
Monitor water quality regularly on high-risk waterbodies (e.g., areas where fish dieoffs have occurred, areas that support infected bryozoan colonies, etc.) 4,7 .

div.head: Avian Cholera
div.p: SGCN with Known Impacts

div.head: Botulism
div.p: SGCN with Known Impacts [1][2][3] Drivers Least Tern Piping Plover Common Loon ▪ Higher temperatures 3 ▪ Low oxygen levels in water 3 ▪ Major fluctuations in water levels 3 ▪ Aquatic animal death and carcass accumulation 5,6 ▪ High levels of organic materials 5,6 SGCN Susceptible to Intoxication

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Warmer temperatures are associated with increased mortality from Iridoviruses in both hatchery environments and the wild, suggesting that future climate conditions may lead to increased impact 3,8 . Drying is thought to inactivate virus, and therefore, more frequent drought conditions could reduce the occurrence of the virus at seasonal waterbodies 3 .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Do not stock fish from hatcheries experiencing an outbreak 8 .
• Continue to screen wild broodstock for MRSIV or other Iridoviruses 8 .
• Avoid moving amphibians and conduct testing if translocations are performed 2,8 .
• Educate public on possibility of spread through fishing gear, boats, boots, and other recreational equipment [14][15][16] .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • There is no vaccine or treatment for ranavirus infection, but sterilization (e.g., bleach, UV light) can be used to treat water or surfaces in captive facilities 2,8 .
• Promote hatchery practices that limit the impact of Iridovirus outbreaks (e.g., sanitization protocols, isolation of rearing units, limited densities, and water quality) 8 .
• Consider the use of water drawdowns to inactivate virus 2 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Improve water and habitat quality at amphibian breeding sites (e.g., via cattle exclosures, reductions in runoff). Pesticides, herbicides, poor water quality, and vegetation loss compound the impacts of ranaviruses 2,6,7 .
• Control non-native species (e.g., American bullfrogs) that may transmit and serve as a reservoir for ranaviruses.

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Encourage the public to report observed amphibian and fish mortality events, including through participation in the Partners in Amphibian and Reptile Conservation Herpetofaunal Disease Alert System (HDAS) 20 .

div.head: Background
div.p: Chytridiomycosis is an infectious amphibian disease caused by the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). Fungal spores spread within waterbodies and infect the skin of susceptible amphibians, impacting respiration and osmoregulatory functions, eventually leading to cardiac arrest for individuals in advanced stages of disease 5 . Susceptibility to infection varies widely among species, and the severity of disease in individuals typically depends on infection dose and life stage 6,7 . Tadpoles (who frequently become infected but do not experience severe disease) and resistant species, such as the American bullfrog, serve as disease reservoirs and are important means of transmission and persistence within populations 8,9 . Species that are larger in size, occur in wetland habitats, and have a limited range are more predisposed to disease [10][11][12] . The primary modes of transmission include environmental (infectious spores in water or on moist substrates), direct contact (host-host), or reservoir species (bullfrog, crayfish 13 ).

div.head: Impacts
div.p: Bd has led to extirpations and population declines for multiple species throughout the world since it was first described in 1998 [14][15][16] . Among Montana's SGCN, the western toad
• Develop communication to public about the risk of Bd and how to prevent introduction and spread [28][29][30] .

In certain scenarios like acute die-offs, consider researching or applying environmental or individual-level treatments (e.g., salts, fungicides, chemical disinfectants, probiotics) to reduce prevalence of Bd, but be aware that effectiveness of treatments may be variable and requires further investigation [28][29][30] .
• Evaluate for the presence of and consider reducing abundance of Bd reservoir host species (e.g., infected amphibian larvae, bullfrogs, crayfish) [28][29][30] .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Consider habitat manipulations to improve adaptive capacity to disease, such as (but not limited to): increased shallow warm water for tadpoles, open basking sites for adults and metamorphic individuals, artificial heat sources, altered water flow or pond drying regime, and/or promoting the abundance of microorganisms that consume zoospores [28][29][30] .
• Explore opportunities to re-establish populations in disease-free locations or areas unlikely to be affected by Bd (e.g., areas at higher elevation, and drier, warmer habitat) 28,29,31 .
• If deemed necessary, consider implementation of captive colonies, head-start programs, and treatment facilities to improve imperiled species recovery [28][29][30][31] .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Develop a long-term surveillance plan that helps to determine Bd prevalence, impacts, and transmission; and monitors overall amphibian population health 30 .
• Monitor for mortality events or population declines that may indicate a disease outbreak.

• Contribute to and stay up to date on the amphibian disease surveillance database at www.amphibiandisease.org. • Inform anglers and water recreation users about risks and transmission routes for WD (contaminated gear/boats spreading spores between waterbodies) and enforce aquatic biosecurity protocols.

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: • Avoid stocking juvenile fish, particularly at times when juvenile susceptible fish are abundant in environment, to reduce impacts of WD on populations 2 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • Promote habitat restoration efforts to increase water flow and reduce erosion, stream degradation, and runoff in order to limit T. tubifex colonization 16 .
• If stocking is needed, ensure that fish are WD-free and/or explore development of WD-resistant fish strains 17 .
• Consider the use of UV radiation in reducing impacts of WD by suppressing abundance of T. tubifex and infectivity of M. cerebralis 2 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Support efforts related to improving overall fish health and adaptive capacity, such as promoting genetic diversity 12 .
Continue surveillance for M. cerebralis in wild fish populations, especially in areas where it has not previously been detected.

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ Differentiate and characterize T. tubifex strains in Montana and their susceptibility to M. cerebralis. ▪ Explore mechanisms of resistance and susceptibility in salmonid species.

div.head: Avian Trematodiasis SGCN with Known Impacts
Drivers
div.p: To date, significant impacts on SGCN have not been reported.
-Distribution and prevalence of trematode-infected faucet snails 2
-Waterfowl migration and concentration at stopover sites 3 -Host status (e.g., nutritional, age) and susceptibility 1 -Environmental conditions (e.g., water temperature) 3,4

div.head: SGCN Susceptible to Infection
div.p: To date, no additional SGCN confirmed as susceptible. Avian trematodiasis is strongly influenced by environmental conditions, particularly temperature and water availability. Warmer lake and wetland temperatures accelerate trematode development within snail hosts, increasing the number of infective stages shed into the environment and heightening transmission risk to waterfowl 12,13 . Additionally, reduced availability of stopover habitat-such as during drought-can force large numbers of birds to congregate at remaining wetlands, intensifying exposure to infected snails and amplifying disease severity. Fluctuating water levels and eutrophication may further shape the distribution and density of snail populations, especially in shallow, nutrient-dense systems that favor snail proliferation 14 . In the event of waterbodies drying out, disease risk may be limited due to reduced survival of aquatic intermediate hosts and trematodes 15 .

div.head: SGCN Potentially Susceptible
div.p: Overall, such ecological shifts are likely to influence the frequency, timing, and geographic extent of trematodiasis outbreaks, with potential for earlier seasonal onset and increased transmission conditions.

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Continue promoting policies and raising public awareness to mitigate the spread of aquatic invasive species, such as boat inspection and disinfection of all equipment 11 .
Consider habitat modification to reduce suitable habitat or disrupt life cycles for faucet snails (e.g., management of aquatic vegetation, periodic drawdowns of water levels) 4,16 .
• Explore biological control methods for faucet snails and other invasive mollusks by supporting native, snail-eating fish or invertebrate populations 4,16 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Promote wetland habitat conservation and improve water quality by reducing nutrient runoff and restoring/maintaining natural hydrological regimes 16 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Continue monitoring for mortality events, determining cause of death, and focus sampling efforts on major spring and fall stop-over areas during seasonal migration 16 .
• Explore use of environmental DNA sampling to detect presence of faucet snails and/or pathogenic trematodes 17 .
• Develop awareness around causes of waterbird mortality (e.g., trematodiasis, botulism, etc.) among hunters, anglers, and the general public and how to report unusual waterfowl mortality events.

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ Montana avian species susceptibility to trematodiasis ▪ Prevalence and intensity of trematode infections in Montana faucet snail populations and transmission risk/dynamics to Montana avifauna ▪ Sublethal effects (e.g., reduced fitness, impaired migration, vulnerability to other disease) of trematode infection in waterfowl

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • There are few known strategies to manage BKD in wild fisheries. Within hatcheries, depopulation is the preferred and most effective management option, but can be performed in combination with quarantine, water sterilization, and chemical treatment of infected individuals 1,7 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Research the impact of water quality on BKD dynamics and if deemed necessary, consider habitat modifications (e.g., improving streamflow) that could reduce the risk of BKD 1,11 .
• Reduce other stressors on fish populations potentially affected by BKD and continue to maintain adequate genetic diversity 14 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Consider pairing a molecular (qPCR) and immunological (ELISA) diagnostic test in surveillance efforts 4 .
• Increase awareness of BKD among public and FWP staff, including clinical signs.

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ Little is known about BKD impacts in wild fish populations, particularly among species of concern such as bull trout and wild strains of westslope cutthroat trout. ▪ There is little research on the potential impacts of climate change on BKD in the western United States.

populations occupying arid regions, suggesting that increases in drought conditions due to rising temperatures and changes in precipitation patterns may increase risk of RHD 3,16 . The association with arid climates and RHDV2's northward expansion in the U.S. highlights possible climatic drivers for disease risk, but further research is needed to better understand the relationship between RHD and climate.

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Implement biosecurity measures (e.g., disinfection of equipment and clothing) when handling animals or working in areas of at-risk populations 5 .

• Support cross-jurisdictional efforts (e.g., Montana Dept. of Livestock, USDA), surveillance activities, and policies (e.g., importation bans) that help prevent spillover from domestic rabbits 17,18 .
• Build public awareness about risks associated with exposing or releasing domestic rabbits into areas where at-risk wild populations exist.

• Advise hunters or falconers to avoid areas with known RHDV2 outbreaks, wear gloves when field dressing harvests, ensure proper disposal of remains, sanitize gear, and prevent birds from consuming dead or diseased rabbits 17,18 .
In the event of an outbreak in a wild population, spread of disease may be limited by ensuring proper disposal of carcasses to avoid potential contact by susceptible hosts or vector species 5,18 .
• If considering vaccination in vulnerable wild populations, be aware of strain type needed as RHDV vaccines do not protect against RHDV2 2,18 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Promote conservation actions that help bolster pygmy rabbit (or other affected SGCN) resilience to RHD outbreaks. These include actions that conserve greater sage-grouse and sagebrush habitat and improve habitat connectivity, which can benefit the population health and conservation of pygmy rabbits, who are obligate sagebrush dwellers 17,18 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Continue to encourage the public, hunters, falconers, and rehabilitation centers to report unusual mortality events in rabbit/hare populations as a part of FWP's passive surveillance program 5,18 .
• If conducting surveillance, be aware that RHD presence in wild populations may be best assessed in late spring during peak transmission times 1 .

div.head: Passerines and colonial waterbird SGCN
div.p: Other Susceptible Montana Species 1 American Goldfinch Lazuli Bunting Pine Siskin Other animals, including mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and fish may also be susceptible.

div.head: Background
div.p: Salmonellosis is a bacterial disease caused by Salmonella bacteria. It affects a wide variety of animals; including mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and fish; and has a worldwide distribution 5,6 . In wild birds it can be a common cause of sporadic mortality events, especially for passerines around bird feeding stations in the winter and in young waterbirds in large breeding colonies 6 . Infected wildlife shed the bacteria in their feces for up to months after infection, and the fecal-to-oral route is the main transmission route. While reptiles, amphibians, and fish can be infected by Salmonella, infections are often asymptomatic, and affected individuals may serve as reservoirs that can further distribute the pathogen in the environment 5 .

div.head: Impacts
div.p: For the majority of wildlife, salmonellosis does not cause population-level impacts. However, salmonellosis outbreaks in passerines using bird feeders in the winter have caused larger mortality events, particularly in red crossbills, pine siskins, and American goldfinches 7 . Data from outbreaks indicate that mortality due to avian salmonellosis can be wide-ranging, multi-county events, involving hundreds to thousands of birds 7 . In some cases, particularly those involving waterfowl, salmonellosis is often reported in combination with multiple other sources of mortality, so it can be difficult to estimate the sole impacts of salmonellosis in certain populations.

div.head: Presence in Montana
div.p: ▪ Salmonellosis has caused wild bird mortality events in Montana, including within the following species: crows, ravens, red crossbills, American goldfinches, pine siskins, evening grosbeaks, house finches, house sparrows, and Cassin's finches 7

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: There is little evidence that salmonellosis is strongly tied to climate or weather. However, outbreaks are common in the winter due to an increased aggregation of animals around limited food sources, and severe winters may lead to increased use of feeders 4 .

div.head: Conservation Actions Prevention
div.p: • Avoid supplying attractants (e.g., garbage, grain spills, bird baths, feeding stations, etc.) that may facilitate mixing of different species, which can facilitate transmission from carrier animals to susceptible animals 8 .

Encourage the public to keep bird feeders and baths clean and sanitized, especially throughout the winter, and to use feeders that minimize transmission risk (e.g., feeders that keep food dry, smaller feeders, and those easier to disinfect) 8 .
• Consider eliminating/reducing point sources of potential bacteria (e.g., sewage, garbage, livestock wastewater discharges) near breeding colonies of aquatic species (e.g., pelicans, gulls) 8 .

div.head: Disease Management
div.p: • Antibiotic therapy may be considered but is challenging to administer in field settings with wild birds and is more easily applied to captive colonies 8,9 .
• Promptly remove attractants (e.g., feeding stations) or point sources of bacteria (e.g., sewage, fecal buildup, garbage, etc.) during outbreak events 8 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Encourage reporting from the public and other agencies and consider online reporting tools.
• Accurate determination of cause of death (or sickness) during reported morbidity/mortality events in birds is important for developing prevention and management strategies 8 .

div.head: Research/Knowledge Gaps
div.p: ▪ Most research available is concerned with salmonella spreading to humans/livestock from wildlife. Very little research is available concerning salmonella impacts to wildlife, though long-term population impacts appear to be minimal to non-existent.

div.head: Drivers
div.p: To date, significant impacts on SGCN have not been reported.
-Vector abundance (ticks and other arthropods) and feeding preferences 1,2 -Density and distribution of mammalian reservoir hosts (rabbits, rodents, voles)

div.head: Background
div.p: Tularemia is a vector-borne disease caused by the highly infectious bacterium, Francisella tularensis. F. tularensis has an exceptionally wide host range, capable of infecting over 250 species of animals (mostly mammals, some birds, and a few amphibians and reptiles) 1 . Ticks are the primary vectors and reservoirs for tularemia, but some insects (e.g., flies, gnats, and mosquitos) and birds can play a significant role by mechanically spreading disease via contaminated mouth parts or excreting feces containing the bacteria 2 . Aside from vector-borne transmission, animals are also readily infected via inhalation and ingestion of, or direct contact with, the bacterium, which can occur through exposure to other host species, contaminated water, soil, or carcasses 3 . The bacterium can persist for weeks to months in the environment 3 . Tularemia is typically detected through observations

div.head: Climate Sensitivity
div.p: Climate variability can affect tularemia through its impacts on the distribution and abundance of tick vectors and reservoir host species (i.e., hares, rabbits, and rodents) 13,14 . Warming temperatures may allow for increased northward expansion and extended periods of reproduction and development for arthropod vectors, increasing the risk of transmission 15 . An increase in drought conditions may limit vector abundance but can also increase host density and transmission risk by concentrating host populations during drought. Volatile weather patterns leading to sporadic, heavy rainfall events may also increase suitable breeding habitat for vectors or result in flooding events capable of facilitating spread of F. tularensis to new locations.
Advise FWP personnel and public (particularly hunters and trappers) on the routes of spread of tularemia (e.g., translocation of infected wildlife, carcasses).
• Partner with human health agencies (e.g., Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services) to develop collaborative approaches for disease monitoring, prevention, and management 2 .
In the event of severe outbreaks that threaten conservation goals, consider judicious use of insecticides in an attempt to lower vector abundance in the environment 17 .

div.head: Species and Habitat Management
div.p: • Protect vulnerable host habitat and reduce other stressors to promote resiliency and adaptive capacity to disease in susceptible populations 17 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Identify and map regions of possible disease foci based on lagomorph and aquatic rodent populations, serologic surveys (in carnivore species), and tick surveys 1,16 .
• Increase opportunistic monitoring of susceptible wildlife species through lab testing of carcasses received at the Montana Wildlife Health Lab.
• Encourage hunters, trappers, and other recreationists to report observations of groups of dead rodents or lagomorphs so that samples can be collected and tested.

div.head: Drivers
div.p: To date, significant impacts on SGCN have not been reported.
-Human-mediated transmission (import of fish and fish byproduct, contaminated equipment, infected bait) [4][5][6] -Presence of reservoir or highly susceptible species 1,4 -Waterway connectivity

div.p: Viral Hemorrhagic Septicemia Virus (VHSV) is a highly contagious and often fatal disease of both marine and freshwater fish. VHSV is well distributed throughout the Northern Hemisphere and is known to infect over 140 fish species 3 . In the United States, VHSV has
Establish a Montana-specific rapid response plan in case of Bsal's introduction (refer to the Rapid Response Template for Bsal provided by the North American Bsal Task Force) 9,10 .

• Potential management actions that may be considered following the invasion of Bsal include the application of antifungals to hosts at affected sites or, in high-priority populations, the capture and removal of amphibians, followed by habitat modifications or treatments (e.g., draining water bodies to kill fungal spores, applying fungicidal treatments to environment), and then release of disease-free individuals back to habitat 9,10 .

div.head: Surveillance and Monitoring
div.p: • Identify and monitor populations and habitat areas that host Montana's high-risk amphibians.

div.head: Background
div.p: Ophidiomycosis (also known as snake fungal disease [SFD]) is a disease of snakes caused by a fungal pathogen, Ophidiomyces ophidiicola (Oo). It is associated with outbreaks of dermatitis in snake populations that involve crusting, ulceration and discoloration of the skin, abnormal molting, and inappropriate basking behavior in affected individuals 7,8 . Infection is thought to occur opportunistically through breaks in the skin or via mucosal introduction 9,10 . Clinical disease and prevalence tend to increase in spring, following brumation.

div.head: Impacts
div.p: It is unclear whether Oo affects overall population viability, but it is has been linked to population declines and notable mortalities in certain species in the eastern United States 3,[11][12][13] . The current and potential impacts of SFD for snake populations in Montana and the greater region remains unknown. Further research and surveillance are needed.

div.head: CHAPTER 10: WILDLIFE VIEWING AND EDUCATION
div.p: Enhancing conservation of SGCN and their habitats through communication, education, citizen science, and wildlife viewing

State Wildlife Action Plans (SWAPs) use the best available science to identify Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN), threats to both, and conservation actions that are needed to conserve, enhance, and recover these species and their habitats. While this chapter is not one of the eight required elements for a SWAP, two of the three broad, overarching pathways for implementing species and habitat conservation, include actions to communicate with a wide spectrum of the public and provide targeted educational messaging. Outreach and communication actions have an important role to play in wildlife and habitat conservation, including SWAP implementation.

This chapter highlights opportunities to further increase FWP's relevance to a broader range of the public. Expanding opportunities for wildlife viewing, engaging the public in citizen science, and delivering new communication and educational messages that improve conservation outcomes for SGCN and HGCN have the potential to reach nonconsumptive users and new constituents. All Montanans, as well as visitors to our state, benefit from the conservation of fish and wildlife. Hunters and anglers in Montana are passionate about conservation and engage regularly with FWP on hunting and fishing regulations, habitat conservation, and other topics related to wildlife management. But much of the public is unaware of the work that FWP does to conserve fish and wildlife, particularly nongame species. This challenge of raising public awareness is not unique to Montana. Recognizing that this lack of understanding and engagement by a large segment of society has implications for the sustainability of fish, wildlife, and their habitats, the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA) formed the Blue Ribbon Panel on Sustaining America's Diverse Fish and Wildlife Resources. The panel made two recommendations:
1. That $1.3 billion in new federal funding be secured and dedicated to support implementation of State Wildlife Action Plans to conserve SGCN and the habitats they depend on.
2. That state wildlife agencies examine the impact of societal changes on the relevancy of fish and wildlife conservation and recommend program changes to engage and serve broader constituencies.
tool for delivering messages that will enhance conservation for SGCN and the habitats they depend on.
4. Explore novel educational partnerships and partner programs.

Education staff will explore ways to continue to partner with organizations such as the Montana State Library, Montana Discovery Foundation, federal agencies, and other organizations on programs such as Adopt-a-Species (a habitat conservation program for Helena school kids) and Master Naturalist. Both programs have significant potential to integrate SWAP species and habitats and to expand outside of the Helena area with additional partnerships and capacity.

div.head: Citizen Science
div.p: Citizen Science engages the public in scientific research and monitoring through participation and collaboration. Professional biologists can train volunteers to follow field protocols and conduct surveys on wildlife to better understand species distribution and monitor trends. Citizen science projects can have multiple benefits, including augmenting wildlife monitoring capacity, increasing support and appreciation for wildlife conservation, improving scientific literacy, and fostering a sense of shared stewardship for wildlife and the habitats they depend on.

FWP and key conservation partners such as Montana Audubon and local Audubon chapters have implemented a number of successful citizen science projects monitoring SGCN and Species of Greatest Information Need (SGIN). Species that are easily recognizable and are surveyed using straightforward methods are great candidates for citizen science monitoring. Recent projects include surveys for chimney swift, common poorwill, common nighthawk, and long-billed curlew. Volunteers are trained to conduct surveys and enter data in real time using apps that can be downloaded to a smart phone, such as Survey123.

There is substantial cross-pollination between citizen science and education, such as The provisions for periodic monitoring of SGCN and their habitats, for monitoring the effectiveness of conservation actions, and for adapting conservation actions as appropriate to respond to new information or changing conditions

The inclusion of a habitat or species as one of greatest conservation concern does not imply that FWP and partners have the capacity to implement all the actions contained in this SWAP; rather, these lists and the accompanying threats and actions lay out options for making conservation progress, alongside and in collaboration with the many partners who engage in this work.

div.head: Monitoring SGCN and HGCN
div.p: Information about the status and trends of wildlife populations and their habitats forms the basis for informed management. However, obtaining such information is resource intensive, so taking this approach for all species would represent a consequential tradeoff to allocating resources for conservation actions (Buxton et al. 2020). As such, only a small number of Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and their habitats have spatially explicit, repeated, species-or habitat-specific monitoring efforts.

A variety of circumstances dictate which species or habitats get specific monitoring efforts. For some SGCN, monitoring is obligated, planned, and executed through species recovery plans (e.g., piping plover, pallid sturgeon, Kootenai River white sturgeon, bull trout), species management plans (e.g., common loon, Columbia River redband trout, Arctic grayling, westslope cutthroat trout, Yellowstone cutthroat trout), or through the terms of conservation easements or lease agreements (e.g., prairie dogs). For these species, monitoring often informs conservation actions over short time periods (e.g., restricting access to a loon nest site). SGCN may also be monitored because they are harvested (e.g., greater sage-grouse, paddlefish), trapped (e.g., fisher), or removed for management of other species. Aside from these groups, SGCN might be the subject of short-term, species-specific monitoring efforts to address key information needs if they are petitioned for Endangered Species Act listing or if their status ranking is uncertain due to a lack of information on the species.

For the majority of terrestrial SGCN and their habitats, FWP relies on monitoring that occurs through a variety of efforts and sources to understand changes to SGCN and their habitats. These include our investment and participation in structured multispecies
• Applicable to a broad geographic scale, including as many FWP regions as possible.
• Encourages partnerships and collaboration and encourages work with good collaborators.
• Maximizes funding partnerships and leverages partner contributions.
• Complements and builds from existing research and data.
• Investigators' experience and expertise match the project plan.
• Encourages training of graduate students and FWP staff.

While the wording of these criteria is subject to change over the life of this SWAP, the concepts have proven to be durable over time. Following proposal scoring and discussion, the research steering committee makes a preliminary recommendation about whether to proceed with each project, or to refine the project proposal or scope, which is then vetted with the FWP Director's Office. We welcome partners to engage with us to conduct research and monitoring, knowing that these are the criteria that FWP uses to prioritize these efforts.

div.head: Partner Involvement
div.p: To gather partner feedback and assess desire for participation, we sent a survey to external partners to learn how they use Montana's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) and how we can make the 2025 SWAP most useful for them. The survey was sent to 198 people across 48 agencies, and 101 people responded, resulting in a 52.6% survey response rate. See Appendix E for a list of the agencies contacted and see Appendix D for a list of the questions that were included in the survey.

One of the survey questions asked, "Are you interested in being on a SWAP External Partner Team?" Eighteen peopled responded "Yes" and 41 people responded "Maybe." Due to the large number of people interested in being on the external team, and due to the complexities of managing 10 different internal teams that also had diverse external representation, we decided not to create an official external team that would have been limited to 10 to 15 people. Instead, we emailed those who responded to the original survey and asked if they or their staff would like to be on an email list of interested external partners where we could provide updates and opportunities for all partners to engage. A total of 236 people across 85 agencies and organizations wanted to receive these email updates. We held three meetings in December 2024, June 2025, and August 2025 to gather feedback on the vertebrate, invertebrate, and plant SGCN, HGCN, focal areas, and our process for threats and conservation actions.

We also provided for partner participation by giving presentations about the 2025 SWAP revision at Montana Chapter of The Wildlife Society (MTTWS) and the Montana Chapter of the American Fisheries Society (MTAFS) conferences. We presented at the 2024 MTTWS and 2025 MTTWS and MTASF annual conferences about the SWAP revision process and
